title: BQP versus BPP
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Do quantum computers fundamentally solve more decision problems efficiently than classical probabilistic ones? Formally, is BQP different from BPP in the absence of any oracle?
status: Open since the formulation of quantum complexity theory. Known oracle separations and candidate applications do not establish the unrelativized separation. See John Watrous (2008), *Quantum Computational Complexity*, arXiv:0804.3401.
solved_when: An unconditional (oracle-free) proof that BQP ≠ BPP, or a proof that BQP = BPP, is established.
why: It settles whether quantum computation fundamentally enlarges efficient computation, beyond what oracle separations and candidate applications can demonstrate.
key_works: John Watrous (2008), *Quantum Computational Complexity*, arXiv:0804.3401.

title: NP-complete problems in BQP
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Can a quantum computer solve an NP-complete problem in polynomial time? Formally, is NP contained in BQP?
status: Open. Grover-type improvements concern search complexity and do not give polynomial-time algorithms for unrestricted NP-complete problems. See Watrous (2008), *Quantum Computational Complexity*, arXiv:0804.3401.
solved_when: A polynomial-time quantum algorithm for any NP-complete decision problem is exhibited, or NP ⊆ BQP is otherwise established (or refuted).
why: It determines whether quantum computing can efficiently solve general combinatorial search rather than only selected structured problems.
key_works: Watrous (2008), *Quantum Computational Complexity*, arXiv:0804.3401.

title: The unrelativized relationship between BQP and PH
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Determine whether BQP is contained in the polynomial hierarchy, whether PH is contained in BQP, or whether they are incomparable.
status: Oracle evidence separates quantum computation from PH, but it does not resolve these containments for ordinary computation.
why: Locates quantum computation relative to classical alternation and approximate counting.
key_works: Scott Aaronson (2010), *BQP and the polynomial hierarchy*, DOI:10.1145/1806689.1806711; Ran Raz and Avishay Tal (2019), *Oracle separation of BQP and PH*, DOI:10.1145/3313276.3316315.

title: Perfect completeness for QMA
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Can every problem verifiable by a quantum proof system be reformulated so that yes-instances have a witness the verifier accepts with certainty — that is, does QMA equal QMA₁ for a standard finite gate set?
status: Open. Recent amplification results improve completeness dramatically but also establish black-box limitations, showing that arbitrarily small error is not the same as perfect completeness (Aaronson, Harris, and Witteveen, 2025; revised 2026, *Limits to black-box amplification in QMA*, arXiv:2509.21131).
solved_when: A proof that QMA = QMA₁ for some specified standard finite gate set, or a proof that they differ, is given.
why: It would clarify whether the nonzero verification error in quantum proofs is essential or merely an artifact of the definitions.
key_works: Scott Aaronson, Phillip Harris, and Freek Witteveen (2025; revised 2026), *Limits to black-box amplification in QMA*, arXiv:2509.21131.

title: Quantum Valiant–Vazirani isolation
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Is there a quantum analogue of the Valiant–Vazirani theorem: a randomized polynomial-time reduction that takes general QMA verification to verification with a unique accepting quantum witness? The reduction should come with suitable completeness and soundness promises.
status: Open for unrestricted QMA. Classical and restricted quantum analogues do not provide a general quantum witness-isolation theorem; see Dorit Aharonov, Michael Ben-Or, Fernando Brandão, and Or Sattath (2008), *The Pursuit of Uniqueness: Extending Valiant-Vazirani Theorem to the Probabilistic and Quantum Settings*, arXiv:0810.4840.
solved_when: Such a randomized polynomial-time reduction exists for unrestricted QMA, achieving suitable completeness and soundness guarantees.
why: It would transfer uniqueness-based algorithms and hardness arguments from the classical setting into quantum complexity.
key_works: Dorit Aharonov, Michael Ben-Or, Fernando Brandão, and Or Sattath (2008), *The Pursuit of Uniqueness: Extending Valiant-Vazirani Theorem to the Probabilistic and Quantum Settings*, arXiv:0810.4840.

title: Error reduction for StoqMA
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Does StoqMA admit general, efficient error reduction that preserves its restricted (stoquastic) verifier structure? More precisely, can the completeness–soundness gap of a StoqMA verification be amplified efficiently without leaving the class?
status: Open since StoqMA's introduction. Dorit Aharonov, Alex B. Grilo, and Yupan Liu (2020/2025), *StoqMA vs. MA: the power of error reduction*, arXiv:2010.02835; DOI:10.22331/q-2025-09-11-1853, show that suitable error reduction would imply StoqMA = MA.
solved_when: A general efficient error-reduction procedure for StoqMA verification is established that preserves its restricted computational structure, or the possibility of such reduction is ruled out.
why: It tests whether stoquastic verification genuinely exceeds classical randomized verification: Aharonov–Grilo–Liu show that suitable error reduction would imply StoqMA = MA.
key_works: Dorit Aharonov, Alex B. Grilo, and Yupan Liu (2020/2025), *StoqMA vs. MA: the power of error reduction*, arXiv:2010.02835; DOI:10.22331/q-2025-09-11-1853.

title: General commuting local Hamiltonians in NP
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Does every commuting local Hamiltonian problem with bounded locality admit a polynomial-size classical certificate for its low-energy promise? Formally, is the general commuting local Hamiltonian problem contained in NP?
status: Open generally. Bostanci–Hwang's 2026 results extend NP containment to important rank-one cases beyond two dimensions, but not to arbitrary commuting interactions. John Bostanci and Yeongwoo Hwang (2026), *Commuting Local Hamiltonians Beyond 2D*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2026.25.
solved_when: A proof that every bounded-locality commuting local Hamiltonian problem has polynomial-size classical certificates for its low-energy promise (or a counterexample showing containment in NP fails).
why: A solution would separate the computational difficulty caused by noncommutativity in local Hamiltonian problems from the difficulty caused by entanglement alone.
key_works: John Bostanci and Yeongwoo Hwang (2026), *Commuting Local Hamiltonians Beyond 2D*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.ITCS.2026.25.

title: No low-energy samplable states
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Can we construct local Hamiltonian families for which no efficiently classically samplable state can be sufficiently low-energy? Formally, this asks for families realizing the NLSS (no low-energy samplable states) conjecture.
status: Open beyond restricted state families. Exclusions of Clifford, almost-Clifford, and fermionic Gaussian low-energy states are partial results, not the full claim. Key work: Kartik Anand (2025), *Constructing Fermionic Hamiltonians with Non-Gaussianic low-energy states*, arXiv:2502.15368.
solved_when: Explicit local Hamiltonian families are constructed such that every sufficiently low-energy state escapes the relevant efficient classical sampling-description class.
why: It would strengthen the evidence that low-energy quantum matter cannot be represented by tractable classical models.
key_works: Kartik Anand (2025), *Constructing Fermionic Hamiltonians with Non-Gaussianic low-energy states*, arXiv:2502.15368.

title: Maximum randomized-versus-quantum separation for total functions
subfield: Quantum query complexity and algebraic algorithms
open: How large can the gap between randomized and quantum query complexity be for a total Boolean function? Formally, determine the optimal exponent in the relation between \(R(f)\) and \(Q(f)\) over all total \(f\).
status: The general gap between known large separations and upper bounds remains unresolved; the 2025 survey records cubic-type separations versus a quartic general upper bound. Key works: Yassine Hamoudi (2025), *A Brief Introduction to Quantum Query Complexity*, arXiv:2508.08852; Aaronson (2021), *Open Problems Related to Quantum Query Complexity*, arXiv:2109.06917.
solved_when: The exponent relating \(R(f)\) and \(Q(f)\) for total functions is pinned down exactly — in particular, closing the gap between the known cubic-type separations and the quartic general upper bound recorded in the 2025 survey.
why: It measures the true quantum speedup achievable without hiding difficulty in a promise, giving a clean benchmark for quantum query algorithms.
key_works: Yassine Hamoudi (2025), *A Brief Introduction to Quantum Query Complexity*, arXiv:2508.08852; Aaronson (2021), *Open Problems Related to Quantum Query Complexity*, arXiv:2109.06917.

title: Optimal quantum complexity of k-distinctness
subfield: Quantum query complexity and algebraic algorithms
open: For each fixed \(k\geq3\), what is the optimal quantum query complexity of deciding whether some value occurs at least \(k\) times in the input? Formally, obtain matching upper and lower bounds for \(k\)-distinctness, and understand how the complexity behaves as \(k\) grows.
status: Open beyond element distinctness. Learning graphs and multidimensional quantum walks yield improved algorithms but do not settle the complete exponent landscape. Key work: Stacey Jeffery and Sebastian Zur (2022), *Multidimensional Quantum Walks, with Application to k-Distinctness*, arXiv:2208.13492.
solved_when: Matching quantum query upper and lower bounds are established for \(k\)-distinctness for every fixed \(k\geq3\), together with an understanding of the exponent landscape as \(k\) grows.
why: The problem is a sharp test of the limits of quantum walks and collision-finding techniques; settling it would clarify whether current algebraic algorithmic methods can reach optimality beyond element distinctness.
key_works: Stacey Jeffery and Sebastian Zur (2022), *Multidimensional Quantum Walks, with Application to k-Distinctness*, arXiv:2208.13492.

title: Computational complexity of Uhlmann transformations
subfield: Quantum query complexity and algebraic algorithms
open: When can a unitary mapping between compatible purifications of mixed states be synthesized efficiently, particularly for succinctly specified mixed states where no privileged purification access is available?
status: Structural completeness and equivalence results exist, but efficient synthesis for important promised families remains unresolved. Key work: John Bostanci, Yuval Efron, Tony Metger, Alexander Poremba, Luowen Qian, and Henry Yuen (2023), *Unitary Complexity and the Uhlmann Transformation Problem*, arXiv:2306.13073.
solved_when: A characterization is given of when such unitary synthesis is efficiently possible — including for promised families of succinctly specified mixed states — resolving whether efficient synthesis holds for the important promised families currently left open.
why: A solution links quantum state conversion, cryptography, and the recovery of encoded information, giving a unified complexity-theoretic handle on these tasks.
key_works: John Bostanci, Yuval Efron, Tony Metger, Alexander Poremba, Luowen Qian, and Henry Yuen (2023), *Unitary Complexity and the Uhlmann Transformation Problem*, arXiv:2306.13073.

title: Permanent anticoncentration
open: How spread out are the values of the permanent of a Gaussian matrix around its natural scale? Prove sufficiently strong lower-tail bounds for the permanent of a Gaussian matrix at its \(\sqrt{n!}\) scale, strong enough to support approximate-sampling reductions.
status: Open in the required general form; note this is distinct from proving that permanent estimation is computationally hard. Key work: Aaronson and Arkhipov (2011), *The Computational Complexity of Linear Optics*, arXiv:1011.3245. Related lines include small-ball probability inequalities and anticoncentration of random polynomials; the problem is also known as the Permanent Anti-Concentration Conjecture.
solved_when: Lower-tail anticoncentration bounds for the permanent of a Gaussian matrix at the \(\sqrt{n!}\) scale are established in the generality needed to support the approximate-sampling reductions for which they are intended.
why: Such bounds convert additive probability-estimation information into useful multiplicative information, which is what the sampling reductions need.
key_works: Aaronson and Arkhipov (2011), *The Computational Complexity of Linear Optics*, arXiv:1011.3245.

title: Average-case hafnian hardness for Gaussian boson sampling
open: Can the worst-to-average-case hardness and anticoncentration behavior established for standard random circuit sampling be extended to the experimentally relevant Gaussian boson sampling distributions? A complete answer would establish these statements for the structured matrix ensembles (hafnians of Gaussian-related matrices) that arise in that setting.
status: Open in robust approximate-sampling formulations; exact hafnian hardness alone does not settle noisy experimental distributions. Key works: Craig S. Hamilton et al. (2017), *Gaussian Boson Sampling*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.119.170501; Daniel Grier et al. (2022), *The Complexity of Bipartite Gaussian Boson Sampling*.
solved_when: Average-case hardness of computing hafnian-type matrix permanents-like quantities for the structured ensembles appearing in Gaussian boson sampling is proven, together with an anticoncentration result for the corresponding output probabilities, in a robust approximate-sampling formulation that covers noisy experimental distributions.
why: It would place Gaussian photonic quantum advantage on firmer complexity foundations; without it, exact hafnian hardness alone does not rule out efficient classical simulation of the noisy distributions actual experiments produce.
key_works: Craig S. Hamilton et al. (2017), *Gaussian Boson Sampling*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.119.170501; Daniel Grier et al. (2022), *The Complexity of Bipartite Gaussian Boson Sampling*.

title: Robust average-case hardness of random-circuit sampling
open: Can we prove that random-circuit sampling is hard on average, even when the sampler is allowed a constant total-variation-distance error — the regime actually relevant to noisy experiments — under defensible average-case assumptions? A formal statement should establish hardness of approximate sampling itself, rather than relying only on exact or extremely high-precision probability estimation.
status: The problem is open at the strongest useful noise-robust level; existing worst-to-average-case reductions do not automatically deliver the constant-error statement. Key work: Adam Bouland, Bill Fefferman, Chinmay Nirkhe, and Umesh Vazirani (2018), *Quantum Supremacy and the Complexity of Random Circuit Sampling*, arXiv:1803.04402.
solved_when: A proof shows average-case hardness of sampling from random circuits to within constant total-variation distance, under stated average-case assumptions, closing the gap left by worst-to-average-case reductions.
why: It separates a genuine mathematical hardness theorem for noisy devices from an extrapolation from exact or high-precision statements, which is what quantum-supremacy experiments actually need.
key_works: Adam Bouland, Bill Fefferman, Chinmay Nirkhe, and Umesh Vazirani (2018), *Quantum Supremacy and the Complexity of Random Circuit Sampling*, arXiv:1803.04402.

title: Sharp state- and observable-dependent Trotter error bounds
open: Can we derive product-formula (Trotter) error bounds that depend on the actual initial state and measured observable, are efficiently evaluable, and remain predictive at useful simulation times?
status: General commutator-based product-formula bounds are established, notably the theory developed in Andrew Childs, Yuan Su, Minh C. Tran, Nathan Wiebe, and Shuchen Zhu (2021), *A Theory of Trotter Error*, arXiv:1912.08854; DOI:10.1103/PhysRevX.11.011020; however, tight instance-specific certificates remain substantially less developed.
solved_when: An efficiently computable error bound is obtained that provably exploits the specific initial state and measured observable and remains predictive (non-vacuous) at useful simulation times.
why: Such bounds could remove large safety margins in Trotterization without silently sacrificing accuracy, directly reducing simulation cost.
key_works: Andrew Childs, Yuan Su, Minh C. Tran, Nathan Wiebe, and Shuchen Zhu (2021), *A Theory of Trotter Error*, arXiv:1912.08854; DOI:10.1103/PhysRevX.11.011020.

title: Certified FeMoco spin-state and energy ordering
open: Can a quantum computer deliver the energy differences that decide FeMoco's spin-state and energy ordering, together with a complete uncertainty budget accounting for the electronic Hamiltonian, the choice of active space, state preparation, and quantum numerical error?
status: Resource-estimation studies establish plausible computational routes, but no certified solution of the relevant chemical ordering exists. Key work: Markus Reiher, Nathan Wiebe, Krysta Svore, Dave Wecker, and Matthias Troyer (2017), *Elucidating Reaction Mechanisms on Quantum Computers*, arXiv:1605.03590.
solved_when: The chemically decisive FeMoco energy differences are computed with a full uncertainty budget spanning the electronic Hamiltonian, active space, state preparation, and quantum numerical error.
why: It would test quantum computing on a scientifically consequential strongly correlated system, namely the FeMoco active site relevant to nitrogenase chemistry.
key_works: Markus Reiher, Nathan Wiebe, Krysta Svore, Dave Wecker, and Matthias Troyer (2017), *Elucidating Reaction Mechanisms on Quantum Computers*, arXiv:1605.03590.

title: Controlled low-temperature phase diagram of the doped Hubbard model
open: Can we produce a controlled map of the low-temperature phase diagram of the two-dimensional doped Hubbard model, resolving its competing phases and correlations? Concretely, this means answers with quantified error control in both the thermodynamic limit and the low-temperature regime.
status: Extensive classical benchmarks constrain portions of the diagram, notably J. P. F. LeBlanc et al. (2015), *Solutions of the Two Dimensional Hubbard Model: Benchmarks and Results from a Wide Range of Numerical Algorithms*, arXiv:1505.02290; quantum simulation must still demonstrate controlled answers in the disputed regimes.
solved_when: The disputed regimes of the two-dimensional doped Hubbard model's low-temperature phase diagram are resolved with error control toward the thermodynamic limit and low temperatures, distinguishing the competing phases (e.g., stripe versus superconducting order).
why: It provides a direct test of proposed microscopic explanations of correlated-electron phenomena, including high-temperature superconductivity and the stripe–superconductivity competition.
key_works: J. P. F. LeBlanc et al. (2015), *Solutions of the Two Dimensional Hubbard Model: Benchmarks and Results from a Wide Range of Numerical Algorithms*, arXiv:1505.02290.

title: Real-time nonabelian gauge dynamics near the continuum
open: Can a quantum computer simulate a genuinely nontrivial real-time observable of SU(3) gauge theory with all systematic errors under control? Concretely, this means computing such an observable with quantified errors from lattice spacing, finite volume, electric-field truncation, state preparation, and quantum execution.
status: Lower-dimensional and truncated demonstrations exist, but these provide context rather than a complete continuum-QCD calculation. Key works: Bauer et al. (2022), *Quantum Simulation for High Energy Physics*, arXiv:2204.03381; Jordan, Lee, and Preskill (2012), *Quantum Algorithms for Quantum Field Theories*, arXiv:1111.3633.
solved_when: A nontrivial real-time SU(3) observable is computed with controlled, quantified errors from each of lattice spacing, finite volume, electric-field truncation, state preparation, and quantum execution.
why: It would open the door to scattering, hadronization, and nonequilibrium strong-interaction physics — real-time phenomena inaccessible to classical lattice methods.
key_works: Bauer et al. (2022), *Quantum Simulation for High Energy Physics*, arXiv:2204.03381; Jordan, Lee, and Preskill (2012), *Quantum Algorithms for Quantum Field Theories*, arXiv:1111.3633.

title: Fixed-angle QAOA conjectures
open: Can the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm achieve a guaranteed MaxCut approximation ratio on regular graphs using angle parameters fixed once and for all, independent of the particular instance? A precise answer would establish or refute, with explicit dependence on QAOA depth and graph size, the fixed-angle performance conjectures on regular MaxCut graph families.
status: The problem remains open conjectural territory. Only shallow cases have been analytically solved, and the conjectures are otherwise supported by numerical evidence, notably Jonathan Wurtz and Danylo Lykov (2021), *Fixed-angle conjectures for the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm on regular MaxCut graphs*, Physical Review A 104, 052419.
solved_when: The fixed-angle performance conjectures for QAOA on regular MaxCut graph families are proved or refuted, with explicit dependence on depth and graph size.
why: A proof would replace expensive instance-by-instance parameter searches with justified reusable angle schedules, making QAOA practical to deploy without optimization overhead.
key_works: Jonathan Wurtz and Danylo Lykov (2021), *Fixed-angle conjectures for the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm on regular MaxCut graphs*, Physical Review A 104, 052419.

title: Valid confidence intervals for adaptive classical shadows
subfield: Quantum machine learning and learning quantum systems
open: Can classical shadows be given statistically valid confidence intervals when the observables are chosen adaptively — that is, after the experimenter has already looked at earlier shadow data — in the presence of realistic measurement errors and repeated adaptive queries?
status: Standard shadow guarantees, as in Hsin-Yuan Huang, Richard Kueng, and John Preskill (2020), *Predicting Many Properties of a Quantum System from Very Few Measurements*, arXiv:2002.08953, cover important predetermined-observable settings; unrestricted adaptive reuse needs additional control.
solved_when: A method exists that provides tight confidence guarantees for observables selected after inspecting shadow data, robust to realistic measurement errors and repeated adaptive queries.
why: It prevents exploratory quantum experiments from reporting selection-biased discoveries, making adaptive data reuse trustworthy.
key_works: Hsin-Yuan Huang, Richard Kueng, and John Preskill (2020), *Predicting Many Properties of a Quantum System from Very Few Measurements*, arXiv:2002.08953.

title: SIC measurements in every finite dimension
subfield: Quantum information, entanglement, and channel capacities
open: Does every finite-dimensional Hilbert space admit a symmetric informationally complete POVM — a set of equiangular rank-one projectors achieving the maximal number of outcomes? Or is there a finite dimension in which no such measurement exists?
status: Open. Exact and numerical constructions are known in many dimensions, but these do not establish the universal statement. Key works include Joseph Renes et al. (2004), *Symmetric informationally complete quantum measurements*, and Paweł Horodecki, Łukasz Rudnicki, and Karol Życzkowski (2020), *Five open problems in theory of quantum information*, arXiv:2002.03233.
solved_when: A proof that SIC-POVMs exist in every finite dimension, or an explicit counterexample dimension with a proof of nonexistence.
why: A positive answer would give a uniform, optimally geometric structure for informationally complete quantum measurements, with implications for equiangular lines and connections to Hilbert's twelfth problem.
key_works: Joseph Renes et al. (2004), *Symmetric informationally complete quantum measurements*; Paweł Horodecki, Łukasz Rudnicki, and Karol Życzkowski (2020), *Five open problems in theory of quantum information*, arXiv:2002.03233.

title: Four mutually unbiased bases in dimension six
subfield: Quantum information, entanglement, and channel capacities
open: Do there exist four mutually unbiased orthonormal bases of \(\mathbb C^6\)? Either exhibit such a quartet explicitly, or prove that no four mutually unbiased bases can coexist in dimension six.
status: Open. Three mutually unbiased bases in dimension six are available; the prime-power construction of complete sets does not settle dimension six. See Horodecki, Rudnicki, and Życzkowski (2020), *Five open problems in theory of quantum information*, arXiv:2002.03233.
solved_when: An explicit construction of four mutually unbiased orthonormal bases of \(\mathbb C^6\) is given, or a proof is supplied that no such quartet exists.
why: It probes the arithmetic obstruction behind optimal complementary measurements, making dimension six the canonical test case where the general theory fails.
key_works: Horodecki, Rudnicki, and Życzkowski (2020), *Five open problems in theory of quantum information*, arXiv:2002.03233.

title: Exact two-way capacity of thermal-loss channels
subfield: Quantum information, entanglement, and channel capacities
open: What is the exact entanglement- or secret-key-generation capacity of a thermal-loss bosonic channel when the two communicating parties are assisted by unlimited two-way classical communication? Today only achievable rates and upper bounds are known, and closing that gap remains open.
status: Exact capacity benchmarks are established for pure-loss channels, but thermal noise leaves important gaps between achievable rates and upper bounds. Key work: Stefano Pirandola, Riccardo Laurenza, Carlo Ottaviani, and Leonardo Banchi (2017), *Fundamental Limits of Repeaterless Quantum Communications*, arXiv:1510.08863.
solved_when: A single formula (or matching achievable rate and converse bound) is established for the two-way assisted entanglement/secret-key capacity of thermal-loss channels, exactly determining capacity for any transmissivity and thermal noise.
why: It sets the ultimate benchmark against which quantum repeaters and frequency transducers in realistic optical links must be judged, telling us the maximum value such devices can add.
key_works: Stefano Pirandola, Riccardo Laurenza, Carlo Ottaviani, and Leonardo Banchi (2017), *Fundamental Limits of Repeaterless Quantum Communications*, arXiv:1510.08863.

title: Low-overhead fault-tolerant blind delegation
open: Can a client delegate a useful quantum computation to an untrusted remote server so that both the input and the program remain private, any cheating is detected, and the scheme still tolerates physical noise — all at a total overhead that competes with non-private alternatives?
status: Universal blind computation exists in theory (Anne Broadbent, Joseph Fitzsimons, and Elham Kashefi (2009), *Universal blind quantum computation*, arXiv:0807.4154; DOI:10.1109/FOCS.2009.36), and fault-tolerant extensions have been developed in principle; what remains unresolved is achieving integrated, useful-scale performance under all these requirements at once.
solved_when: A working demonstration of delegated computation at useful scale achieves input and program privacy, cheat detection, and noise tolerance simultaneously, with total overhead competitive with non-private approaches.
why: It would allow confidential use of remote quantum hardware, letting clients exploit quantum servers without revealing their data or algorithms.
key_works: Anne Broadbent, Joseph Fitzsimons, and Elham Kashefi (2009), *Universal blind quantum computation*, arXiv:0807.4154; DOI:10.1109/FOCS.2009.36.

title: Finite-size qLDPC computation advantage
open: Can a complete finite-size quantum computation be demonstrated in which a quantum LDPC architecture uses fewer total physical resources than a well-optimized surface-code implementation achieving the same failure probability?
status: Strong partial results exist in the form of low-overhead memory designs and simulations, but memory savings do not automatically survive universal gates and routing. Key works: Sergey Bravyi et al. (2024), *High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory*, arXiv:2308.07915; DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-07107-7.
solved_when: An end-to-end finite-size computation — including universal gates and routing, not just memory — is exhibited where the qLDPC architecture's total physical resource count (e.g., qubits) is lower than a well-optimized surface-code implementation at equal failure probability.
why: It tests whether high-rate codes actually reduce the cost of computation, not merely of storing quantum information.
key_works: Sergey Bravyi et al. (2024), *High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory*, arXiv:2308.07915; DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-07107-7.

title: Fault tolerance against radiation-induced correlated bursts
open: Under what architecture-level conditions can radiation-induced error bursts be detected, contained, and corrected without introducing a persistent logical-error floor, and can those conditions be validated experimentally?
status: Catastrophic correlated error bursts from radiation have been observed in large superconducting-qubit arrays (Matt McEwen et al., 2022, *Resolving catastrophic error bursts from cosmic rays in large arrays of superconducting qubits*, arXiv:2104.05219); shielding or average error reduction alone is not a full fault-tolerance argument.
solved_when: The architecture-level conditions are determined and experimentally validated using measured radiation-induced error bursts, demonstrating detection, containment, and correction with no persistent logical-error floor.
why: A rare chip-wide radiation event can defeat error-correcting codes designed around local faults, so average error reduction alone cannot guarantee fault tolerance.
key_works: Matt McEwen et al. (2022), *Resolving catastrophic error bursts from cosmic rays in large arrays of superconducting qubits*, arXiv:2104.05219.

title: Fault-tolerant quantum random-access memory
open: Can we build a coherently addressable quantum random-access memory that survives faults and still delivers a real application-level advantage? Formally, the target is a memory whose query fidelity is quantified, with the full hardware, routing, initialization, and correction costs accounted for.
status: QRAM architectures date to 2007–2008, beginning with Vittorio Giovannetti, Seth Lloyd, and Lorenzo Maccone (2008), *Quantum random access memory*, arXiv:0708.1879; however, asymptotic query depth does not establish scalable fault-tolerant feasibility.
solved_when: A fault-tolerant QRAM construction exists with quantified query fidelity and bounded total hardware, routing, initialization, and correction overheads, such that an application using it retains its claimed advantage.
why: Many attractive quantum algorithms assume coherent data access, and that access dominates their practical cost; without a fault-tolerant QRAM, these algorithms lose their advantage in practice.
key_works: Vittorio Giovannetti, Seth Lloyd, and Lorenzo Maccone (2008), *Quantum random access memory*, arXiv:0708.1879.

title: Autonomous bosonic correction during computation
subfield: Passive memories, bosonic codes, and qudits
open: Can a bosonic quantum processor autonomously stabilize its encoded states while simultaneously performing useful computation — gates, measurement, and reset — all without fast classical feedback?
status: Autonomous stabilization and beyond-break-even memories have been achieved as partial milestones, but useful computation still requires operations compatible with these stabilization schemes. Key works include Sivak et al. (2023), *Real-time quantum error correction beyond break-even*, arXiv:2211.09116; Réglade et al. (2024), *Quantum control of a cat qubit with bit-flip times exceeding ten seconds*.
solved_when: A single demonstration combines autonomous stabilization with a compatible gate set, measurement, and reset, and shows the complete encoded process outperforms an unencoded implementation.
why: It removes the need for fast classical feedback, a major engineering bottleneck in scaling bosonic processors.
key_works: Sivak et al. (2023), *Real-time quantum error correction beyond break-even*, arXiv:2211.09116; Réglade et al. (2024), *Quantum control of a cat qubit with bit-flip times exceeding ten seconds*.

title: High-throughput shuttling through large ion-trap networks
open: Can ions be routed through large trap networks — across many junctions — with heating, loss, timing variation, and congestion all kept within bounded limits, while computation elsewhere proceeds continuously and in parallel? Formally, the goal is a transport scheme that maintains these guarantees at arbitrary network scale rather than only for small demonstrated primitives.
status: Quantum-CCD and racetrack architectures demonstrate essential primitives, not arbitrary-scale transport reliability (J. M. Pino et al. (2021), *Demonstration of the trapped-ion quantum-CCD computer architecture*, arXiv:2003.01293; S. A. Moses et al. (2023), *A Race Track Trapped-Ion Quantum Processor*, arXiv:2305.03828).
solved_when: A shuttling scheme routes ions through many junctions of a large ion-trap network while keeping heating, loss, timing variation, and congestion bounded, and supporting continuous parallel computation.
why: It converts long-lived isolated qubits into a scalable connected processor; without reliable arbitrary-scale transport, trap networks remain demonstrations of primitives rather than usable machines.
key_works: J. M. Pino et al. (2021), *Demonstration of the trapped-ion quantum-CCD computer architecture*, arXiv:2003.01293; S. A. Moses et al. (2023), *A Race Track Trapped-Ion Quantum Processor*, arXiv:2305.03828.

title: Continuous loading during error-corrected computation
open: Can lost atoms be continuously replenished in a neutral-atom array while the system is simultaneously performing repeated syndrome extraction and logical gates, without disturbing stored information or invalidating calibration?
status: Continuous operation of a coherent 3,000-qubit system was reported in 2025 (Neng-Chun Chiu et al. (2025), *Continuous operation of a coherent 3,000-qubit system*, arXiv:2506.20660); continuous replenishment combined with full error-corrected computation remains a stronger, unrealized target.
solved_when: An experiment demonstrates continuous atom replenishment concurrent with full error-corrected computation, with stored quantum information preserved and calibration maintained throughout.
why: Atom loss must become a recoverable service event rather than a run-ending failure, enabling sustained rather than finite-duration error-corrected operation.
key_works: Neng-Chun Chiu et al. (2025), *Continuous operation of a coherent 3,000-qubit system*, arXiv:2506.20660.

title: Optical-power scaling of large atom processors
open: Can a large neutral-atom processor scale in qubit count and active-gate throughput without a proportional increase in the expensive optical power it consumes? Formally, this asks for architectures in which array size and gate rate grow superlinearly relative to laser power, intensity instability, scattered light, and cooling demand.
status: Large coherent arrays and rapid qubit replenishment have been demonstrated, most notably in Chiu et al. (2025), *Continuous operation of a coherent 3,000-qubit system*, arXiv:2506.20660, but affordable sustained optical operation remains a separate, unaddressed scaling target.
solved_when: A demonstrated architecture achieves larger array size and higher active-gate throughput while the required laser power, intensity instability, scattered light, and cooling demand grow subproportionally with that scaling.
why: Qubit count alone does not translate into computational capacity an operator can economically sustain; without solving this, the cost of running ever-larger atom processors grows as fast as their size.
key_works: Chiu et al. (2025), *Continuous operation of a coherent 3,000-qubit system*, arXiv:2506.20660.

title: Repeater advantage with finite memories and real latency
open: Can a real quantum repeater system, built from practical components, beat the fundamental repeaterless bound on entanglement-distribution rate? Formally, this means exceeding the appropriate repeaterless benchmark at useful rates once finite memory lifetime, heralding delay, multiplexing, local gates, and all unsuccessful attempts are accounted for.
status: Capacity bounds define the target rate that must be exceeded, but partial repeater components demonstrated so far do not yet show the complete rate advantage. The relevant benchmark is set by Pirandola et al. (2017), *Fundamental Limits of Repeaterless Quantum Communications*, arXiv:1510.08863.
solved_when: An experimental repeater demonstration surpasses the capacity bound established for repeaterless communication at useful rates, with the reported rate including every loss mechanism in the record: finite memory lifetime, heralding delay, multiplexing overhead, local gates, and unsuccessful attempts.
why: A solution determines whether entanglement can be distributed economically beyond direct-link limitations; without it, scaling quantum networks beyond point-to-point links remains speculative.
key_works: Pirandola et al. (2017), *Fundamental Limits of Repeaterless Quantum Communications*, arXiv:1510.08863.

title: Reliable zero-noise extrapolation under model mismatch
open: Can zero-noise extrapolation be made trustworthy when the extrapolation model itself is wrong? Specifically, produce calibrated uncertainty intervals for the zero-noise estimate in settings where noise scaling changes the noise mechanism, circuit behavior, or drift trajectory rather than simply multiplying a fixed error rate.
status: Extrapolation methods exist, but plausible curve fits do not guarantee valid zero-noise estimates when the model is misspecified. Background: Zhenyu Cai et al. (2023), *Quantum Error Mitigation*, arXiv:2210.00921; DOI:10.1103/RevModPhys.95.045005.
solved_when: A method is given that outputs uncertainty intervals for zero-noise estimates which are calibrated (i.e., valid coverage) under model mismatch — where scaling alters the noise mechanism, circuit behavior, or drift trajectory — rather than only under a correctly specified noise model.
why: Without it, extrapolation can yield systematically biased "corrected" experimental results that appear reliable but are not; with it, error-mitigated experiments would carry trustworthy error bars.
key_works: Zhenyu Cai et al. (2023), *Quantum Error Mitigation*, arXiv:2210.00921; DOI:10.1103/RevModPhys.95.045005.

title: Scalable characterization of correlated gate errors
open: Can the error features most relevant to logical computation be recovered through experiments of feasible scale, without assuming that average gate fidelity determines them? Formally, the question asks for a scalable characterization procedure whose measured data identify the correlated error structure that matters for fault tolerance, rather than a single headline fidelity per gate.
status: Benchmarking metrics capture selected operational quantities, but many distinct correlated channels can share similar headline scores. Proctor et al. (2017), *What randomized benchmarking actually measures*, arXiv:1702.01853; Bausch et al. (2024), *Learning high-accuracy error decoding for quantum processors*.
solved_when: A characterization method exists that recovers the operationally relevant correlated error features of gates using experiment counts that scale feasibly with system size, and its output demonstrably distinguishes channels that share similar average-gate-fidelity scores.
why: Reliable fault-tolerance predictions require more than one number per gate; without scalable recovery of correlated error structure, decoding and threshold estimates rest on assumptions the benchmarking data do not actually test.
key_works: Proctor et al. (2017), *What randomized benchmarking actually measures*, arXiv:1702.01853; Bausch et al. (2024), *Learning high-accuracy error decoding for quantum processors*.

title: Asymptotic stabilizer rank of magic-state tensor powers
subfield: Many-body structure, simulation resources, and sensing
open: How does the stabilizer rank of tensor powers of key magic states such as the T state grow asymptotically? A precise answer, for both exact and approximate stabilizer rank, is still missing.
status: Current decomposition algorithms and lower bounds leave substantial uncertainty in the optimal exponential behavior. See Sergey Bravyi and David Gosset (2016), *Improved classical simulation of quantum circuits dominated by Clifford gates*, arXiv:1601.07601.
solved_when: Tight asymptotic characterizations of both the exact and approximate stabilizer-rank growth of tensor powers of important resource states such as the T state are established, closing the gap between known decomposition algorithms and lower bounds.
why: This growth rate controls a major family of classical simulation algorithms for non-Clifford circuits, so pinning it down fixes the true cost of simulating quantum circuits dominated by Clifford gates.
key_works: Sergey Bravyi and David Gosset (2016), *Improved classical simulation of quantum circuits dominated by Clifford gates*, arXiv:1601.07601.

title: The general multipartite quantum entropy cone
subfield: Many-body structure, simulation resources, and sensing
open: What are the possible entropy vectors of general quantum states shared among four or more parties, and which homogeneous entropy inequalities do they obey? Equivalently, characterize the unrestricted multipartite quantum entropy cone beyond the well-understood stabilizer case.
status: Stabilizer-state cones and other restricted families are better understood than the unrestricted quantum cone; a key work is Noah Linden, František Matúš, Mary Beth Ruskai, and Andreas Winter (2013), *The Quantum Entropy Cone of Stabiliser States*, arXiv:1302.5453.
solved_when: A complete characterization is available of all homogeneous entropy inequalities and achievable entropy vectors for general four-party and larger quantum states.
why: The cone governs which information-sharing patterns quantum systems can exhibit, thereby constraining the design of coding and communication protocols.
key_works: Noah Linden, František Matúš, Mary Beth Ruskai, and Andreas Winter (2013), *The Quantum Entropy Cone of Stabiliser States*, arXiv:1302.5453.

title: R10-12. Unrestricted lower bounds for finding a welded-tree path
open: Can a quantum algorithm output an explicit entrance-to-exit path in the standard randomly welded-tree oracle problem using only subexponentially many queries, or does every such algorithm require exponentially many queries? A proof of an exponential quantum-query lower bound for producing the full path — with no restrictions on the algorithm — is the target.
status: Quantum walks can find the exit efficiently without retaining a path. The 2023 "power of forgetting" result — Andrew M. Childs, Matthew Coudron, and Amin Shiraz Gilani (2023), *Quantum algorithms and the power of forgetting*, arXiv:2211.12447 — establishes a separation for a restricted class of genuine, rooted algorithms; the unrestricted path-finding question remains stronger. The problem is also highlighted in Scott Aaronson (2021), *Open Problems Related to Quantum Query Complexity*, arXiv:2109.06917.
solved_when: An exponential quantum-query lower bound is established for outputting an explicit entrance-to-exit path in the standard randomly welded-tree oracle problem, with no restrictions on the algorithm class; alternatively, a substantially faster path-output algorithm is found.
why: It separates learning that an endpoint is reachable from producing an inspectable classical witness of reachability.
key_works: Andrew M. Childs, Matthew Coudron, and Amin Shiraz Gilani (2023), *Quantum algorithms and the power of forgetting*, arXiv:2211.12447; Scott Aaronson (2021), *Open Problems Related to Quantum Query Complexity*, arXiv:2109.06917.

title: R10-13. The PPT-squared conjecture beyond established special cases
open: Is the composition of any two positive-partial-transpose (PPT) quantum channels always entanglement breaking, or do there exist two valid PPT channels whose composition still transmits entanglement to a reference?
status: Qutrit and other structured cases are established, per Junhyeong An and Soojoon Lee (2026), *Beyond the Positive Partial Transpose Squared Conjecture: The Qutrit Case*, arXiv:2607.15947. An August 2026 preprint, Sang-Jun Park (2026), *Every PPT channel has finite entanglement breaking index*, arXiv:2608.13551, reports finite entanglement-breaking index for every PPT channel; however, eventual destruction under repeated composition is weaker than destruction after two PPT stages.
solved_when: A proof that every composition of two PPT channels is entanglement breaking, or an explicit counterexample: two valid PPT channels whose composed channel retains entanglement with a reference.
why: It fixes how quickly successive bound-entanglement-compatible noise processes destroy all transmissible entanglement — whether two PPT stages already suffice or more are needed.
key_works: Sang-Jun Park (2026), *Every PPT channel has finite entanglement breaking index*, arXiv:2608.13551; Junhyeong An and Soojoon Lee (2026), *Beyond the Positive Partial Transpose Squared Conjecture: The Qutrit Case*, arXiv:2607.15947.

title: R10-15. Essential tensor-stable positive maps over ordinary complex numbers
open: Does there exist, over the ordinary complex numbers, a finite-dimensional complex-linear map that stays positive under every tensor power yet is neither completely positive nor completely copositive? Either construct such a map \(\Phi\) with \(\Phi^{\otimes n}\) positive for all positive integers \(n\), or prove that no such map exists.
status: Nontrivial positivity for any prescribed finite number of tensor powers is possible, but this does not settle the question for all \(n\). Constructions using nonstandard hypercomplex numbers exist; however, they do not settle existence over ordinary \(\mathbb C\). Key works: Alexander Müller-Hermes, David Reeb, and Michael M. Wolf (2015), *Positivity of linear maps under tensor powers*, arXiv:1502.05630; Mirte van der Eyden, Tim Netzer, and Gemma De las Cuevas (2022), *Halos and undecidability of tensor stable positive maps*, arXiv:2110.02113.
solved_when: An explicit finite-dimensional complex-linear map \(\Phi\) is given with \(\Phi^{\otimes n}\) positive for every positive integer \(n\) and \(\Phi\) neither completely positive nor completely copositive; or a proof is supplied that no such map exists over \(\mathbb C\).
why: A solution would clarify whether positivity can remain stable under unlimited composition without arising from the familiar completely positive structures.
key_works: Alexander Müller-Hermes, David Reeb, and Michael M. Wolf (2015), *Positivity of linear maps under tensor powers*, arXiv:1502.05630; Mirte van der Eyden, Tim Netzer, and Gemma De las Cuevas (2022), *Halos and undecidability of tensor stable positive maps*, arXiv:2110.02113.

title: R10-16. Decidability of tensor-stable positivity
open: Given an exactly specified finite-dimensional map with rational complex coefficients, decide whether all its tensor powers are positive, or prove that no algorithm can decide this for every input.
status: The 2022 analysis by Mirte van der Eyden, Tim Netzer, and Gemma De las Cuevas, *Halos and undecidability of tensor stable positive maps* (arXiv:2110.02113; DOI:10.1088/1751-8121/ac726e), proves undecidability for a related matrix-multiplication-tensor positivity problem and develops connections to tensor-stable maps, but it does not settle the ordinary all-tensor-powers decision problem.
solved_when: Either an algorithm is exhibited that, for every finite-dimensional map with rational complex coefficients, decides whether all its tensor powers are positive, or a proof is given that no such algorithm exists for all inputs.
why: It determines whether a complete automated classifier for this channel-related positivity property is possible.
key_works: Mirte van der Eyden, Tim Netzer, and Gemma De las Cuevas (2022), *Halos and undecidability of tensor stable positive maps*, arXiv:2110.02113; DOI:10.1088/1751-8121/ac726e.

title: R10-18. Joint dimension–accuracy optimality of diamond-norm channel tomography
open: How many forward queries to a black-box quantum channel are needed to learn it to diamond-norm error \(\varepsilon\)? Formally, decide whether the general \(O(d^4/\varepsilon^2)\) dependence for a \(d\)-dimensional channel is jointly optimal in dimension and accuracy even when ancillas, collective measurements, and adaptive strategies are allowed.
status: The 2026 revision (Mele and Bittel, *Optimal learning of quantum channels in diamond distance*, arXiv:2512.10214) establishes optimal dimension and Kraus-rank dependence at constant accuracy, with an upper bound \(O(d_{\rm in}d_{\rm out}k/\varepsilon^2)\); however, the matching separate parameter bounds do not automatically establish a matching joint lower bound.
solved_when: Matching upper and lower bounds are established for the query complexity of learning an arbitrary noisy \(d\)-dimensional channel to diamond-norm error \(\varepsilon\), resolving whether the \(O(d^4/\varepsilon^2)\) dependence is jointly optimal; at constant accuracy this means matching the upper bound \(O(d_{\rm in}d_{\rm out}k/\varepsilon^2)\) in dimension and Kraus rank \(k\).
why: It pins down the fundamental experimental cost of learning worst-case channel behavior rather than selected average observables.
key_works: Antonio Anna Mele and Lennart Bittel (2025/2026), *Optimal learning of quantum channels in diamond distance*, arXiv:2512.10214.

title: R10-23. Efficient capacity-achieving HSW square-root decoding
open: Can we build, for general finite classical–quantum memoryless channels, capacity-achieving codes whose Holevo–Schumacher–Westmoreland square-root decoding measurement is implemented by a polynomial-size circuit? Formally, the construction must be efficiently described and account for all costs — codeword-state preparation, block encoding, conditioning, and measurement synthesis — rather than assuming an exponential codebook oracle.
status: The coding theorem establishes the existence of good measurements but not efficient circuits for them. Algorithms for Petz recovery and pretty-good measurements — see András Gilyén, Seth Lloyd, Iman Marvian, Yihui Quek, and Mark M. Wilde (2022), *Quantum algorithm for Petz recovery channels and pretty good measurements*, arXiv:2006.16924; DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.128.220502 — provide implementations under access and conditioning assumptions that need not remain efficient for HSW code families. The HSW framework itself is treated in Mark M. Wilde (2017), *Quantum Information Theory*, second edition, Section 20.3.
solved_when: An explicit capacity-achieving code family for general finite classical–quantum memoryless channels is given whose HSW square-root decoding measurement admits a polynomial-size implementation, with all preparation, block-encoding, conditioning, and measurement-synthesis costs charged and remaining efficient.
why: It converts a communication-capacity existence theorem into an executable receiver architecture, making HSW decoding physically implementable rather than merely provably existent.
key_works: Mark M. Wilde (2017), *Quantum Information Theory*, second edition, Section 20.3; András Gilyén, Seth Lloyd, Iman Marvian, Yihui Quek, and Mark M. Wilde (2022), *Quantum algorithm for Petz recovery channels and pretty good measurements*, arXiv:2006.16924; DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.128.220502.

title: R10-24. An unrestricted strong converse for blind mixed-state compression
open: For an arbitrary finite-dimensional source \(\rho^{AR}\), does reference-preserving reconstruction fidelity necessarily vanish whenever the compression rate drops below \(S(CQ)\), where \(C,Q\) are the nonredundant Koashi–Imoto components? The question allows completely arbitrary encoding and decoding channels, with no structural assumptions on the decoder.
status: The optimal first-order rate is established. The 2025 strong-converse revision of Zahra Baghali Khanian, *Strong Converse Bounds for Compression of Mixed States*, arXiv:2206.09415 (2022; revised 2025), proves results under additional decoder assumptions rather than the unrestricted statement; the underlying rate result builds on Zahra Baghali Khanian and Andreas Winter (2022), *General Mixed State Quantum Data Compression with and without Entanglement Assistance*, arXiv:1912.08506.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of the unrestricted strong converse: for any sequence of encoding and decoding channels with compression rate below \(S(CQ)\), the reference-preserving fidelity tends to zero.
why: It settles whether operating below the fundamental rate causes complete failure, rather than merely preventing fidelity from approaching one.
key_works: Zahra Baghali Khanian and Andreas Winter (2022), *General Mixed State Quantum Data Compression with and without Entanglement Assistance*, arXiv:1912.08506; Zahra Baghali Khanian (2022; revised 2025), *Strong Converse Bounds for Compression of Mixed States*, arXiv:2206.09415.

title: R10-26. The entropy photon-number inequality for arbitrary independent inputs
open: Does the entropy photon-number inequality hold for all independent input states, not just Gaussian ones? Formally, for independent \(n\)-mode input states \(A\) and \(B\) mixed on a beamsplitter of transmissivity \(\eta\), prove the entropy photon-number inequality.
status: Conjectured in 2007 and still discussed as open at a June 2026 specialist symposium. The established quantum entropy-power inequality (Giacomo De Palma, Andrea Mari, and Vittorio Giovannetti (2014), *A generalization of the Entropy Power Inequality to Bosonic Quantum Systems*, arXiv:1402.0404) and the one-mode Gaussian optimizer theorems (Giacomo De Palma, Dario Trevisan, and Vittorio Giovannetti (2017), *Gaussian States Minimize the Output Entropy of One-Mode Quantum Gaussian Channels*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.118.160503) do not establish the full arbitrary-input statement.
solved_when: A proof (or disproof) of the inequality for arbitrary independent \(n\)-mode inputs at a beamsplitter of arbitrary transmissivity \(\eta\), covering all modes \(n\) — not restricted to Gaussian inputs.
why: It would provide sharp entropy constraints for optical mixing processes and strengthen capacity analyses of bosonic communication systems.
key_works: Giacomo De Palma, Andrea Mari, and Vittorio Giovannetti (2014), *A generalization of the Entropy Power Inequality to Bosonic Quantum Systems*, arXiv:1402.0404; Giacomo De Palma, Dario Trevisan, and Vittorio Giovannetti (2017), *Gaussian States Minimize the Output Entropy of One-Mode Quantum Gaussian Channels*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.118.160503.

title: R10-27. Minimum-output-entropy additivity with a nonunital qubit factor
status: Unital-qubit results and several other special classes are established. High-dimensional counterexamples to general additivity do not answer this qubit-factor question.
why: Identifies whether a single noisy qubit channel can participate in the entangled-input mechanisms responsible for entropy nonadditivity.
key_works: Christopher King (2002), *Additivity for unital qubit channels*, Journal of Mathematical Physics 43, 4641–4653; Alexander S. Holevo (2015), *Gaussian optimizers and the additivity problem in quantum information theory*, arXiv:1501.00652.

title: R10-28. Intermediate-\(p\) multiplicativity for identity-mixed Werner–Holevo channels
open: Does multiplicativity of the maximal output \(p\)-norm hold for identity-mixed Werner–Holevo channels in the intermediate range of \(p\)? Formally, one asks whether the multiplicativity property extends to the interior values of \(p\) that lie between the known endpoints.
status: Multiplicativity at \(p=2\) is proved for the mixed family; the unmixed Werner–Holevo channel is understood for \(1\le p\le2\). These endpoint and boundary results do not cover the stated interior region. Key works: Spiros Michalakis (2007), *Multiplicativity of the maximal output 2-norm for depolarized Werner-Holevo channels*, arXiv:0707.1722; Nilanjana Datta (2004), *Multiplicativity of Maximal p-Norms in Werner-Holevo Channels for \(1\le p\le2\)*, arXiv:quant-ph/0410063.
solved_when: Multiplicativity of the maximal output \(p\)-norm is proved for the identity-mixed Werner–Holevo family over the intermediate-\(p\) region not covered by the \(p=2\) result and the \(1\le p\le2\) analysis of the unmixed channel.
why: It isolates a highly symmetric surviving test case for maximal-output-norm multiplicativity after broad conjectures in the area failed.
key_works: Spiros Michalakis (2007), *Multiplicativity of the maximal output 2-norm for depolarized Werner-Holevo channels*, arXiv:0707.1722; Nilanjana Datta (2004), *Multiplicativity of Maximal p-Norms in Werner-Holevo Channels for \(1\le p\le2\)*, arXiv:quant-ph/0410063.

title: R10-32. Infinite coherence cost without pairwise reversibility
open: Can a Gibbs-preserving channel demand unbounded coherence for exact implementation by thermal operations even when no recovery channel can exactly restore any pair of orthogonal input states (i.e., it is not pairwise reversible)? Formally, either construct such a channel or prove that pairwise reversibility is necessary for divergent coherence cost.
status: Tajima–Takagi prove infinite coherence cost for a class of pairwise-reversible channels satisfying an additional energy-related condition; their final 2025 paper explicitly leaves open whether every cost-diverging Gibbs-preserving channel must be pairwise reversible (Hiroyasu Tajima and Ryuji Takagi (2025), *Gibbs-Preserving Operations Requiring Infinite Amount of Quantum Coherence*, arXiv:2404.03479; DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.134.170201).
solved_when: Either a Gibbs-preserving channel that is not pairwise reversible is constructed and shown to require infinite coherence for exact implementation by thermal operations, or it is proved that every cost-diverging Gibbs-preserving channel must be pairwise reversible.
why: It identifies the physical mechanism behind thermodynamic operations that appear mathematically free but cannot be implemented with finite coherence resources.
key_works: Hiroyasu Tajima and Ryuji Takagi (2025), *Gibbs-Preserving Operations Requiring Infinite Amount of Quantum Coherence*, arXiv:2404.03479; DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.134.170201.

title: QMA versus QCMA
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Do quantum proofs buy more verification power than classical proofs for a quantum verifier? Formally, are QMA and QCMA equal or distinct as unrelativized complexity classes?
status: The unrelativized question remains open. Classical-oracle separations were obtained by John Bostanci, Jonas Haferkamp, Chinmay Nirkhe, and Mark Zhandry (2026), *Separating QMA from QCMA with a Classical Oracle*, STOC 2026; the older "find a classical-oracle separation" formulation is therefore not the remaining problem.
solved_when: An unrelativized proof (or refutation) that QMA ≠ QCMA, or QMA = QCMA, is established — that is, no reliance on a classical oracle.
why: It determines whether useful evidence for quantum verification can be intrinsically quantum rather than merely classical information.
key_works: John Bostanci, Jonas Haferkamp, Chinmay Nirkhe, and Mark Zhandry (2026), *Separating QMA from QCMA with a Classical Oracle*, STOC 2026.

title: The power of unentangled quantum witnesses
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Does a verifier gain real power from receiving two quantum witnesses that are promised to be unentangled — that is, does QMA(2) strictly contain QMA, or do the two classes coincide?
status: The ordinary complexity-class question remains open. A September 2026 preprint establishes a quantum-oracle separation and resolves the associated no-disentanglers conjecture, but not the unrelativized equality (John Bostanci et al. (2026), *A quantum oracle separation between QMA(2) and QMA*, arXiv:2609.02865).
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that QMA(2) = QMA, or a separation of the two classes, is established in the standard, unrelativized setting.
why: It determines exactly how much computational power a mere promise about independence between witnesses provides, which is the crux of understanding quantum proof systems with multiple provers.
key_works: John Bostanci et al. (2026), *A quantum oracle separation between QMA(2) and QMA*, arXiv:2609.02865.

title: The quantum PCP conjecture
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Is it QMA-hard to estimate the ground-state energy density of a bounded-locality, bounded-degree Hamiltonian to constant additive accuracy? Equivalently, does a quantum analogue of the classical PCP theorem hold for the local Hamiltonian problem under constant-factor approximation of the energy?
status: Open. Good quantum codes, NLTS constructions, and recent locally testable-code results do not by themselves establish the quantum PCP conjecture. Key works include Dorit Aharonov, Itai Arad, and Thomas Vidick (2013), *The Quantum PCP Conjecture*, arXiv:1309.7495, and Sevag Gharibian (2026), *Hardness of Approximation for Ground State Problems*.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of QMA-hardness of approximating the ground-state energy density of bounded-locality, bounded-degree Hamiltonians to a constant additive accuracy is established.
why: It determines whether extensive quantum entanglement remains computationally essential at nonzero energy density, deciding whether the classical PCP phenomenon extends to quantum proof systems or genuinely breaks down.
key_works: Dorit Aharonov, Itai Arad, and Thomas Vidick (2013), *The Quantum PCP Conjecture*, arXiv:1309.7495; Sevag Gharibian (2026), *Hardness of Approximation for Ground State Problems*.

title: Negative-partial-transpose bound entanglement
subfield: Quantum information, entanglement, and channel capacities
open: Can a quantum state with negative partial transpose be bound-entangled — that is, undistillable? Formally: does there exist an NPT state such that no joint measurement on any finite number of copies yields a singlet?
status: Open. A July 2026 preprint by Kishor Bharti, Rishikesh Gajjala, and Tobias Haug (2026), *Two-copy nondistillability of Werner states: sharp partial-trace inequalities and finite-copy extensions*, arXiv:2607.24479, solves the two-copy Werner-state case but explicitly leaves the arbitrary-copy endpoint unresolved.
solved_when: An explicit NPT state is proven undistillable across every finite number of copies (or, conversely, it is proven that every NPT state becomes distillable at some finite copy number).
why: It decides whether entanglement that is detectable by the PPT criterion can nevertheless remain permanently unusable for singlet distillation.
key_works: Kishor Bharti, Rishikesh Gajjala, and Tobias Haug (2026), *Two-copy nondistillability of Werner states: sharp partial-trace inequalities and finite-copy extensions*, arXiv:2607.24479.

title: Exact quantum capacity of the depolarizing channel
subfield: Quantum information, entanglement, and channel capacities
open: What is the exact quantum capacity of the qubit depolarizing channel across its entire nontrivial parameter range? In particular, where in this range does the regularized coherent information genuinely exceed any single-letter quantity?
status: Open. Improved upper bounds, coding constructions, and strong-converse results do not yield the exact capacity curve. Key works include Tulja Varun Kondra et al. (2026), *Sharp Quantum Capacity Thresholds: Exponential Strong Converses for Degradable and Antidegradable Channels*, arXiv:2608.01308, and Zhiwei Song et al. (2026), *Approximate majorization and high-order capacity of quantum depolarizing channels*.
solved_when: The capacity is determined exactly as a function of the depolarizing parameter over the nontrivial range, settling whether regularization is essential and where.
why: It provides a fundamental benchmark for transmitting quantum information through symmetric noise, the canonical model for which all capacity questions should ideally be answerable.
key_works: Tulja Varun Kondra et al. (2026), *Sharp Quantum Capacity Thresholds: Exponential Strong Converses for Degradable and Antidegradable Channels*, arXiv:2608.01308; Zhiwei Song et al. (2026), *Approximate majorization and high-order capacity of quantum depolarizing channels*.

title: Exact output majorization for depolarizing channels
subfield: Quantum information, entanglement, and channel capacities
open: Does the exact output-majorization conjecture hold for tensor powers of depolarizing channels? That is, can the approximate majorization guarantees already established for these channels be strengthened to exact majorization, or is there a counterexample?
status: Open. Work from September 2026 establishes approximate majorization and sharp higher-order consequences for quantum depolarizing channels, but leaves the exact conjecture unresolved (Zhiwei Song, Xin Wang, Marco Tomamichel, and Kun Fang (2026), *Approximate majorization and high-order capacity of quantum depolarizing channels*, arXiv:2609.37240).
solved_when: The exact output-majorization conjecture for tensor powers of depolarizing channels is either proved in full generality or refuted by an explicit counterexample.
why: A tight answer would sharply constrain the benefit of entangled inputs in channel coding, replacing approximate bounds with exact structural information about the depolarizing channel's output majorization behavior.
key_works: Zhiwei Song, Xin Wang, Marco Tomamichel, and Kun Fang (2026), *Approximate majorization and high-order capacity of quantum depolarizing channels*, arXiv:2609.37240.

title: Polynomial-time dihedral hidden subgroup algorithms
subfield: Quantum query complexity and algebraic algorithms
open: Is there a polynomial-time quantum algorithm for the dihedral hidden subgroup problem or, equivalently, the dihedral coset problem? A proof of meaningful limitations for broad algorithmic models would also qualify as an answer.
status: Open. A claimed August 2026 solution was explicitly refuted: as shown by Aparna Gupte, Seyoon Ragavan, and Mark Zhandry (2026), *The ePrint:2026/1591 Quantum Algorithm Does Not Solve DCP* (ePrint:2026/1693), that algorithm cannot recover even the required secret bit with non-negligible advantage. For background see Andrew Childs and Wim van Dam (2010), *Quantum algorithms for algebraic problems*, arXiv:0812.0380.
solved_when: Either a polynomial-time quantum algorithm for the dihedral hidden subgroup or dihedral coset problem is given, or such an algorithm is ruled out for a broad algorithmic model.
why: A solution would substantially change the quantum algorithmic landscape for lattice-related problems, including unique shortest-vector problems.
key_works: Andrew Childs and Wim van Dam (2010), *Quantum algorithms for algebraic problems*, arXiv:0812.0380; Aparna Gupte, Seyoon Ragavan, and Mark Zhandry (2026), *The ePrint:2026/1591 Quantum Algorithm Does Not Solve DCP*, ePrint:2026/1693.

title: R10-01. An eleven-qubit, three-logical-qubit code with weight-four checks
open: Does there exist an \([[11,3,3]]\) qubit stabilizer code with eight independent commuting generators, each of Pauli weight at most four? Arbitrary connectivity and non-CSS constructions are permitted.
status: The 2026 low-weight-code analysis leaves the minimum possible maximum generator weight at four or five. Weight-five constructions exist; weight four remains unresolved. See Fuchuan Wei, Zhengyi Han, Austin Yubo He, Zimu Li, and Zi-Wen Liu (2026), *Theory of low-weight quantum codes*, arXiv:2601.19848.
solved_when: An explicit \([[11,3,3]]\) stabilizer code is exhibited with eight independent commuting generators, each of weight at most four; alternatively, a proof that no such code exists.
why: It closes a small but concrete gap in check-complexity for hardware-efficient error correction, pinning the minimum possible maximum generator weight for this code family.
key_works: Fuchuan Wei, Zhengyi Han, Austin Yubo He, Zimu Li, and Zi-Wen Liu (2026), *Theory of low-weight quantum codes*, arXiv:2601.19848.

title: R10-02. The square-root distance conjecture for weight-four stabilizer codes
open: Prove or refute that every qubit stabilizer code encoding at least one logical qubit and generated by weight-at-most-four checks satisfies \(d=O(\sqrt n)\), **without assuming geometric locality**.
status: Explicitly conjectured in 2026. Weight-three generators impose much stronger limitations; weight-four toric-code families attain square-root distance.
why: Would identify an intrinsic check-weight obstruction, rather than a hardware-layout obstruction.
key_works: Wei et al. (2026), *Theory of low-weight quantum codes*, arXiv:2601.19848.

title: R10-03. An absolutely maximally entangled state of eight ququarts
open: Does there exist an absolutely maximally entangled state of eight ququarts — a pure state on \((\mathbb C^4)^{\otimes 8}\) whose reduction to every four-party subset is \(I_{256}/256\)? Either construct such a state or prove that none exists.
status: The 2026 classification of seven-party absolutely maximally entangled states explicitly identifies AME(8,4) as a remaining existence problem; settling the seven-party cases does not settle this eight-party instance. See Fei Shi, Xiande Zhang, Qi Zhao, and Lvzhou Li (2026), *Complete Existence Classification of Seven-Partite Absolutely Maximally Entangled States*, arXiv:2608.01011.
solved_when: An explicit pure state on \((\mathbb C^4)^{\otimes 8}\) is exhibited whose reduction to every four-party subsystem is maximally mixed, \(I_{256}/256\), or a proof is given that no such state exists.
why: It supplies — or rules out — a particularly small perfect tensor, with applications to erasure correction, secret sharing, and tensor-network constructions.
key_works: Fei Shi, Xiande Zhang, Qi Zhao, and Lvzhou Li (2026), *Complete Existence Classification of Seven-Partite Absolutely Maximally Entangled States*, arXiv:2608.01011.
aliases: AME(8,4); eight-leg perfect tensor of bond dimension four.

title: R10-04. Optimal length of permutation-invariant codes correcting \(t\) errors
open: Does the shortest two-dimensional permutation-invariant qubit code that corrects \(t\) arbitrary errors always have length \(t^2 + t\)? A formal statement would determine, for every \(t\), the minimum length \(n\) of such a code.
status: A 2026 numerical study by Liam J. Bond, Jiří Minář, Māris Ozols, Arghavan Safavi-Naini, and Vladyslav Visnevskyi (2026), *Permutation-invariant codes: a numerical study and qudit constructions*, arXiv:2603.10981, conjectures the equivalent distance bound \(n\ge(3d^2+1)/4\), with evidence of saturation. However, general constructions and numerical optima do not establish the proposed formula for every \(t\). Related constructions appear in Arda Aydin, Max A. Alekseyev, and Alexander Barg (2024), *A family of permutationally invariant quantum codes*, Quantum 8, 1321.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation with counterexample) that the minimum length of a two-dimensional permutation-invariant qubit code correcting \(t\) arbitrary errors equals \(t^2 + t\) for every \(t\); equivalently, in the distance formulation, that the bound \(n \ge (3d^2+1)/4\) holds and is saturated for all relevant \(d\).
why: It determines the optimal redundancy required for error correction in settings where individual particles cannot be distinguished or addressed, such as certain physical architectures.
key_works: Liam J. Bond, Jiří Minář, Māris Ozols, Arghavan Safavi-Naini, and Vladyslav Visnevskyi (2026), *Permutation-invariant codes: a numerical study and qudit constructions*, arXiv:2603.10981; Arda Aydin, Max A. Alekseyev, and Alexander Barg (2024), *A family of permutationally invariant quantum codes*, Quantum 8, 1321.

title: R10-05. A seven-qubit code encoding three orthogonal states and correcting one error
open: Does there exist a seven-qubit quantum code that encodes three orthogonal logical states and corrects any single error — in particular, one with no stabilizer (additive) structure? Formally, determine whether a rank-three projector on seven qubits satisfies all distance-three Knill–Laflamme conditions, or prove that no such \(((7,3,3))_2\) code exists.
status: The March 2026 rational-certificate table still gives \(2\le K_{\max}(7,3)\le3\); the upper endpoint is not known to be achievable. The relevant bound is Gerard Anglès Munné and Felix Huber (2026), *SDP bounds on quantum codes: rational certificates*, arXiv:2603.19901.
solved_when: Either an explicit nonadditive \(((7,3,3))_2\) code (a rank-three projector meeting all distance-three Knill–Laflamme conditions) is constructed, or a certificate proves impossibility — thereby determining whether \(K_{\max}(7,3)=3\) or \(K_{\max}(7,3)=2\).
why: It tests whether abandoning stabilizer structure improves one of the smallest single-error-correcting quantum codes, where additive constructions are fully understood.
key_works: Gerard Anglès Munné and Felix Huber (2026), *SDP bounds on quantum codes: rational certificates*, arXiv:2603.19901.

title: R10-06. A nine-qubit, thirteen-dimensional, distance-three code
open: Does there exist a nine-qubit quantum code of dimension thirteen that corrects one arbitrary error? Formally: construct a \(((9,13,3))_2\) code, or prove that every such code has dimension at most twelve — with the search covering arbitrary codes, not just codeword-stabilized ones.
status: A twelve-dimensional nonadditive code is known, and the 2026 certified bounds remain \(12\le K_{\max}(9,3)\le13\). Searches restricted to codeword-stabilized constructions do not exclude arbitrary codes. Key works: Sixia Yu, Qing Chen, C. H. Lai, and C. H. Oh (2008), *Nonadditive Quantum Error-Correcting Code*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.101.090501; A. Rigby, J. C. Olivier, and P. Jarvis (2019), *Heuristic construction of codeword stabilized codes*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevA.100.062303; Anglès Munné and Huber (2026), arXiv:2603.19901.
solved_when: Either an explicit \(((9,13,3))_2\) code is given, or it is proved that \(K_{\max}(9,3)=12\), closing the gap \(12\le K_{\max}(9,3)\le13\).
why: It closes a longstanding one-dimension gap in a canonical nonadditive-code benchmark.
key_works: Sixia Yu, Qing Chen, C. H. Lai, and C. H. Oh (2008), *Nonadditive Quantum Error-Correcting Code*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.101.090501; A. Rigby, J. C. Olivier, and P. Jarvis (2019), *Heuristic construction of codeword stabilized codes*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevA.100.062303; Anglès Munné and Huber (2026), arXiv:2603.19901.

title: R10-07. Semi-Clifford normal forms for two odd-prime-dimensional qudits
open: Can every two-qudit gate at every finite level of the Clifford hierarchy be factored as \(U=C_1DC_2\), with Clifford gates \(C_1, C_2\) and a diagonal gate \(D\), when each qudit has odd-prime dimension? The question is settled at the third level but open for all higher levels.
status: The 2025 one-qubit-or-qudit classification does not settle two-qudit higher levels; its concluding conjectures explicitly extend the normal-form question to two qudits. Key works: Nadish de Silva and Oscar Lautsch (2025), *The Clifford hierarchy for one qubit or qudit*, arXiv:2501.07939; I. Chen and N. de Silva (2024), *Characterising semi-Clifford gates using algebraic sets*, Communications in Mathematical Physics 405, 201.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation, via explicit counterexample) that every two-qudit gate in every finite level of the Clifford hierarchy over odd-prime local dimension admits the semi-Clifford factorization \(U=C_1DC_2\).
why: A positive answer would give systematic gate-teleportation and synthesis structures for higher-dimensional fault-tolerant computation.
key_works: Nadish de Silva and Oscar Lautsch (2025), *The Clifford hierarchy for one qubit or qudit*, arXiv:2501.07939; I. Chen and N. de Silva (2024), *Characterising semi-Clifford gates using algebraic sets*, Communications in Mathematical Physics 405, 201.

title: R10-10. Aaronson–Ambainis influence for all bounded low-degree polynomials
open: Must every bounded low-degree polynomial on the hypercube have a coordinate with substantial influence? Formally, prove or refute that every multilinear \(p:\{-1,1\}^N\to[0,1]\) of degree at most \(d\) and variance at least \(\varepsilon\) has some coordinate of influence at least \((\varepsilon/d)^C\) for a universal constant \(C\).
status: The conjecture remains open in general. September 2026 results obtain sharp inequalities for completely bounded polynomials and associated quantum algorithms, but those additional structural assumptions do not cover every bounded polynomial. Key works: Scott Aaronson and Andris Ambainis (2014), *The Need for Structure in Quantum Speedups*, Theory of Computing 10, 133–166; Francisco Escudero Gutiérrez, Miquel Saucedo, and Carlos Palazuelos (2026), *Optimal inequalities for completely bounded polynomials and the limitations of quantum query algorithms*, arXiv:2609.05201.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) of the influence lower bound \((\varepsilon/d)^C\) for all bounded multilinear polynomials of degree at most \(d\) and variance at least \(\varepsilon\), with \(C\) a universal constant.
why: A proof would explain why substantial quantum query advantages require exploitable structure rather than merely low polynomial degree.
key_works: Scott Aaronson and Andris Ambainis (2014), *The Need for Structure in Quantum Speedups*, Theory of Computing 10, 133–166; Francisco Escudero Gutiérrez, Miquel Saucedo, and Carlos Palazuelos (2026), *Optimal inequalities for completely bounded polynomials and the limitations of quantum query algorithms*, arXiv:2609.05201.

title: R10-11. Exact parity in higher-depth QAC⁰
open: Can polynomial-size, constant-depth quantum circuits built from arbitrary one-qubit gates and unbounded-fanin Toffoli gates compute parity exactly, when supplied with only polynomially many initialized ancillas and no free unbounded-fanout primitive?
status: Recent lower-bound work (Joshi, Tal, Vasconcelos, and Wright, 2025/2026, *Improved Lower Bounds for QAC0*, arXiv:2512.14643; DOI:10.1145/3798129.3800922) excludes exact parity at depth three even with unrestricted size and ancillas, and establishes approximation limitations at depth two. General higher constant depth remains unresolved. Earlier foundational treatment in Cristopher Moore (1999), *Quantum Circuits: Fanout, Parity, and Counting*.
