solved_when: A proof (or construction) resolves exact parity computation for general constant depth in this model; the existing lower-bound work already excludes exact parity at depth three even with unrestricted size and ancillas, so the open question is settled for all higher constant depths.
why: It determines whether genuinely quantum interference can defeat the classical constant-depth obstruction to parity in this gate model.
key_works: Cristopher Moore (1999), *Quantum Circuits: Fanout, Parity, and Counting*; Malvika Raj Joshi, Avishay Tal, Francisca Vasconcelos, and John Wright (2025/2026), *Improved Lower Bounds for QAC0*, arXiv:2512.14643; DOI:10.1145/3798129.3800922.

title: R10-14. Absolute PPT versus absolute separability for two qutrits
open: Does every \(3\times3\) bipartite state whose spectrum stays PPT under every global unitary also stay separable under every global unitary? Equivalently, are the absolutely-PPT and absolutely-separable sets equal for \(3\otimes3\) systems?
status: Open for two qutrits. March 2026 work by Nalan Wang, Lin Chen, and Zhiwei Song (2026), *Extreme points of absolutely PPT states with exactly three distinct eigenvalues*, arXiv:2603.20717, classifies relevant extreme points with three distinct eigenvalues, but does not establish equality of the full absolutely-PPT and absolutely-separable sets.
solved_when: The equality (or a counterexample) of the full absolutely-PPT set and the absolutely-separable set in \(3\otimes3\) is established.
why: It tests whether the spectrum alone can conceal entanglement beyond all partial-transpose tests, even after arbitrary global basis changes.
key_works: Nalan Wang, Lin Chen, and Zhiwei Song (2026), *Extreme points of absolutely PPT states with exactly three distinct eigenvalues*, arXiv:2603.20717.

title: R10-19. Finite collapse of the exact PPT entanglement-cost hierarchy
open: Does the exact PPT entanglement-cost hierarchy of Lami–Mele–Regula collapse to a finite level — that is, is their Conjecture S33 true? A formal proof or refutation is sought.
status: The 2025 paper of Ludovico Lami, Francesco A. Mele, and Bartosz Regula (2025), *Computable entanglement cost under positive partial transpose operations* (arXiv:2405.09613; Physical Review Letters 134, 090202, Supplemental Material, Conjecture S33), establishes efficient approximation through converging hierarchies and reports numerical support for collapse. Approximate computability is already established; universal exact collapse is not.
solved_when: Conjecture S33 of Lami–Mele–Regula (Physical Review Letters 134, 090202, Supplemental Material, Conjecture S33) is proved or refuted; if proved, the level at which the hierarchy collapses should be identified.
why: A positive answer would remove the remaining hierarchy limit from an operational entanglement-cost formula, making the exact cost directly computable rather than only approximable through converging hierarchies.
key_works: Ludovico Lami, Francesco A. Mele, and Bartosz Regula (2025), *Computable entanglement cost under positive partial transpose operations*, arXiv:2405.09613; Physical Review Letters 134, 090202, Supplemental Material, Conjecture S33.

title: R10-20. Sub-ebit implementation of the elegant joint measurement
open: Can the two-qubit elegant joint measurement be implemented exactly and deterministically by LOCC using a pure resource state of entanglement entropy below one ebit, if that state is allowed higher Schmidt rank? Formally, only the classical outcome of the measurement must be reproduced.
status: One ebit is known to suffice by teleportation. The 2026 analysis explicitly leaves open the higher-rank, sub-ebit possibility. See Seiseki Akibue, Jisho Miyazaki, and Hiroyuki Osaka (2025/2026), *Optimizing Entanglement Manipulation via Algebraic-Geometric Decompositions and Semidefinite Programming Hierarchies*, arXiv:2501.17394.
solved_when: A higher-Schmidt-rank pure resource state with entanglement entropy strictly below one ebit is shown to yield an exact, deterministic LOCC implementation of the elegant joint measurement's classical outcome — or such a state is proved impossible.
why: It tests whether extra resource dimension can lower the entanglement cost of a fixed distributed measurement, which currently costs one ebit via teleportation.
key_works: Seiseki Akibue, Jisho Miyazaki, and Hiroyuki Osaka (2025/2026), *Optimizing Entanglement Manipulation via Algebraic-Geometric Decompositions and Semidefinite Programming Hierarchies*, arXiv:2501.17394.
aliases: EJM cost; symmetric joint measurement cost.

title: R10-21. A strict asymptotic distillation gap between SEP and PPT operations
open: Is there a bipartite state whose entanglement can be distilled at a strictly higher asymptotic rate under PPT operations than under every separable operation? Formally, exhibit a state \(\rho\) with \(D_{\rm SEP}(\rho)<D_{\rm PPT}(\rho)\), where the rates are asymptotic singlet-distillation rates with vanishing error — a single-copy success-probability gap does not suffice.
status: The 2026 analysis explicitly identifies this separation as unresolved despite progress on single-copy optimization. Key work: Akibue, Miyazaki, and Osaka (2025/2026), *Optimizing Entanglement Manipulation via Algebraic-Geometric Decompositions and Semidefinite Programming Hierarchies*, arXiv:2501.17394, Section 5.5.
solved_when: A bipartite state \(\rho\) is exhibited together with a proof that its asymptotic singlet-distillation rate with vanishing error under PPT operations strictly exceeds that under separable operations.
why: It would show that the PPT relaxation overestimates the entanglement asymptotically usable even relative to all separable operations, invalidating PPT rate bounds as tight proxies for operational distillation.
key_works: Akibue, Miyazaki, and Osaka (2025/2026), *Optimizing Entanglement Manipulation via Algebraic-Geometric Decompositions and Semidefinite Programming Hierarchies*, arXiv:2501.17394, Section 5.5.

title: R10-29. A strict advantage of fully interleaved superchannel discrimination
open: In the realization-based superchannel-discrimination model, determine whether fully general causal interleaving can achieve a strictly better asymmetric error exponent than nested adaptive strategies. Supply an explicit pair exhibiting a gap, or prove equality under clearly stated access rules.
status: Hirche establishes achievable and converse quantities for several strategy classes but leaves gaps between the general interleaved and more restricted formulations; classical cases do not settle the quantum question. Key work: Christoph Hirche (2023), *Quantum Network Discrimination*, arXiv:2103.02404; DOI:10.22331/q-2023-07-25-1064.
solved_when: Either an explicit pair of superchannels is given for which the general interleaved strategy achieves a strictly larger asymmetric error exponent than every nested adaptive strategy, or equality of the exponents is proven under clearly stated access rules.
why: It determines whether access to a process's temporal structure has operational value beyond repeated use of the process as a single higher-order object.
key_works: Christoph Hirche (2023), *Quantum Network Discrimination*, arXiv:2103.02404; DOI:10.22331/q-2023-07-25-1064.

title: R10-30. Polynomial entanglement lower bounds for one-round quantum routing
open: Does there exist an explicit, efficiently computable Boolean family \(f_n(x,y)\) such that any constant-error, one-round simultaneous-message protocol that routes an unknown qubit to the party selected by \(f_n\) requires initial entanglement of formation at least \(n^c\) for some \(c>0\)? In other words, can one-round quantum routing be shown to need polynomially much entanglement?
status: The September 2026 revision of Bogner's work proves an \(\Omega(\log n)\) entanglement-of-formation lower bound for inner-product routing, allowing arbitrary mixed shared resources and error at most \(0.09\); polynomial lower bounds remain open. Key works: Kevin Bogner (2026), *Robust logarithmic entanglement lower bound for f-routing*, arXiv:2608.05775v3; René Allerstorfer, Harry Buhrman, Alex May, Florian Speelman, and Philip Verduyn Lunel (2024), *Relating Non-Local Quantum Computation to Information Theoretic Cryptography*, Quantum 8, 1387.
solved_when: An explicit efficiently computable Boolean family \(f_n(x,y)\) is exhibited, together with a proof that any constant-error, one-round simultaneous-message protocol routing an unknown qubit to the party selected by \(f_n\) requires initial entanglement of formation at least \(n^c\) for some \(c>0\).
why: Such a bound would establish substantial resource requirements for nonlocal quantum computation and strengthen the foundations of position-based cryptographic security.
key_works: Kevin Bogner (2026), *Robust logarithmic entanglement lower bound for f-routing*, arXiv:2608.05775v3; René Allerstorfer, Harry Buhrman, Alex May, Florian Speelman, and Philip Verduyn Lunel (2024), *Relating Non-Local Quantum Computation to Information Theoretic Cryptography*, Quantum 8, 1387.

title: R10-31. Causally faithful routed-circuit decompositions
open: Does every finite-dimensional unitary admit a routed-circuit representation in which the absence of a permitted directed route exactly captures each operational no-influence relation? If not, characterize the obstruction and exhibit a minimal counterexample.
status: The lattice-theoretic characterization of September 2026 advances ordinary unitary causal decompositions, but universal faithful realization in the richer routed-circuit formalism remains a separate target, also developed through thesis and workshop work. Key works: Tein van der Lugt and Robin Lorenz (2026), *Unitary causal decompositions: a characterisation via lattice theory*, arXiv:2508.11762; DOI:10.22331/q-2026-09-30-2218. Tein van der Lugt (2025), *Causal and Compositional Structure in Quantum Theory*, doctoral thesis, DOI:10.5287/ORA-VQ7OPD7AP. Augustin Vanrietvelde, Hlér Kristjánsson, and Jonathan Barrett (2021), *Routed Quantum Circuits*, arXiv:2011.08120.
solved_when: Either a universal construction realizing every finite-dimensional unitary as a causally faithful routed circuit is given, or a counterexample is exhibited together with a characterization of the obstruction.
why: A solution would connect experimentally meaningful causal independence to compositional circuit structure without introducing fictitious causal paths.
key_works: Tein van der Lugt and Robin Lorenz (2026), *Unitary causal decompositions: a characterisation via lattice theory*, arXiv:2508.11762; DOI:10.22331/q-2026-09-30-2218. Tein van der Lugt (2025), *Causal and Compositional Structure in Quantum Theory*, doctoral thesis, DOI:10.5287/ORA-VQ7OPD7AP. Augustin Vanrietvelde, Hlér Kristjánsson, and Jonathan Barrett (2021), *Routed Quantum Circuits*, arXiv:2011.08120.

title: Spectral gap amplification without destroying locality
subfield: Computational complexity and quantum proof systems
open: Can a local Hamiltonian's promise gap be amplified to a constant fraction of its extensive energy scale without destroying locality or the relevant low-energy structure? Formally, is there an efficient reduction that achieves such spectral gap amplification while preserving bounded locality?
status: Open in the form needed for quantum PCP. October 2026 work addresses combinatorial soundness amplification, which is not a general spectral amplification theorem: Mitali Bafna, Quynh T. Nguyen, and Tina Zhang (2026), *Gap Amplification for Local Hamiltonians with Combinatorial Soundness*, arXiv:2610.04952.
solved_when: A procedure is given that amplifies the promise gap of a local Hamiltonian to a constant fraction of its extensive energy scale, via an efficient reduction that preserves bounded locality and the relevant low-energy structure.
why: It would supply a potential missing component of a quantum PCP proof; without it, current amplification techniques do not yield general spectral amplification.
key_works: Mitali Bafna, Quynh T. Nguyen, and Tina Zhang (2026), *Gap Amplification for Local Hamiltonians with Combinatorial Soundness*, arXiv:2610.04952.

title: Tight quantum triangle-finding bounds
subfield: Quantum query complexity and algebraic algorithms
open: What is the true bounded-error quantum query complexity of detecting a triangle in a graph given by its adjacency matrix? In particular, is the current upper bound tight, and how does the complexity scale with the sparsity of the graph?
status: Open. Improved and derandomized algorithms do not close the upper–lower-bound gap. Key works include Guanzhong Li and Lvzhou Li (2023), *Derandomization of quantum algorithm for triangle finding*, arXiv:2309.13268; François Le Gall and Shogo Nakajima (2015), *Quantum Algorithm for Triangle Finding in Sparse Graphs*, arXiv:1507.06878.
solved_when: Matching upper and lower bounds are established for the bounded-error quantum query complexity of triangle detection in the adjacency-matrix model, including tight dependence on graph sparsity.
why: Triangle finding is a central test case for quantum graph algorithms beyond unstructured search, and tight bounds here would sharpen our understanding of what speedups quantum queries offer for structured graph problems.
key_works: Guanzhong Li and Lvzhou Li (2023), *Derandomization of quantum algorithm for triangle finding*, arXiv:2309.13268; François Le Gall and Shogo Nakajima (2015), *Quantum Algorithm for Triangle Finding in Sparse Graphs*, arXiv:1507.06878.

title: Efficient nonabelian hidden subgroup algorithms for graph isomorphism
subfield: Quantum query complexity and algebraic algorithms
open: Can a quantum computer efficiently solve the hidden subgroup problem over the symmetric group for the instances produced by graph isomorphism? Concretely, this asks for an algorithm that overcomes the known measurement and postprocessing barriers that have blocked nonabelian Fourier sampling approaches.
status: Open. Abelian Fourier sampling and several nonabelian special cases have been analyzed but do not resolve these instances. See Childs and van Dam (2010), *Quantum algorithms for algebraic problems*, arXiv:0812.0380; DOI:10.1103/RevModPhys.82.1.
solved_when: An efficient (polynomial-time) quantum algorithm is given that solves the symmetric-group hidden subgroup instances arising from graph isomorphism, including efficient measurement of the relevant quantum states and efficient classical postprocessing of the measurement outcomes.
why: A solution would extend quantum algebraic speedups beyond the abelian group structures underlying factoring and discrete logarithms, and would place graph isomorphism in BQP.
key_works: Childs and van Dam (2010), *Quantum algorithms for algebraic problems*, arXiv:0812.0380; DOI:10.1103/RevModPhys.82.1.

title: Tight complexity under restricted unitary access
subfield: Quantum query complexity and algebraic algorithms
open: Classify natural search, estimation, and learning tasks when access permits only \(U\), rather than freely supplying \(U^\dagger\), controlled-\(U\), transpose, and conjugate operations.
status: A newly sharpened frontier. Recent separations show that familiar oracle conventions can hide essential computational resources, but a complete task-by-task classification is absent. Key works include Ewin Tang, John Wright, and Mark Zhandry (2026), *Quantum oracles, weak and strong*; and Blake Holman, Ronak Ramachandran, and Justin Yirka (2025), *Quantum Search with In-Place Queries*.
solved_when: A task-by-task classification of natural search, estimation, and learning tasks under \(U\)-only access is achieved, determining for each whether the restricted model incurs a complexity separation from the standard oracle model.
why: It makes algorithmic speedups meaningful for experimentally supplied quantum processes, where inverses, controlled versions, transposes, and conjugates may not be freely available.
key_works: Ewin Tang, John Wright, and Mark Zhandry (2026), *Quantum oracles, weak and strong*; Blake Holman, Ronak Ramachandran, and Justin Yirka (2025), *Quantum Search with In-Place Queries*.

title: Generic accuracy amplification for state and unitary synthesis
subfield: Quantum query complexity and algebraic algorithms
open: Which state-generation and unitary-synthesis complexity classes permit exponentially improved accuracy with only polynomial overhead? That is, for which such classes can the fidelity of an output state or implemented transformation be boosted, at a cost that grows only polynomially?
status: Open in general. Standard decision-problem amplification techniques do not automatically amplify the fidelity of an output state or implemented transformation. Related work appears in Bostanci et al. (2023), *Unitary Complexity and the Uhlmann Transformation Problem*, arXiv:2306.13073.
solved_when: A characterization exists of the state-generation and unitary-synthesis complexity classes that admit exponentially improved accuracy with only polynomial overhead (or a demonstration that such amplification fails for a class, with the accompanying separation).
why: Without generic amplification, small synthesis errors become an unaccounted resource when quantum algorithms are composed, so their accumulated effect escapes the complexity accounting.
key_works: Bostanci et al. (2023), *Unitary Complexity and the Uhlmann Transformation Problem*, arXiv:2306.13073.

title: Permanent-of-Gaussians conjecture
open: Is it average-case hard, for random matrices with independent complex Gaussian entries, to approximate the permanent to the precision and success probability required for boson-sampling hardness? A formal answer would establish the appropriate average-case #P-hardness of this task, going beyond worst-case results.
status: Open since the original boson-sampling proposal. Worst-case permanent hardness is insufficient for this purpose. Key work: Scott Aaronson and Alex Arkhipov (2011), *The Computational Complexity of Linear Optics*, arXiv:1011.3245; DOI:10.1145/1993636.1993682.
solved_when: Approximating the permanent of independent complex Gaussian matrices, at the precision and success probability needed for approximate boson-sampling hardness, is proven hard on average (average-case #P-hardness established).
why: It supplies the missing complexity assumption behind robust linear-optical sampling advantage; without it, the claimed quantum advantage of boson sampling rests on an unproven average-case hardness foundation.
key_works: Scott Aaronson and Alex Arkhipov (2011), *The Computational Complexity of Linear Optics*, arXiv:1011.3245; DOI:10.1145/1993636.1993682.

title: Sharp loss and distinguishability boundaries in photonic sampling
open: When photons are lost, partially distinguishable, or unevenly squeezed, at what point does photonic sampling stop being a plausible quantum-advantage experiment and become efficiently classically simulable? Formally, determine the tight simulable-versus-hard boundaries as photon survival probability, distinguishability, squeezing strength, and mode count scale together.
status: Numerous sufficient simulation regimes and hardness regimes are known, but their boundaries do not meet, so they do not yet form a complete phase diagram. Key works include Grier et al. (2022), *The Complexity of Bipartite Gaussian Boson Sampling*, DOI:10.22331/q-2022-11-28-863, and Hamilton et al. (2017), *Gaussian Boson Sampling*.
solved_when: A complete phase diagram is given in which the sufficient simulation regimes and the plausibly-hard regimes meet at sharp boundaries across the joint scaling of photon survival, distinguishability, squeezing, and mode count.
why: It identifies which component improvements in photonic devices actually preserve computational hardness, telling experimentalists where quantum advantage survives realistic imperfections.
key_works: Grier et al. (2022), *The Complexity of Bipartite Gaussian Boson Sampling*, DOI:10.22331/q-2022-11-28-863; Hamilton et al. (2017), *Gaussian Boson Sampling*.

title: Efficient certification of hard sampling distributions
open: Can we efficiently certify that a quantum device's outputs are close to a specified hard sampling distribution, using feasible classical computation and samples, under explicit restrictions strong enough to make certification possible but weak enough to exclude realistic spoofers?
status: Open as a general practical certification problem; efficient tests usually certify selected statistics, assumptions, or restricted alternatives. Key works: Bouland et al. (2018), *Quantum Supremacy and the Complexity of Random Circuit Sampling*, arXiv:1803.04402; Aaronson and Arkhipov (2011), *The Computational Complexity of Linear Optics*. Related to property testing with computationally bounded adversaries.
solved_when: A certification procedure exists whose classical computation and sample cost are feasible, with explicit restrictions stated on the sampler/adversary that both enable certification and rule out realistic spoofing strategies.
why: A sampler's apparent complexity is not evidence that it sampled the intended distribution, so quantum advantage claims lack grounding until such certification exists.
key_works: Bouland et al. (2018), *Quantum Supremacy and the Complexity of Random Circuit Sampling*, arXiv:1803.04402; Aaronson and Arkhipov (2011), *The Computational Complexity of Linear Optics*.

title: Low-temperature mixing times of quantum Gibbs samplers
open: Can we prove useful mixing-time bounds for quantum Gibbs samplers on explicit noncommuting many-body Hamiltonians in the low-temperature regime? That is, establish quantitative rapid-mixing guarantees even at temperatures where correlations and metastability already make classical sampling difficult.
status: Efficiently implementable generators satisfying exact detailed balance exist — see Chi-Fang Chen, Michael J. Kastoryano, and András Gilyén (2023; revised 2025), *An efficient and exact noncommutative quantum Gibbs sampler*, arXiv:2311.09207 — but their existence does not imply rapid mixing for arbitrary low-temperature systems.
solved_when: A proof is given that an efficiently implementable quantum Gibbs sampler with exact detailed balance mixes rapidly — with explicit, quantitative mixing-time bounds — for explicit noncommuting many-body Hamiltonians at low temperature.
why: State preparation can dominate the cost of otherwise efficient simulation, so genuine mixing bounds would remove the main bottleneck in quantum Gibbs-sampling pipelines.
key_works: Chi-Fang Chen, Michael J. Kastoryano, and András Gilyén (2023; revised 2025), *An efficient and exact noncommutative quantum Gibbs sampler*, arXiv:2311.09207.

title: End-to-end Gibbs-sampling advantage for frustrated magnets
open: Can a quantum device prepare and measure the thermal state of a specified frustrated magnet at lower total cost than any classical approach, with the accounting including mixing, initialization, error correction, and observable estimation?
status: This is an application-level target, not a consequence of having an efficient Lindbladian implementation; an efficient and exact noncommutative quantum Gibbs sampler exists (Chen, Kastoryano, and Gilyén (2023/2025), *An efficient and exact noncommutative quantum Gibbs sampler*, arXiv:2311.09207), but the end-to-end advantage remains undemonstrated.
solved_when: An end-to-end demonstration shows the specified frustrated magnet's Gibbs state can be prepared and measured — covering mixing, initialization, error correction, and observable estimation — at a total cost beating classical methods in the finite-temperature regimes of interest.
why: It could resolve finite-temperature regimes of frustrated magnets that reliable classical sampling cannot reach, where the Monte Carlo sign problem blocks standard methods.
key_works: Chen, Kastoryano, and Gilyén (2023/2025), *An efficient and exact noncommutative quantum Gibbs sampler*, arXiv:2311.09207.

title: Certifiable initial overlap for phase estimation
open: Can we efficiently certify a useful lower bound on a prepared state's overlap with the target eigenstate, without first solving the hard spectral problem itself? Formally: given a prepared state and a Hamiltonian, produce a verifiable lower bound on the overlap using resources substantially less than those needed for full phase estimation of the spectrum.
status: System-specific heuristics and bounds exist, but a broadly useful certification procedure for strongly correlated chemistry remains missing. Related work includes Joonho Lee et al. (2022/2023), *Is there evidence for exponential quantum advantage in quantum chemistry?*, arXiv:2208.02199; the problem also connects to a posteriori certification in numerical eigenvalue problems.
solved_when: An efficient certification procedure exists that outputs a certified lower bound on the initial overlap for broadly relevant instances, including strongly correlated chemistry systems, where no such procedure is currently available.
why: Resource estimates for quantum phase estimation become misleading when they assume an unverified state-preparation success probability; a certified lower bound makes these cost estimates trustworthy.
key_works: Joonho Lee et al. (2022/2023), *Is there evidence for exponential quantum advantage in quantum chemistry?*, arXiv:2208.02199.

title: Reliable ground-state preparation for strongly correlated instances
open: Can we prepare ground states of strongly correlated molecules or materials with guarantees that hold across an entire specified class of instances, rather than only on isolated favorable cases? More precisely, the goal is a preparation method with demonstrated scaling guarantees or reproducible success over a defined class of strongly correlated systems.
status: Adiabatic, variational, filtering, and phase-estimation approaches currently offer partial solutions, and no unrestricted efficient algorithm is expected. Related considerations include multireference electronic structure and avoiding metastable optimization solutions. Key works: Lee et al. (2022/2023), *Is there evidence for exponential quantum advantage in quantum chemistry?*, arXiv:2208.02199; Markus Reiher et al. (2017), *Elucidating Reaction Mechanisms on Quantum Computers*.
solved_when: A state-preparation method exists whose scaling guarantees or reproducible success have been demonstrated across a specified class of strongly correlated molecules or materials, not merely on individual favorable instances.
why: It converts raw Hamiltonian-simulation capability into dependable scientific calculations; without reliability across a class of instances, quantum simulations of strongly correlated systems cannot be trusted as a scientific tool.
key_works: Lee et al. (2022/2023), *Is there evidence for exponential quantum advantage in quantum chemistry?*, arXiv:2208.02199; Markus Reiher et al. (2017), *Elucidating Reaction Mechanisms on Quantum Computers*.

title: Long-time local-observable simulation beyond generic light cones
open: Can verifiable physical promises — such as hydrodynamic behavior or rapid mixing — be leveraged to estimate local observables of a lattice Hamiltonian at long times, at a cost substantially below that of generic full-state simulation?
status: Nearly optimal general lattice-evolution algorithms exist; favorable long-time reductions require additional promises and are not generic fast-forwarding. Key work: Jeongwan Haah, Matthew Hastings, Robin Kothari, and Guang Hao Low (2018/2020), *Quantum algorithm for simulating real time evolution of lattice Hamiltonians*, arXiv:1801.03922.
solved_when: An algorithm is given that, under an explicitly stated physical promise (e.g., hydrodynamic or mixing), estimates long-time local observables with cost asymptotically below the generic full-state simulation cost for the same Hamiltonian and time.
why: In many physical systems, transport and equilibration properties matter more than reconstructing the entire wavefunction, so cheap local-observable estimates at long times would deliver the physically relevant quantity without paying for the full state.
key_works: Jeongwan Haah, Matthew Hastings, Robin Kothari, and Guang Hao Low (2018/2020), *Quantum algorithm for simulating real time evolution of lattice Hamiltonians*, arXiv:1801.03922.

title: Certified truncation of unbounded bosonic and gauge degrees of freedom
open: Can we derive practical, state-dependent bounds on how large a bosonic or gauge-field mode cutoff must be for a simulation to faithfully reproduce the physics, including regimes with particle production and long-time dynamics? More formally, the goal is a certification that truncating the infinite-dimensional Hilbert space to a given cutoff incurs bounded, quantifiable error for the interacting models of interest.
status: Rigorous truncation bounds exist only for selected models and regimes, and universal small cutoffs cannot be assumed. Key works: Stephen Jordan, Keith Lee, and John Preskill (2012), *Quantum Algorithms for Quantum Field Theories*, arXiv:1111.3633; Christian Bauer et al. (2022), *Quantum Simulation for High Energy Physics*, arXiv:2204.03381.
solved_when: A method exists for deriving state-dependent truncation bounds applicable to interacting bosonic and gauge-field simulations, with control over error in regimes involving particle production and long-time dynamics.
why: It determines whether a finite qubit encoding accurately represents an infinite-dimensional physical system — the prerequisite for any trustworthy quantum simulation of such field theories.
key_works: Stephen Jordan, Keith Lee, and John Preskill (2012), *Quantum Algorithms for Quantum Field Theories*, arXiv:1111.3633; Christian Bauer et al. (2022), *Quantum Simulation for High Energy Physics*, arXiv:2204.03381.

title: Useful fault-tolerant simulation of open many-body systems
open: Can we demonstrate a genuine, practical quantum-computing advantage for simulating a specified driven-dissipative many-body system once the full overhead of the pipeline is paid for? That is, for a concrete open-system model, show a favorable end-to-end crossover accounting for the cost of implementing the Lindbladian, the mixing to steady state, the required measurements, and fault tolerance.
status: Polynomial simulation theorems for open many-body systems are established — notably Martin Kliesch, Thomas Barthel, Christian Gogolin, Michael Kastoryano, and Jens Eisert (2011), *A dissipative quantum Church-Turing theorem*, arXiv:1105.3986 — but these asymptotic results do not establish a favorable scientific crossover for practical advantage.
solved_when: A specified driven-dissipative many-body model is simulated end to end — including Lindbladian implementation, steady-state mixing, measurement, and fault tolerance — with a demonstrable practical advantage over the best classical alternative for the same task.
why: It unlocks quantitative calculations of dissipative phases, transport, and nonequilibrium steady states that are out of reach classically.
key_works: Martin Kliesch, Thomas Barthel, Christian Gogolin, Michael Kastoryano, and Jens Eisert (2011), *A dissipative quantum Church-Turing theorem*, arXiv:1105.3986.

title: Quantum-assisted nitrogenase reaction kinetics
open: Can quantum computation deliver a validated reaction pathway for biological nitrogen fixation, not just benchmark electronic energies? Concretely, this means resolving competing intermediates, environmental effects, and the rate-determining steps of the full catalytic mechanism.
status: This is a downstream application gap beyond existing FeMoco resource estimates; accurate energies alone do not determine a complete catalytic mechanism. Key works: Reiher et al. (2017), *Elucidating Reaction Mechanisms on Quantum Computers*, arXiv:1605.03590; Vera von Burg et al. (2021), *Quantum computing enhanced computational catalysis*, arXiv:2007.14460.
solved_when: A quantum-assisted computation yields a complete nitrogenase reaction pathway that accounts for competing intermediates and environmental effects and identifies the rate-determining steps, with validation against experimental kinetics.
why: It turns resource estimates for FeMoco-style energy calculations into actual mechanistic understanding of the catalyst, bridging quantum computation and real catalysis rather than producing benchmark numbers.
key_works: Reiher et al. (2017), *Elucidating Reaction Mechanisms on Quantum Computers*, arXiv:1605.03590; Vera von Burg et al. (2021), *Quantum computing enhanced computational catalysis*, arXiv:2007.14460.

title: Validated quantum advantage in industrial catalysis
open: Can a quantum calculation change a real catalyst-selection or process-design decision more accurately or more cheaply than the strongest available classical workflow?
status: Detailed catalytic case studies and resource estimates exist, but decision-level advantage requires preparation, uncertainty, and experimental validation together. Key work: Vera von Burg et al. (2021), *Quantum computing enhanced computational catalysis*, arXiv:2007.14460.
solved_when: A demonstrated case exists in which a quantum computation, with full state preparation, uncertainty quantification, and experimental validation, alters a concrete catalyst-selection or process-design decision and outperforms the best classical workflow in accuracy or cost.
why: It would establish an economically meaningful chemistry use case for quantum computing, moving the field beyond abstract complexity claims.
key_works: Vera von Burg et al. (2021), *Quantum computing enhanced computational catalysis*, arXiv:2007.14460.

title: Coupled electronic–nuclear nonadiabatic dynamics
open: Can we simulate a chemically important nonadiabatic process end-to-end, with errors under control at every level — electronic correlation, nuclear motion, conical-intersection behavior, and the measured reaction observables?
status: Electronic-structure algorithms are more mature than complete coupled-dynamics workflows; any claimed favorable scaling must include the costs of initial-state preparation and readout, not just the core simulation. Key works: Lee et al. (2022/2023), *Is there evidence for exponential quantum advantage in quantum chemistry?*, arXiv:2208.02199; Jordan, Lee, and Preskill (2012), *Quantum Algorithms for Quantum Field Theories*.
solved_when: A chemically important nonadiabatic process is simulated as a complete coupled electron–nuclear dynamics workflow in which the errors in electronic correlation, nuclear motion, conical-intersection behavior, and reaction observables are all controlled, and the favorable scaling accounts for initial-state preparation and readout as well as the dynamics itself.
why: It targets photochemistry and reaction dynamics — phenomena that static energy calculations fundamentally cannot capture.
key_works: Lee et al. (2022/2023), *Is there evidence for exponential quantum advantage in quantum chemistry?*, arXiv:2208.02199; Jordan, Lee, and Preskill (2012), *Quantum Algorithms for Quantum Field Theories*.

title: Real-frequency response of strongly correlated materials
open: Can we obtain controlled spectral functions and transport responses for strongly correlated materials in regimes where analytic continuation from imaginary time and the entanglement growth of classical real-time simulation both fail? Formally, the goal is a construction yielding such real-frequency quantities with quantified error control.
status: Ground-state and imaginary-time benchmarks are substantial (e.g., LeBlanc et al. (2015), *Solutions of the Two Dimensional Hubbard Model*, arXiv:1505.02290; Haah et al. (2018/2020), *Quantum algorithm for simulating real time evolution of lattice Hamiltonians*), but reliable long-time, real-frequency results remain model- and regime-dependent.
solved_when: Controlled spectral functions and transport responses are obtained in regimes where analytic continuation and classical real-time entanglement growth are major obstacles, with reliability no longer model- and regime-dependent.
why: These quantities are directly comparable with spectroscopy and transport experiments, closing the gap between benchmark calculations and measured material properties.
key_works: LeBlanc et al. (2015), *Solutions of the Two Dimensional Hubbard Model*, arXiv:1505.02290; Haah et al. (2018/2020), *Quantum algorithm for simulating real time evolution of lattice Hamiltonians*.

title: Finite-density QCD with controlled state preparation
open: Can we prepare and measure finite-baryon-density gauge-theory states on a quantum computer with controlled, verifiable quality? Specifically, can such state preparation be achieved with demonstrated resource scaling, gauge fidelity, and continuum extrapolation?
status: Quantum-simulation proposals address the classical sign problem conceptually, but avoiding that problem does not automatically make state preparation efficient. A relevant reference is Christian Bauer et al. (2022), *Quantum Simulation for High Energy Physics*, arXiv:2204.03381.
solved_when: A preparation-and-measurement protocol for finite-baryon-density gauge-theory states is demonstrated with explicit resource scaling, quantified gauge fidelity, and a performed continuum extrapolation.
why: It would give access to dense strongly interacting matter beyond the reach of standard Monte Carlo methods.
key_works: Christian Bauer et al. (2022), *Quantum Simulation for High Energy Physics*, arXiv:2204.03381.

title: Quantum preconditioners with honest implementation cost
open: Can we construct preconditioners for quantum linear-system solvers whose benefit survives an honest accounting of costs? Formally, the total gate complexity of the solver — including the preconditioner's construction, block encoding, application, and data-access costs — should improve once all these are counted.
status: General matrix-transformation machinery is established via quantum singular value transformation (András Gilyén, Yuan Su, Guang Hao Low, and Nathan Wiebe (2019), *Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for quantum matrix arithmetics*, arXiv:1806.01838); however, a classical preconditioner is not automatically an efficient quantum oracle, so no such honestly cheap quantum preconditioner is known.
solved_when: A preconditioner is constructed and proven to reduce the quantum linear-system solver's total gate complexity after including its construction, block encoding, application, and data-access costs.
why: Condition-number dependence can erase nominal linear-algebra speedups, so an honestly cheap preconditioner is what makes the quantum advantage real rather than notional.
key_works: András Gilyén, Yuan Su, Guang Hao Low, and Nathan Wiebe (2019), *Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for quantum matrix arithmetics*, arXiv:1806.01838.

title: Output-aware quantum linear algebra
open: For which applications can a quantum linear-system solver deliver an end-to-end advantage, once the cost of extracting the desired classical output from the solution state is accounted for? More formally, classify the settings where the classical output of interest can be recovered cheaply enough that quantum state preparation and linear-system solving still beat classical alternatives overall.
status: Preparing a solution state is well understood under suitable access assumptions, but recovering a full classical solution generally changes the complexity. Key framework: Gilyén et al. (2019), *Quantum singular value transformation and beyond*, arXiv:1806.01838.
solved_when: A classification exists of applications for which the desired classical output is extractable at a cost low enough that the quantum pipeline — state preparation plus linear-system solving — yields an end-to-end advantage over classical methods.
why: It prevents state-output quantum algorithms from being misrepresented as fast drop-in replacements for arbitrary classical solvers, clarifying where genuine end-to-end speedups exist.
key_works: Gilyén et al. (2019), *Quantum singular value transformation and beyond*, arXiv:1806.01838.

title: Nonlinear differential equations beyond strong dissipativity
open: Can quantum algorithms for nonlinear differential equations achieve provable speedups in regimes beyond strongly dissipative dynamics, or is there a sharp barrier there? More precisely, either extend Carleman-based techniques to useful nonlinearity and dissipation regimes where they currently fail, or prove matching limitations showing such guarantees are impossible.
status: Carleman-based algorithms establish quantum advantages in restricted dissipative regimes, per Jin-Peng Liu et al. (2021), *Efficient quantum algorithm for dissipative nonlinear differential equations*, arXiv:2011.03185; unrestricted nonlinear evolution cannot inherit those guarantees.
solved_when: An algorithm (or impossibility result) covers nonlinear ODEs outside the strongly dissipative, weakly nonlinear regime where current methods apply, with runtime guarantees comparable to those achieved in the dissipative case — or, dually, a proof that unrestricted nonlinear evolution cannot inherit those guarantees.
why: It decides whether quantum methods are applicable to realistic nonlinear dynamics or only to carefully conditioned examples, which determines their practical relevance for simulation.
key_works: Jin-Peng Liu et al. (2021), *Efficient quantum algorithm for dissipative nonlinear differential equations*, arXiv:2011.03185.

title: Stiff nonlinear dynamics with certified quantum truncation
open: Can quantum algorithms for stiff nonlinear differential equations retain a genuine speedup once the costs of solution growth, normalization, and output estimation are all accounted for, through adaptive truncation and conditioning strategies?
status: Existing nonlinear quantum algorithms, such as Liu et al. (2021), *Efficient quantum algorithm for dissipative nonlinear differential equations*, arXiv:2011.03185, expose these dependencies but do not solve general stiffness and adaptive-error control.
solved_when: Adaptive truncation and conditioning strategies for stiff nonlinear equations are developed whose cost analysis includes solution growth, normalization, and output estimation, and which still preserve a quantum advantage over the best classical methods for general stiff instances.
why: Stiffness pervades chemistry, plasma physics, and multiscale engineering, so a certified, end-to-end quantum method here would target simulation problems of real practical weight rather than idealized instances.
key_works: Liu et al. (2021), *Efficient quantum algorithm for dissipative nonlinear differential equations*, arXiv:2011.03185.

title: Practical amplitude-estimation advantage for Monte Carlo
open: Can a quantum computer demonstrate an end-to-end advantage on a consequential Monte Carlo expectation-estimation problem, covering the full workflow from reversible sampling through payoff evaluation, fault tolerance, and final statistical confidence?
status: Quadratic query improvements for Monte Carlo are established, following Ashley Montanaro (2015), *Quantum speedup of Monte Carlo methods*, arXiv:1504.06987; however, their wall-clock and energy advantages are not automatic, a concern emphasized by Ryan Babbush et al. (2021), *Focus beyond quadratic speedups for error-corrected quantum advantage*.
solved_when: A full-workflow demonstration is achieved — reversible sampling, payoff evaluation, fault tolerance, and statistical confidence all included — showing a practical wall-clock or energy advantage, not merely the established quadratic query improvement.
why: Monte Carlo estimation is ubiquitous, but the known quadratic speedup can be consumed by the cost of expensive coherent oracles, so the practical benefit remains unproven.
key_works: Ashley Montanaro (2015), *Quantum speedup of Monte Carlo methods*, arXiv:1504.06987; Ryan Babbush et al. (2021), *Focus beyond quadratic speedups for error-corrected quantum advantage*.

title: Useful quantum backtracking on structured search
open: Can quantum backtracking deliver a genuine practical advantage on real structured search problems once the full cost of building the search tree and checking constraints reversibly is paid? In other words, identify and demonstrate specific structured constraint families where quantum backtracking beats strong classical heuristics under these fully charged conditions.
status: Quantum speedups in tree size are established, as in Ashley Montanaro (2015/2016), *Quantum walk speedup of backtracking algorithms*, arXiviv:1509.02374; practical advantage depends on the actual tree and implementation overhead.
solved_when: Concrete structured constraint families are identified and demonstrated where quantum backtracking outperforms strong classical heuristics after reversible constraint checking and search-tree construction are charged.
why: It would connect quantum search to real combinatorial workloads rather than idealized tree-size abstractions, showing where the established speedups survive practical implementation overhead.
key_works: Ashley Montanaro (2015/2016), *Quantum walk speedup of backtracking algorithms*, arXiv:1509.02374.

title: QAOA beyond overlap-gap barriers
open: Can the quantum approximate optimization algorithm be made to beat classical average-case hardness barriers on structured optimization problems? In particular, what problem structure, depth scaling, or algorithmic modification yields a provable, useful approximation improvement outside known overlap-gap obstructions?
status: Low-depth barriers and landscape results rule out several naive routes, and exceeding these barriers is not established by successful small-instance optimization. Key work: Mark Xin Hong Goh (2026), *The overlap gap property and its implication for the quantum approximate optimisation algorithm*, doctoral thesis.
solved_when: A rigorous guarantee of approximation improvement beyond the overlap-gap thresholds is demonstrated, at an explicit depth scaling, on a defined problem distribution.
why: It would separate meaningful optimization progress from parameter-fitting demonstrations on small instances.
key_works: Mark Xin Hong Goh (2026), *The overlap gap property and its implication for the quantum approximate optimisation algorithm*, doctoral thesis.

title: Trainable, expressive, non-dequantizable variational models
subfield: Quantum machine learning and learning quantum systems
open: Can we exhibit a variational quantum model family that is simultaneously useful in practice, efficiently trainable, expressive enough for its task, and not efficiently replaceable by a comparably informed classical model?
status: These properties have been studied individually, but satisfying all three at once with convincing scaling evidence remains a central gap in quantum machine learning theory. Key work: Martin Larocca et al. (2025), *Barren Plateaus in Variational Quantum Computing*, arXiv:2405.00781; DOI:10.1038/s42254-025-00813-9.
solved_when: A model family is exhibited that demonstrably achieves all three properties — efficient trainability, sufficient expressivity for its task, and no efficient classical surrogate with comparable information access — supported by convincing scaling evidence.
why: It avoids the common tradeoff in which quantum advantage is sacrificed simply to eliminate barren plateaus during training.
key_works: Martin Larocca et al. (2025), *Barren Plateaus in Variational Quantum Computing*, arXiv:2405.00781; DOI:10.1038/s42254-025-00813-9.

title: Noise-resilient trainability at useful circuit depth
subfield: Quantum machine learning and learning quantum systems
open: Can a quantum machine-learning circuit retain an informative gradient — or some alternative efficient training signal — at the circuit depths required for a practical advantage, when realistic device noise and finite sampling budgets are present?
status: Noise-free initialization fixes do not solve the noise-induced loss of training signal. Key works: Jarrod McClean et al. (2018), *Barren plateaus in quantum neural network training landscapes*, arXiv:1803.11173; Larocca et al. (2025), *Barren Plateaus in Variational Quantum Computing*.
solved_when: A training method is demonstrated that maintains informative gradients or an equivalent efficient training signal, under measured noise and finite sampling budgets, at circuit depths needed for a target advantage.
why: Training can fail before the underlying model loses formal expressive power, so noise — not expressivity — becomes the binding constraint on useful variational quantum computing.
key_works: Jarrod McClean et al. (2018), *Barren plateaus in quantum neural network training landscapes*, arXiv:1803.11173; Larocca et al. (2025), *Barren Plateaus in Variational Quantum Computing*.

title: Adaptive generalization from quantum experimental data
subfield: Quantum machine learning and learning quantum systems
open: Can a quantum experimental learner that adaptively chooses its measurements, reuses learned representations, and encounters distribution shift be guaranteed to generalize? Formally, derive sharp generalization and sample-complexity bounds for such an adaptive quantum learner.
status: Quantum learning advantages exist for selected data models, as shown in Hsin-Yuan Huang et al. (2022), *Quantum advantage in learning from experiments*, arXiv:2112.00778; DOI:10.1126/science.abn7293, but they do not provide a universal adaptive generalization theory.
solved_when: A generalization and sample-complexity theory is derived that covers adaptive measurement selection, representation reuse, and distribution shift, with sharp quantitative guarantees.
why: It makes learned scientific predictions trustworthy outside the training experiment.
key_works: Hsin-Yuan Huang et al. (2022), *Quantum advantage in learning from experiments*, arXiv:2112.00778; DOI:10.1126/science.abn7293.

title: Quantum kernel advantage under matched data access
subfield: Quantum machine learning and learning quantum systems
open: Can a quantum kernel method provably learn something a classical learner cannot, when both are charged the same way for data loading, sampling access, preprocessing, and model selection? More precisely, establish a learning separation that survives dequantization-style attacks under matched data-access assumptions.
status: Dequantization results have shown that apparently quantum speedups can depend on unequal access assumptions, as in Ewin Tang (2019), *A quantum-inspired classical algorithm for recommendation systems*, arXiv:1807.04271; related work includes M. Cerezo et al. (2021), *Variational Quantum Algorithms*, kernel-method lower bounds, and sample-and-query data structures.
solved_when: A rigorous separation (or matching lower bound) is proved between quantum kernel methods and classical learners under identical access costs for data loading, sampling access, preprocessing, and model selection.
why: It separates a genuine computational advantage from a mere input-model advantage, so claimed quantum learning speedups can be trusted rather than artifacts of unequal access.
key_works: Ewin Tang (2019), *A quantum-inspired classical algorithm for recommendation systems*, arXiv:1807.04271; M. Cerezo et al. (2021), *Variational Quantum Algorithms*.

title: Practical quantum processing of massive classical streams
subfield: Quantum machine learning and learning quantum systems
open: Can a quantum processor deliver a measured end-to-end advantage on a streaming task over massive classical data, counting every resource from sketch construction and coherent processing through repeated inference to the final model output?
status: Haimeng Zhao et al. (2026), *Exponential quantum advantage in processing massive classical data*, establishes important model-specific exponential advantages; practical wall-clock advantage remains a separate, unachieved target.
solved_when: A classical-data streaming task is experimentally realized in which the measured total-resource cost — including sketch construction, coherent processing, repeated inference, and model output — is lower than that of the best classical alternative.
why: Success would make quantum learning relevant even when the input data does not originate in a quantum experiment, removing a key practical barrier to applying quantum machine learning to everyday classical data.
key_works: Haimeng Zhao et al. (2026), *Exponential quantum advantage in processing massive classical data*.

title: Quantum-data learning advantage after storage and error correction
subfield: Quantum machine learning and learning quantum systems
open: Can a quantum learner retain its sample-complexity advantage once the full overhead of preserving, routing, and jointly processing quantum training data is paid for in the experiment? More precisely, can an end-to-end demonstration show the advantage survives the complete experimental system, not just the idealized measurement step?
status: Exponential measurement advantages are established for selected tasks, notably in Huang et al. (2022), *Quantum advantage in learning from experiments*, arXiv:2112.00778; however, sample count alone does not account for the complete experimental system, and no demonstration yet includes storage and processing overheads.
solved_when: An experimental demonstration shows a quantum learner's sample advantage persisting after the costs of quantum data storage, routing, and joint processing are included in the complete experimental system.
why: It determines whether quantum memory is economically justified as part of a learning pipeline.
key_works: Huang et al. (2022), *Quantum advantage in learning from experiments*, arXiv:2112.00778.

title: Efficient measurement of difficult many-body observables
subfield: Quantum machine learning and learning quantum systems
open: Can we design measurement ensembles, implementable on near-term hardware, that estimate physically important nonlocal many-body observables with manageable sample complexity in cases where standard classical-shadow constructions have large shadow norms? Equivalently, find ensembles whose shadow norm for such observables is small without sacrificing experimental feasibility.
status: Classical shadows do not make every observable efficiently estimable; favorable measurement design remains task-specific. The framework originates with Huang, Kueng, and Preskill (2020), *Predicting Many Properties of a Quantum System from Very Few Measurements*, arXiv:2002.08953.
solved_when: A concrete, experimentally implementable measurement ensemble is identified, together with a sample-complexity bound showing that physically important nonlocal observables with large standard shadow norms can be estimated efficiently using that ensemble.
why: Measurement cost can dominate otherwise efficient state preparation, so without such designs the practical advantage of efficient preparation is lost at readout.
key_works: Huang, Kueng, and Preskill (2020), *Predicting Many Properties of a Quantum System from Very Few Measurements*, arXiv:2002.08953.

title: Exact distillation rates for Werner-state families
subfield: Quantum information, entanglement, and channel capacities
open: What is the optimal asymptotic singlet-distillation rate for each state in the distillable region of the specified Werner-state families, and how much do collective processing protocols improve on that rate? Formally, determine the complete rate function over the distillable region, including the exact gain achievable with collective operations.
status: Distillability and distillation rate are different questions, and the question of rate remains open: recent finite-copy threshold results do not determine the complete rate function. Key work: Bharti, Gajjala, and Haug (2026), *Two-copy nondistillability of Werner states*, arXiv:2607.24479.
solved_when: The full asymptotic singlet-distillation rate function is determined across the distillable region of the specified Werner-state families, quantifying the benefit of collective processing.
why: It quantifies the usable entanglement content of these states rather than merely deciding whether some entanglement can be extracted at all.
key_works: Bharti, Gajjala, and Haug (2026), *Two-copy nondistillability of Werner states*, arXiv:2607.24479.

title: Exact reliability and strong-converse exponents
subfield: Quantum information, entanglement, and channel capacities
open: For important quantum channels, can we determine the exact error-decay (reliability) and success-decay (strong-converse) exponents as functions of the rate, rather than merely showing that they decay exponentially?
status: A September 2026 preprint — Salman Beigi and Marco Tomamichel (2026), *Strong Converses for Quantum Channel Capacities from Blowing-Up Lemmata*, arXiv:2609.11771 — claims general exponential strong converses for finite-dimensional memoryless capacities; exact exponent functions remain a finer question.
solved_when: Exact exponent functions of the rate are identified for the relevant quantum channels, matching achievable lower bounds and converse upper bounds.
why: Converts asymptotic capacity characterizations into quantitative finite-blocklength guidance.
key_works: Salman Beigi and Marco Tomamichel (2026), *Strong Converses for Quantum Channel Capacities from Blowing-Up Lemmata*, arXiv:2609.11771.

title: Publicly verifiable quantum computation from weaker assumptions
open: Can a classical verifier publicly check an arbitrary quantum computation without relying on quantum indistinguishability obfuscation? More precisely, can publicly verifiable classical verification of general quantum computations be based on substantially weaker or better-understood assumptions?
status: New September 2026 constructions provide public verification under strong assumptions; existence under those assumptions is not the remaining gap. Key work: Alexandru Gheorghiu, Aparna Gupte, Vojtěch Havlíček, and Yunchao Liu (2026), *Verifiable Quantum Advantage and Computation via Quantum Circuit Obfuscation*, arXiv:2609.40289.
solved_when: A construction is given that achieves publicly verifiable classical verification of general quantum computations under assumptions substantially weaker or better understood than quantum indistinguishability obfuscation.
why: It would weaken the cryptographic foundations needed for auditable quantum cloud services, replacing a strong and poorly understood assumption with more standard ones.
key_works: Alexandru Gheorghiu, Aparna Gupte, Vojtěch Havlíček, and Yunchao Liu (2026), *Verifiable Quantum Advantage and Computation via Quantum Circuit Obfuscation*, arXiv:2609.40289.

title: Practical classical verification with realistic constants
open: Can a useful quantum workload be classically verified end-to-end — prover, verifier, communication, and fault-tolerance overhead included — with constants small enough that the workload's quantum advantage survives? Formally, this asks for an implementation whose measured costs, not just asymptotic scaling, preserve the advantage of the verified computation.
status: Quasilinear asymptotic resource constructions were reported in September 2026 (Finn Holler and Anand Natarajan (2026), *Classical Verification of Quantum Computation with Quasilinear Resources, from Compiled Nonlocal Games*, arXiv:2609.38060, building on Urmila Mahadev (2018), *Classical Verification of Quantum Computations*, arXiv:1804.01082); practical constants and complete systems remain separate open questions.
solved_when: A working implementation of classical verification for a useful quantum workload exists, with measured prover, verifier, communication, and fault-tolerance costs that do not destroy the workload's advantage.
why: It turns classical verification from an asymptotic possibility into a usable tool, since polynomial or quasilinear overhead alone can still swamp a real quantum speedup.
key_works: Finn Holler and Anand Natarajan (2026), *Classical Verification of Quantum Computation with Quasilinear Resources, from Compiled Nonlocal Games*, arXiv:2609.38060; Urmila Mahadev (2018), *Classical Verification of Quantum Computations*, arXiv:1804.01082.

title: Practical quantum fully homomorphic encryption
open: Can a quantum fully homomorphic encryption scheme evaluate useful quantum circuits with overhead low enough for real-world use? In particular, can the complete cost — key management, non-Clifford gate evaluation, noise accumulation, and decryption — be reduced and validated experimentally on circuits of genuine computational interest?
status: Cryptographic constructions exist, but compactness and polynomial complexity do not establish practical deployment. Key work: Urmila Mahadev (2017; revised 2023), *Classical Homomorphic Encryption for Quantum Circuits*, arXiv:1708.02130.
solved_when: A full experimental evaluation of homomorphically evaluating useful quantum circuits is demonstrated, measuring the complete overhead including key management, non-Clifford evaluation, noise, and decryption, with overheads reduced to levels supporting practical deployment.
why: It permits computation on encrypted quantum data without revealing it to the server, enabling delegated quantum computation on confidential inputs.
key_works: Urmila Mahadev (2017; revised 2023), *Classical Homomorphic Encryption for Quantum Circuits*, arXiv:1708.02130.

title: Noise-tolerant unclonable credentials
open: Can we build unclonable signing tokens or credentials whose security survives explicit storage noise, recovery operations, repeated verification, and device imperfections? Formally, the goal is to construct and demonstrate such tokens that remain unclonable under a realistic noisy-device model rather than idealized noiseless memory.
status: Memory-efficient cryptographic constructions advanced in 2026 with the work of Andrew Huang, Omri Shmueli, Vinod Vaikuntanathan, and Mark Zhandry (2026), *Unclonable Cryptography in Linear Quantum Memory*, CRYPTO 2026; however, asymptotically small quantum keys are not yet a complete noisy-device solution.
solved_when: A construction of unclonable signing tokens or credentials is given and demonstrated, with security surviving explicit storage noise, recovery operations, repeated verification, and device imperfections.
why: It would turn no-cloning-based cryptography from a theoretical possibility into usable persistent credentials.
key_works: Andrew Huang, Omri Shmueli, Vinod Vaikuntanathan, and Mark Zhandry (2026), *Unclonable Cryptography in Linear Quantum Memory*, CRYPTO 2026.

title: High-throughput cryptographically certified randomness
open: Can a quantum random-number generator be operated at a genuinely competitive bit rate while every output remains cryptographically certified — net of the costs of cryptographic challenges, seed consumption, finite-statistical analysis, hardware noise, and verification?
status: Single-device cryptographic certification protocols are established, notably Zvika Brakerski et al. (2018), *A Cryptographic Test of Quantumness and Certifiable Randomness from a Single Quantum Device*, arXiv:1804.00640; achieving useful operating rates and a complete security accounting remains an open engineering target.
solved_when: A working system achieves a positive, competitive net rate of certified random bits after fully accounting for cryptographic challenges, seed use, finite statistics, hardware noise, and verification costs.
why: It delivers verifiable randomness without requiring trust in the device's internal implementation.
key_works: Zvika Brakerski et al. (2018), *A Cryptographic Test of Quantumness and Certifiable Randomness from a Single Quantum Device*, arXiv:1804.00640.

title: Minimum realistic resources for RSA-2048 factoring
open: What is the minimum realistic resource cost — in physical qubits, runtime, energy, and reliability — required to factor an RSA-2048 modulus under explicitly measured hardware assumptions? A defensible answer would fix a best-achieved tradeoff among these quantities, anchored to characterized device parameters rather than idealized ones.
status: Estimates continue to improve. Gidney's 2025 sub-million-noisy-qubit proposal is a resource analysis, not an experimental factorization (Craig Gidney (2025), *How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers with less than a million noisy qubits*, arXiv:2505.15917).
solved_when: A resource analysis exists that specifies the physical-qubit count, runtime, energy, and reliability targets for factoring RSA-2048, with every assumption drawn from explicitly measured hardware parameters.
why: It grounds cryptographic migration timelines and quantum-hardware roadmaps in auditable cost estimates rather than speculation.
key_works: Craig Gidney (2025), *How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers with less than a million noisy qubits*, arXiv:2505.15917.

title: Honest quantum resource models for lattice cryptanalysis
open: Can we produce reproducible end-to-end quantum resource estimates for the leading quantum attacks on lattice-based cryptography? Such estimates should honestly account for coherent memory, reversible sieving, classical preprocessing, and error-correction overheads.
status: Current literature makes it easy to conflate algorithmic proposals with realistic lower-level costs, and refuted hidden-subgroup shortcuts — such as those exposed in Gupte, Ragavan, and Zhandry (2026), *The ePrint:2026/1591 Quantum Algorithm Does Not Solve DCP*, ePrint:2026/1693 — illustrate the need for independently checked analyses; Babbush et al. (2021), *Focus beyond quadratic speedups for error-corrected quantum advantage*, informs how error-correction overheads should be weighed.
solved_when: Reproducible end-to-end resource estimates exist for the leading quantum lattice attacks, covering coherent memory, reversible sieving, classical preprocessing, and error correction.
why: It separates meaningful quantum threats to lattice cryptography from analyses that rest on unsupported oracle-cost assumptions, directly informing which post-quantum parameters are actually needed.
key_works: Gupte, Ragavan, and Zhandry (2026), *The ePrint:2026/1591 Quantum Algorithm Does Not Solve DCP*, ePrint:2026/1693; Babbush et al. (2021), *Focus beyond quadratic speedups for error-corrected quantum advantage*.

title: Circuit-level single-shot decoding in practical qLDPC devices
open: Can single-shot decoding be made to work in a practical qLDPC device, where syndrome extraction uses realistic circuits, measurements are correlated, leakage is present, and classical latency is bounded? In other words, can a circuit-level implementation preserve the finite-size advantage that single-shot decoding promises in theory?
status: Single-shot decoding of good quantum LDPC codes is established theoretically (Shouzhen Gu et al. (2024), *Single-Shot Decoding of Good Quantum LDPC Codes*, arXiv:2306.12470; DOI:10.1007/s00220-024-04951-6), so the generic existence of single-shot decoders should not be relisted as open; the open question is the circuit-level, practical integration.
solved_when: An integrated demonstration of single-shot decoding on a qLDPC code under realistic syndrome circuits, measurement correlations, leakage, and bounded classical latency that provably (or demonstrably) retains a finite-size advantage over repeated-measurement alternatives.
why: It would cut the time spent on repeated syndrome measurements and simplify the classical control stack required for fault tolerance, making good qLDPC codes practical rather than merely theoretically decodable.
key_works: Shouzhen Gu et al. (2024), *Single-Shot Decoding of Good Quantum LDPC Codes*, arXiv:2306.12470; DOI:10.1007/s00220-024-04951-6.

title: Practical constants for good quantum locally testable codes
open: Can we pin down explicit, finite-size tradeoffs among rate, distance, check weight, soundness, and construction complexity for good quantum locally testable codes — that is, turn asymptotic existence into concrete, usable parameters?
status: A September 2026 preprint — William Gay and Fernando Granha Jeronimo (2026), *Asymptotically Good Quantum Locally Testable Codes*, arXiv:2609.20780 — claims asymptotically good qubit QLTCs. The remaining target is practical parameters, not their bare asymptotic existence.
solved_when: Explicit finite-size tradeoffs among rate, distance, check weight, soundness, and construction complexity for good qubit QLTCs are obtained, with usable constants rather than bare asymptotic existence.
why: It determines whether local testability can materially improve real architectures.
key_works: William Gay and Fernando Granha Jeronimo (2026), *Asymptotically Good Quantum Locally Testable Codes*, arXiv:2609.20780.

title: Efficient decoding matched to good QLTC constructions
open: Can we equip the new asymptotically good quantum locally testable code constructions with explicit, efficient decoders and provable noise tolerance? That is, for these QLTC families, produce a decoding algorithm whose computational cost is compatible with repeated physical error correction, together with a proof of the noise levels it corrects.
status: Good QLTC constructions exist — Gay and Jeronimo (2026), *Asymptotically Good Quantum Locally Testable Codes*, arXiv:2609.20780 — and single-shot decoding is known for good quantum LDPC codes via Gu et al. (2024), *Single-Shot Decoding of Good Quantum LDPC Codes*; related classical work concerns algorithmic decoding of locally testable codes. However, a local tester and a distance theorem are not automatically a practical decoder.
solved_when: An explicit decoding algorithm is given for a good QLTC construction, with a proven noise tolerance threshold and computational cost per round compatible with repeated physical error correction.
why: It turns an existence construction into an operational code family: a local tester and a distance theorem alone do not yield a practical decoder.
key_works: Gay and Jeronimo (2026), *Asymptotically Good Quantum Locally Testable Codes*, arXiv:2609.20780; Gu et al. (2024), *Single-Shot Decoding of Good Quantum LDPC Codes*.

title: Lossless four-dimensional cubical complexes
open: Do explicit bounded-degree, sufficiently imbalanced, two-sided lossless four-dimensional cubical complexes exist? More precisely, the goal is an explicit construction of such complexes meeting all the conditions required by the corresponding quantum locally testable code construction.
status: The September 2026 construction identifies these complexes as an unresolved combinatorial input. Key work: Itay Cohen, Itai Leigh, Assaf Reiner, Amnon Ta-Shma, and Elad Tzalik (2026), *Good Quantum Locally Testable Codes from Lossless Cubical Complexes*, arXiv:2610.00525.
solved_when: An explicit family of bounded-degree, sufficiently imbalanced, two-sided lossless four-dimensional cubical complexes is constructed that satisfies every condition required by the corresponding QLTC construction.
why: It would supply a distinct structured route to strong quantum code parameters through quantum locally testable codes from lossless cubical complexes.
key_works: Itay Cohen, Itai Leigh, Assaf Reiner, Amnon Ta-Shma, and Elad Tzalik (2026), *Good Quantum Locally Testable Codes from Lossless Cubical Complexes*, arXiv:2610.00525.

title: Reed–Solomon product expansion over binary extension fields
open: Does Conjecture 5.6 of Bafna–Li–Nguyen hold — namely, that the specified bounded-ratio, pairwise-coprime subgroup evaluation sets of sizes \(2^{m_i}+1\) yield constant product expansion for Reed–Solomon codes at rates bounded away from one?
status: Explicitly conjectural in the September 2026 paper; broader unrestricted subgroup variants are false. See Mitali Bafna, Anqi Li, and Quynh T. Nguyen (2026), *Good Quantum Locally Testable Codes from Product Expansion*, arXiv:2609.26735, Conjecture 5.6.
solved_when: The conjecture is proved or refuted for those evaluation sets, at rates bounded away from one, with constant (rate-independent) product expansion.
why: It supplies structured local codes needed in quantum locally testable-code constructions.
key_works: Mitali Bafna, Anqi Li, and Quynh T. Nguyen (2026), *Good Quantum Locally Testable Codes from Product Expansion*, arXiv:2609.26735, Conjecture 5.6.

title: Practical addressable transversal non-Clifford gates
open: Can we build a practical, integrated implementation of addressable transversal non-Clifford logical gates within finite good quantum error-correcting code blocks? That is, can such gates be realized while accounting for the real costs of measured state preparation, decoding, parallelism, and physical-connectivity constraints?
status: Good-code constructions supporting addressable and parallelizable transversal gates already exist — Z. He et al. (2025), *Quantum Codes with Addressable and Transversal Non-Clifford Gates*, arXiv:2502.01864, and Virgile Guémard (2025), *Good quantum codes with addressable and parallelizable transversal non-Clifford gates*, arXiv:2510.19809 — but the practical integrated implementation remains the target.
solved_when: A finite good-code block realizes addressable transversal non-Clifford logical gates in an integrated implementation whose measured-preparation, decoding, parallelism, and physical-connectivity costs are quantified and practically acceptable.
why: It would reduce reliance on large standalone magic-state factories, cutting a major overhead in universal fault-tolerant quantum computation.
key_works: Z. He et al. (2025), *Quantum Codes with Addressable and Transversal Non-Clifford Gates*, arXiv:2502.01864; Virgile Guémard (2025), *Good quantum codes with addressable and parallelizable transversal non-Clifford gates*, arXiv:2510.19809.

title: Geometric implementation costs of nonlocal quantum codes
open: Do the celebrated rate and distance advantages of qLDPC codes survive once their nonlocal connectivity must be physically realized? Determine tight tradeoffs between those code advantages and the physical costs of long-range couplers, shuttling, photonic links, and routing congestion.
status: Abstract sparse connectivity does not imply cheap geometric implementation; the problem remains open. Key works: Bravyi et al. (2024), *High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory*, arXiv:2308.07915; Guémard (2025), *Good quantum codes with addressable and parallelizable transversal non-Clifford gates*.
solved_when: A tight (matching upper and lower bound) tradeoff is established between qLDPC rate/distance advantages and the geometric implementation costs of long-range couplers, shuttling, photonic links, and routing congestion.
why: Without such tradeoffs, architectural comparisons can treat long-range operations as free, invalidating comparisons between qLDPC and local-code architectures.
key_works: Bravyi et al. (2024), *High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory*, arXiv:2308.07915; Guémard (2025), *Good quantum codes with addressable and parallelizable transversal non-Clifford gates*.

title: Decoding mixed erasure, Pauli, leakage, and coherent noise
open: Can we build decoders with explicit guarantees or calibrated uncertainty for the realistic case where erasures, Pauli errors, leakage, and coherent noise act simultaneously, rather than tuning separately for each idealized channel? A satisfying solution would be a decoding framework whose correctness or confidence bounds are provable (or quantitatively calibrated) under a unified noise model combining these mechanisms.
status: Erasure-aware and channel-specific decoding methods are known to offer gains, but a robust unified treatment remains architecture-dependent and is not yet established. Key works include Yue Wu, Shimon Kolkowitz, Shruti Puri, and Jeff Thompson (2022), *Erasure conversion for fault-tolerant quantum computing in alkaline earth Rydberg atom arrays*, arXiv:2201.03540; and Matt McEwen et al. (2021), *Removing leakage-induced correlated errors in superconducting quantum error correction*.
solved_when: A decoder exists that handles erasure, Pauli, leakage, and coherent noise within a single framework, and comes with explicit performance guarantees or calibrated uncertainty quantification for that combined noise model — replacing separately optimized channel-specific decoders.
why: Real quantum devices do not maintain a single stationary textbook noise channel, so separately optimized decoders lose their assumed guarantees in practice; a unified treatment makes error correction reliable under actual hardware conditions.
key_works: Yue Wu, Shimon Kolkowitz, Shruti Puri, and Jeff Thompson (2022), *Erasure conversion for fault-tolerant quantum computing in alkaline earth Rydberg atom arrays*, arXiv:2201.03540; Matt McEwen et al. (2021), *Removing leakage-induced correlated errors in superconducting quantum error correction*.

title: Decoder robustness outside the training distribution
open: Can a learned quantum decoder detect when the noise it faces has drifted away from its training distribution — through shifted rates, rare faults, or unseen correlations — and respond safely rather than silently issuing overconfident logical corrections? Formally, the goal is a decoder that remains reliable out-of-distribution, flagging or abstaining when its corrections are no longer trustworthy.
status: Learned decoders achieve strong benchmark accuracy (Johannes Bausch et al. (2024), *Learning high-accuracy error decoding for quantum processors*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-08148-8), but accuracy on familiar noise is not a guarantee under drift or adversarially selected rare events.
solved_when: A decoder demonstrably detects noise shifts, rare faults, and unseen correlations, and avoids producing overconfident logical corrections in those regimes; success is a demonstrated safety behavior under distribution drift and adversarially selected rare events, not merely strong benchmark accuracy on familiar noise.
why: Decoder failure under drift becomes a hidden logical-error floor that benchmark accuracy on familiar noise will never reveal.
key_works: Johannes Bausch et al. (2024), *Learning high-accuracy error decoding for quantum processors*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-08148-8.

title: Bounded-latency decoding without backlog
open: Can a quantum error-correcting decoder run continuously at the physical syndrome rate with a hard bound on tail latency — even through difficult error bursts — while keeping logical accuracy competitive with the best offline decoders? Formally, the goal is a decoding architecture whose worst-case response time, not merely its average throughput, meets the real-time feedback deadline of the device.
status: High-accuracy decoding and real-time demonstrations exist separately or at limited scales; worst-case sustained throughput remains an architectural constraint. Key works: Bausch et al. (2024), *Learning high-accuracy error decoding for quantum processors*; Google Quantum AI (2025), *Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold*.
solved_when: A demonstrated decoder sustains real-time operation at the physical syndrome rate with bounded worst-case (tail) latency across difficult bursts, with no growing backlog, while achieving logical accuracy competitive with state-of-the-art high-accuracy decoders.
