why: Average decoder speed is insufficient when feedback deadlines are strict; without bounded tail latency, corrections arrive too late during bursts and the logical error rate degrades.
key_works: Bausch et al. (2024), *Learning high-accuracy error decoding for quantum processors*; Google Quantum AI (2025), *Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold*.

title: Logical-error floors at large distance and long duration
open: Does the suppression of logical errors persist when surface-code memories are pushed to much larger code distances and far longer run times, once realistic fault mechanisms — correlated bursts, leakage, calibration changes, and decoder faults — are included? Formally, the question is whether the observed below-threshold scaling extrapolates to the extremely small failure probabilities relevant for large-scale computation under these non-ideal conditions.
status: Below-threshold surface-code memories have been demonstrated, but extrapolation to extremely small failure probabilities requires additional evidence. Key demonstration: Google Quantum AI (2025), *Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold*, arXiv:2408.13687; DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-08449-y.
solved_when: An experimental demonstration shows continued error suppression with increasing code distance over long-duration runs while incorporating correlated bursts, leakage, calibration changes, and decoder faults, providing direct evidence for the extrapolated extremely small logical-failure probabilities rather than relying on extrapolation alone.
why: Large algorithms depend on the tail of the error distribution, not only its typical behavior; without validated suppression of rare logical failures at scale, resource estimates for fault-tolerant computation rest on unverified extrapolations.
key_works: Google Quantum AI (2025), *Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold*, arXiv:2408.13687; DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-08449-y.

title: Leakage-removal protocols without hidden correlated damage
open: Can leakage detection and reset be designed so that leakage propagation is suppressed without the cure itself introducing errors — from resets, measurements, or spectator qubits — that outweigh the logical benefit of removing the leakage? Formally, find leakage-removal protocols whose net effect on the logical error rate is positive once all overhead-induced correlated errors are accounted for.
status: Leakage-removal methods have been demonstrated, notably removing leakage-induced correlated errors in superconducting quantum error correction (Matt McEwen et al. (2021), arXiv:2102.06131), but a scalable joint optimization of leakage removal together with the complete syndrome circuit remains open. Related work concerns fault containment in multilevel physical systems.
solved_when: A leakage-removal protocol is demonstrated in which reset-induced, measurement-induced, and spectator errors are each kept below the logical benefit of leakage suppression, with the suppression verified across the complete syndrome-extraction circuit rather than a fragment of it.
why: Leakage takes qubits out of the computational subspace, violating the assumptions on which many decoder models rest, so unremoved leakage silently corrupts the logical error correction stack.
key_works: Matt McEwen et al. (2021), *Removing leakage-induced correlated errors in superconducting quantum error correction*, arXiv:2102.06131.

title: Long universal logical computations with auditable success
open: Can a quantum processor execute a long, universal logical computation — combining memory, entangling gates, non-Clifford gates, measurement, and feed-forward — whose end-to-end failure can be independently audited rather than merely inferred? Formally, the goal is a demonstration in which all logical operations are performed fault-tolerantly and the total failure budget is certified by an independent check.
status: Below-threshold memory and component demonstrations exist as partial milestones, but they do not establish arbitrary long universal execution. Key works: Google Quantum AI (2025), *Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold*; Bravyi et al. (2024), *High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory*.
solved_when: A demonstration runs a long computation incorporating memory, entangling gates, non-Clifford gates, measurement, and feed-forward, with an independently checkable end-to-end failure budget.
why: It tests the actual product that fault tolerance promises, going beyond memory and isolated component demonstrations to arbitrary long universal logical execution.
key_works: Google Quantum AI (2025), *Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold*; Bravyi et al. (2024), *High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory*.

title: Actual T-state cultivation under coherent fault propagation
open: Can full T-state cultivation — from distillation through escape to downstream consumption — be experimentally certified under realistic physical noise, rather than a Clifford-simulable surrogate that sidesteps coherent fault propagation?
status: September 2026 work by Tim Chan, Armands Strikis, Zhu Sun, and Zhenyu Cai (2026) (*Diagnosing and Restoring the Degraded Fault Distance of Magic State Cultivation*, arXiv:2609.17706) diagnoses a T-versus-S fault-distance discrepancy and supplies corrective flags, but experimental full-protocol certification remains a separate, open task.
solved_when: The complete cultivation protocol, including escape and downstream use of the T states, has been certified under physical noise, without reliance on Clifford-simulable stand-ins.
why: It prevents optimistic magic-state resource estimates from overlooking coherent logical faults that a simulable surrogate would hide.
key_works: Tim Chan, Armands Strikis, Zhu Sun, and Zhenyu Cai (2026), *Diagnosing and Restoring the Degraded Fault Distance of Magic State Cultivation*, arXiv:2609.17706.

title: Continuous magic-state factories with verified yield
open: Can a magic-state factory be run continuously while its long-run production quality is actually verified — tracking accepted-state fidelity, rejection correlations, drift, downtime, and the usable delivery rate to the consuming computation?
status: Existing protocol resource estimates and selected-state demonstrations do not establish long-run production yield. Key works: Craig Gidney et al. (2024), *Magic state cultivation: growing T states as cheap as CNOT gates*, arXiv:2409.17595; Chan et al. (2026), *Diagnosing and Restoring the Degraded Fault Distance of Magic State Cultivation*.
solved_when: A continuously operating factory demonstrates a measured long-run production yield, with accepted-state fidelity, rejection correlations, drift, downtime, and usable delivery rate all tracked and reported over sustained operation.
why: Non-Clifford (magic-state) throughput can set the total runtime of a fault-tolerant computer, so unverified long-run yield leaves the machine's effective speed unknown.
key_works: Craig Gidney et al. (2024), *Magic state cultivation: growing T states as cheap as CNOT gates*, arXiv:2409.17595; Chan et al. (2026), *Diagnosing and Restoring the Degraded Fault Distance of Magic State Cultivation*.

title: Tight spacetime overhead of fault tolerance
open: How much total spacetime overhead is truly required to make a quantum computation fault-tolerant? More precisely, can the asymptotic and finite-size gaps between known lower bounds and achievable spacetime overhead be closed under explicitly specified noise and architecture assumptions?
status: Constant qubit overhead has strong constructions. An August 2026 preprint rules out constant total spacetime overhead in its model; the tight achievable tradeoff remains finer. Key works: Matthias Christandl, Omar Fawzi, and Ashutosh Goswami (2025), *Fault-tolerant quantum computation with constant overhead for general noise*, arXiv:2512.02760; Bharti, Haug, and Andrew Tanggara (2026), arXiv:2608.26272.
solved_when: Matching lower and upper bounds on spacetime overhead are established — asymptotically and at finite size — for an explicitly specified noise and architecture model.
why: It separates savings in qubit count from the total computational cost of fault tolerance, clarifying what constant-qubit-overhead constructions actually cost in time.
key_works: Matthias Christandl, Omar Fawzi, and Ashutosh Goswami (2025), *Fault-tolerant quantum computation with constant overhead for general noise*, arXiv:2512.02760; Bharti, Haug, and Andrew Tanggara (2026), arXiv:2608.26272.

title: Low-overhead conversion between heterogeneous logical codes
open: Can we convert logical information between memory-efficient and gate-efficient code families cheaply enough to be worth doing? That is, can a conversion procedure be given a complete fault-tolerance proof and still show a net benefit once ancillas, routing, and decoding are all counted?
status: Code switching and teleportation primitives exist, but useful finite-size combinations are not determined by those primitives alone. He et al. (2025), *Quantum Codes with Addressable and Transversal Non-Clifford Gates*, arXiv:2502.01864; Christandl et al. (2025), *Fault-tolerant quantum computation with constant overhead for general noise*.
solved_when: A conversion procedure between heterogeneous logical code families is exhibited with a full fault-tolerance proof, and a resource accounting including ancillas, routing, and decoding shows a net benefit over staying in a single code.
why: No single code need be best at storage, movement, and non-Clifford computation, so cheap conversion would let an architecture use each code where it excels.
key_works: He et al. (2025), *Quantum Codes with Addressable and Transversal Non-Clifford Gates*, arXiv:2502.01864; Christandl et al. (2025), *Fault-tolerant quantum computation with constant overhead for general noise*.

title: Joint scheduling of logical routing, factories, and memory
open: Can we jointly schedule logical routing, factory operation, and memory management in a fault-tolerant quantum computer so that the whole schedule is optimal — accounting simultaneously for finite factory rates, stochastic failures, limited connectivity, and logical-memory decay? In other words, is there a method that optimizes the complete fault-tolerant schedule, rather than each resource in isolation, and certifies its resource estimates?
status: Component-wise optimization is not generally globally optimal. Key works include Gidney (2025), *How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers with less than a million noisy qubits*, arXiv:2505.15917; Babbush et al. (2021), *Focus beyond quadratic speedups for error-corrected quantum advantage*.
solved_when: A scheduling method exists that jointly optimizes routing, factories, and memory under finite factory rates, stochastic failures, limited connectivity, and logical-memory decay, and produces certified resource estimates for complete fault-tolerant schedules.
why: Congestion and starvation can erase gains predicted by isolated gate counts, so whole-system optimization is needed for resource estimates to reflect real performance.
key_works: Gidney (2025), *How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers with less than a million noisy qubits*, arXiv:2505.15917; Babbush et al. (2021), *Focus beyond quadratic speedups for error-corrected quantum advantage*.

title: Repair and replacement during logical computation
open: Can a fault-tolerant quantum computation keep running — with its encoded logical data intact and its fault-tolerance assumptions still valid — while failed qubits, control channels, or entire modules are replaced on the fly? Formally, this asks for protocols that reconfigure hardware during logical computation without interrupting service or invalidating the error model.
status: Reconfiguration and continuous hardware replenishment are emerging capabilities, but complete logical service continuity remains a stronger, unreached target. Key works include Neng-Chun Chiu et al. (2025), *Continuous operation of a coherent 3,000-qubit system*, arXiv:2506.20660, and Bravyi et al. (2024), *High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory*.
solved_when: A scheme exists that replaces failed physical components mid-computation while preserving encoded data and maintaining fault-tolerance guarantees; the natural success criterion is demonstrated logical service continuity through such replacement events.
why: Long computations must survive outright component failures, not merely stochastic gate errors; without repair-and-replacement capability, runtime is capped by the lifetime of the weakest physical element.
key_works: Neng-Chun Chiu et al. (2025), *Continuous operation of a coherent 3,000-qubit system*, arXiv:2506.20660; Bravyi et al. (2024), *High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory*.

title: Physical realization of three-dimensional passive self-correction
subfield: Passive memories, bosonic codes, and qudits
open: Can a physically credible three-dimensional passive quantum memory be implemented in the laboratory, exhibiting a quantum lifetime that grows with system size at a fixed nonzero temperature? Formally, this means realizing a 3D passive self-correcting memory whose storage time increases with the number of physical qubits while thermal noise remains present.
status: A May 2026 preprint claims an abstract geometrically local 3D self-correcting stabilizer Hamiltonian; its laboratory realization remains a distinct unresolved problem. (See Shankar Balasubramanian, Margarita Davydova, and Ting-Chun Lin (2026), *A passive self-correcting quantum memory in three dimensions*, arXiv:2605.10943.)
solved_when: A laboratory implementation of a three-dimensional passive memory demonstrates increasing quantum lifetime with system size at a fixed nonzero temperature.
why: A solution would reduce or eliminate the need for continuous measurement and active feedback to maintain quantum information.
key_works: Shankar Balasubramanian, Margarita Davydova, and Ting-Chun Lin (2026), *A passive self-correcting quantum memory in three dimensions*, arXiv:2605.10943.

title: Robustness of self-correction to implementation perturbations
subfield: Passive memories, bosonic codes, and qudits
open: Do passive self-correcting quantum memories retain their protection when the protecting Hamiltonian itself is built imperfectly? Establish useful stability bounds for passive self-correcting constructions under imperfect couplings, unwanted interactions, disorder, and realistic bath dynamics.
status: Abstract lifetime theorems do not by themselves certify a fabricated Hamiltonian. Key works: Balasubramanian, Davydova, and Lin (2026), *A passive self-correcting quantum memory in three dimensions*, arXiv:2605.10943.
solved_when: Quantitative lifetime bounds are proven that hold under imperfect couplings, unwanted interactions, disorder, and realistic bath dynamics, certifying that a fabricated (non-ideal) Hamiltonian still self-corrects for a stated lifetime.
why: Self-correction is useful only if it survives errors in the mechanism meant to provide protection; abstract lifetime theorems alone do not certify a fabricated Hamiltonian.
key_works: Balasubramanian, Davydova, and Lin (2026), *A passive self-correcting quantum memory in three dimensions*, arXiv:2605.10943.

title: Universal fault tolerance with finite-energy GKP states
subfield: Passive memories, bosonic codes, and qudits
open: Can universal fault-tolerant logical computation be demonstrated using physically prepared finite-energy GKP states, with realistic envelope effects incorporated into the gates, recovery, and measurement?
status: The GKP encoding and many component protocols are established, but the ideal infinite-energy codewords assumed in that theory are not physical resources. (Key work: Daniel Gottesman, Alexei Kitaev, and John Preskill (2001), *Encoding a qubit in an oscillator*, arXiv:quant-ph/0008040.)
solved_when: A demonstration of universal logical computation on GKP-encoded qubits uses finite-energy (physically preparable) states and accounts for realistic envelope effects in its gates, recovery, and measurement.
why: Success would deliver efficient bosonic error correction with favorable concatenation overhead, moving GKP codes from idealized resource assumptions toward practical hardware.
key_works: Daniel Gottesman, Alexei Kitaev, and John Preskill (2001), *Encoding a qubit in an oscillator*, arXiv:quant-ph/0008040.

title: GKP correction optimized for photon loss and physical gates
subfield: Passive memories, bosonic codes, and qudits
open: Can GKP-state encodings, recovery maps, and gate schedules be jointly designed around the noise that actually occurs — photon loss combined with finite-energy distortions — rather than the idealized displacement-only channel? In other words, what is the optimal scheme when the correction strategy is tailored to the dominant physical error processes instead of a convenient effective model?
status: Noise-model-specific improvements exist, but the optimal physical architecture remains unsettled. Key works: Gottesman, Kitaev, and Preskill (2001), *Encoding a qubit in an oscillator*, arXiv:quant-ph/0008040; V. V. Sivak et al. (2023), *Real-time quantum error correction beyond break-even*.
solved_when: Encodings, recovery maps, and gate schedules are found and validated that are jointly optimized for photon loss and finite-energy distortions, not a displacement-only channel.
why: The effective noise model used for convenience can differ from the device's actual dominant error, so corrections designed for the wrong channel fail to protect what matters.
key_works: Gottesman, Kitaev, and Preskill (2001), *Encoding a qubit in an oscillator*, arXiv:quant-ph/0008040; V. V. Sivak et al. (2023), *Real-time quantum error correction beyond break-even*.

title: Fast bias-preserving universal cat-qubit gates
subfield: Passive memories, bosonic codes, and qudits
open: Can a cat-qubit processor run a useful universal gate set without destroying the noise bias that makes cat qubits attractive? Formally: implement universal gates such that the suppressed (bit-flip) error channel is not reintroduced strongly enough to eliminate the encoded architecture's overhead advantage.
status: Long bit-flip lifetimes and concatenated demonstrations are important partial results (Ulysse Réglade et al. (2024), *Quantum control of a cat qubit with bit-flip times exceeding ten seconds*; Harald Putterman et al. (2025), *Hardware-efficient quantum error correction via concatenated bosonic qubits*, arXiv:2409.13025), but gates can introduce the suppressed error channel, and a bias-preserving universal gate set has not been achieved.
solved_when: A universal gate set is demonstrated on cat qubits while preserving noise bias sufficiently that the complete encoded architecture — memory plus gates — retains its overhead advantage over an unbiased alternative.
why: A good biased memory is not automatically a good biased computer: gates themselves can introduce the suppressed error channel, eroding the advantage the memory provides.
key_works: Ulysse Réglade et al. (2024), *Quantum control of a cat qubit with bit-flip times exceeding ten seconds*; Harald Putterman et al. (2025), *Hardware-efficient quantum error correction via concatenated bosonic qubits*, arXiv:2409.13025.

title: Correlated-noise control in concatenated bosonic codes
subfield: Passive memories, bosonic codes, and qudits
open: Can correlated faults introduced by shared hardware — common ancillas, pumps, couplers, and recovery circuits — be quantified and suppressed so that concatenating bosonic codes continues to improve logical performance rather than degrading it?
status: Hardware-efficient concatenated bosonic correction has been demonstrated, but the independence assumptions needed for scalability remain untested. Key work: Putterman et al. (2025), *Hardware-efficient quantum error correction via concatenated bosonic qubits*, arXiv:2409.13025.
solved_when: A quantitative characterization of the correlations arising from each shared mechanism is achieved, together with a demonstrated suppression scheme under which concatenation yields continued improvement in logical performance at experimentally relevant scales.
why: The promise of concatenation rests on independence of fault mechanisms; when a single physical mechanism produces correlated faults, the expected logical-performance gains can vanish.
key_works: Putterman et al. (2025), *Hardware-efficient quantum error correction via concatenated bosonic qubits*, arXiv:2409.13025.

title: Scalable fault-tolerant qudit computation
subfield: Passive memories, bosonic codes, and qudits
open: Does encoding and processing information in more than two levels per physical system ever reduce the total computational cost of a fault-tolerant machine, once leakage, control selectivity, measurement, and decoder complexity are all included?
status: Beyond-break-even qudit correction and high-dimensional control are reported, but scalable universal advantage over qubit encodings remains architecture-specific. Key works: Benjamin L. Brock et al. (2025), *Quantum error correction of qudits beyond break-even*; Guémard (2025), *Good quantum codes with addressable and parallelizable transversal non-Clifford gates*.
solved_when: A scalable architecture is demonstrated in which qudit encodings achieve a lower total computational cost than an equivalent qubit encoding, accounting for leakage, control selectivity, measurement, and decoder complexity.
why: Higher local dimension may reduce hardware count, but it can increase every other control burden; settling this determines whether qudits are a genuine scaling resource or a trade-off.
key_works: Benjamin L. Brock et al. (2025), *Quantum error correction of qudits beyond break-even*; Guémard (2025), *Good quantum codes with addressable and parallelizable transversal non-Clifford gates*.

title: Microscopic identification of dominant two-level defects
open: Which atomic-scale defects are actually responsible for loss in a given fabrication stack, and can their abundance be causally tied to qubit relaxation and device-to-device variability? A satisfying answer would identify the defect species and show how their measured concentrations quantitatively explain observed quality factors and variability.
status: Defect models and materials improvements are substantial, but a universal predictive microscopic account is still lacking. See Nathalie de Leon et al. (2021), *Materials challenges and opportunities for quantum computing hardware*, DOI:10.1126/science.abb2823.
solved_when: A microscopic defect model is established that identifies the dominant atomic-scale defects in specific fabrication stacks and demonstrably connects defect abundance to qubit relaxation and variability.
why: It would replace empirical process iteration with targeted manufacturing fixes, attacking qubit loss at its physical source.
key_works: Nathalie de Leon et al. (2021), *Materials challenges and opportunities for quantum computing hardware*, DOI:10.1126/science.abb2823.

title: Reproducible low-loss superconducting interfaces at scale
open: Can superconducting quantum devices be fabricated so that interface loss is controlled reproducibly across entire wafers and batches, rather than demonstrated only in a few champion devices? Formally, the goal is predictive relationships linking processing conditions, defect populations, coherence, and fabrication yield at wafer- and batch-level scale.
status: High-coherence individual devices have been demonstrated, but these do not establish a scalable distribution of device quality. See de Leon et al. (2021), *Materials challenges and opportunities for quantum computing hardware*, DOI:10.1126/science.abb2823.
solved_when: Interface loss is controlled at wafer- and batch-level, with validated predictive relationships connecting processing, defect populations, coherence, and fabrication yield — not merely isolated high-coherence devices.
why: Large processors are limited by their weakest devices and by correlated process failures, so scaling hinges on a reproducible distribution of device quality rather than record-setting outliers.
key_works: de Leon et al. (2021), *Materials challenges and opportunities for quantum computing hardware*, DOI:10.1126/science.abb2823.

title: Nonequilibrium quasiparticle control under active operation
open: Can superconducting qubits be operated through realistic readout, reset, control, and radiation exposure while quasiparticle generation and transport are predicted and suppressed — without paying for that suppression with added noise?
status: Existing quasiparticle mitigation efforts and burst observations have identified the relevant mechanisms, but complete operational control remains unresolved. Key works include McEwen et al. (2022), *Resolving catastrophic error bursts from cosmic rays in large arrays of superconducting qubits*, arXiv:2104.05219, and Philip Krantz et al. (2019), *A quantum engineer’s guide to superconducting qubits*.
solved_when: A scheme demonstrates quasiparticle generation and transport predicted and suppressed during realistic readout, reset, control, and radiation exposure, with no compensating noise introduced.
why: Quasiparticles cause both local relaxation of individual qubits and correlated failures across devices, so uncontrolled quasiparticles threaten both single-qubit fidelity and large-scale error-correcting architectures.
key_works: McEwen et al. (2022), *Resolving catastrophic error bursts from cosmic rays in large arrays of superconducting qubits*, arXiv:2104.05219; Philip Krantz et al. (2019), *A quantum engineer’s guide to superconducting qubits*.

title: Parallel high-fidelity fluxonium gates in dense processors
open: Can a dense fluxonium processor preserve its favorable gate performance when many qubits are operated at once under realistic conditions — simultaneous gates, frequency crowding, spectator coupling, fabrication spread, and repeated error-correction cycles?
status: Coupler and small-system gate advances are partial results; isolated-pair fidelity does not establish dense-array behavior. Key works: Guinn et al. (2024), *Tunable inductive coupler for high-fidelity gates between fluxonium qubits*, DOI:10.1103/PRXQuantum.5.020326; *CNOT gates in inductively coupled multi-fluxonium systems*, arXiv:2512.11756.
solved_when: Fluxonium gate fidelity demonstrated to persist under simultaneous operation in a dense array, with performance maintained across frequency crowding, spectator coupling, fabrication spread, and repeated error-correction cycles — not merely in isolated qubit pairs.
why: It tests whether fluxonium's coherence advantages survive processor integration, determining whether the platform can scale beyond laboratory demonstrations.
key_works: Guinn et al. (2024), *Tunable inductive coupler for high-fidelity gates between fluxonium qubits*, DOI:10.1103/PRXQuantum.5.020326; *CNOT gates in inductively coupled multi-fluxonium systems*, arXiv:2512.11756.

title: Cryogenic wiring without prohibitive heat load
open: Can control and readout wiring for superconducting quantum processors be scaled up while staying within a complete refrigerator budget — accounting for conductive heat load, microwave dissipation, thermalization, crosstalk, and maintenance? Formally, the goal is an interconnect architecture whose total thermal and dissipation burden remains bounded as line counts grow, rather than accumulating per independent line.
status: Engineering studies for hundred-qubit systems establish useful baselines, but extrapolation by adding independent lines is not sustainable indefinitely. Key work: Simon Krinner et al. (2019), *Engineering cryogenic setups for 100-qubit scale superconducting circuit systems*, arXiv:1806.07862.
solved_when: A wiring scheme is demonstrated in which conductive heat, microwave dissipation, thermalization, crosstalk, and maintenance all remain within a complete refrigerator budget at scale, without relying on simple extrapolation by adding independent lines.
why: Physical wiring can become the scaling wall before qubit fabrication does; solving it removes a bottleneck that would otherwise block larger superconducting processors regardless of qubit quality.
key_works: Simon Krinner et al. (2019), *Engineering cryogenic setups for 100-qubit scale superconducting circuit systems*, arXiv:1806.07862.

title: Cryogenic control electronics with full noise accounting
open: Can cryogenic control electronics be integrated directly alongside a superconducting quantum processor, reducing system cost and wiring complexity without any net degradation of qubit performance? Formally, the goal is a controller design whose full noise accounting — power dissipation, phase noise, electromagnetic interference, and shared-control faults — yields a favorable complete-system tradeoff.
status: Component demonstrations exist, but none establishes a favorable complete-system tradeoff. Key works: Krinner et al. (2019), *Engineering cryogenic setups for 100-qubit scale superconducting circuit systems*; Marco Fellous-Asiani et al. (2023), *Optimizing resource efficiencies for scalable full-stack quantum computers*, arXiv:2209.05469.
solved_when: A low-temperature controller is integrated with superconducting qubits and the complete-system tradeoff is favorable, with all dissipated power, phase noise, electromagnetic interference, and shared-control fault effects accounted for and shown not to degrade the qubits.
why: It moves classical control closer to the processor without worsening the refrigerator load or the noise environment, which is what makes deep-cryogenic integration practical rather than counterproductive.
key_works: Krinner et al. (2019), *Engineering cryogenic setups for 100-qubit scale superconducting circuit systems*; Marco Fellous-Asiani et al. (2023), *Optimizing resource efficiencies for scalable full-stack quantum computers*, arXiv:2209.05469.

title: Fast multiplexed readout with bounded correlated error
open: Can a superconducting quantum processor read out many qubits at once — fast — while keeping every correlated failure mode under joint control? Formally, can simultaneous readout throughput be increased while assignment error, measurement-induced transitions, resonator collisions, and backaction on unmeasured qubits are jointly bounded?
status: Fast readout and multiplexed readout each exist individually, but a joint, scalable error model treating their correlated failure modes together remains an open system-level challenge. See Krantz et al. (2019), *A quantum engineer's guide to superconducting qubits*; Google Quantum AI (2025), *Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold*.
solved_when: A readout architecture is demonstrated that increases simultaneous readout throughput while keeping assignment error, measurement-induced transitions, resonator collisions, and backaction on unmeasured qubits jointly bounded, with the bounds characterized under a scalable joint error model.
why: Syndrome extraction exercises the readout system repeatedly, so even small correlations in readout errors accumulate and become consequential for error correction.
key_works: Krantz et al. (2019), *A quantum engineer’s guide to superconducting qubits*; Google Quantum AI (2025), *Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold*.

title: Adaptive calibration that improves logical reliability
open: Can a large superconducting processor keep itself calibrated — using online parameter tracking and periodic recalibration — so that logical failure rates actually go down? In other words, demonstrate that adaptive calibration yields a net improvement in logical reliability after subtracting the costs of calibration interruptions, estimator error, and any instability introduced by the feedback loop.
status: Real-time tracking of fluctuating relaxation rates is advancing, but improved physical estimates do not automatically imply better logical operation. Key work: F. Berritta et al. (2026), *Real-Time Adaptive Tracking of Fluctuating Relaxation Rates*, DOI:10.1103/gk1b-stl3.
solved_when: A working system demonstrates that online parameter tracking plus recalibration reduces logical failures relative to a non-adaptive baseline, with the improvement persisting after accounting for downtime from calibration interruptions, estimator mistakes, and feedback-induced instability.
why: Large processors cannot rely on a permanently stationary calibration, so without adaptive schemes their logical performance degrades as parameters drift.
key_works: F. Berritta et al. (2026), *Real-Time Adaptive Tracking of Fluctuating Relaxation Rates*, DOI:10.1103/gk1b-stl3.

title: Microscopic origin of anomalous ion-trap heating
open: What microscopic mechanism, or set of mechanisms, is the dominant source of anomalous electric-field noise that heats trapped ions near surfaces? A satisfactory answer should identify the noise sources across relevant surfaces and temperatures and yield predictions that remain valid as fabrication and cleaning procedures change.
status: Decades of measurements now tightly constrain candidate models, yet no single predictive microscopic explanation covers the full experimental landscape. A key resource is Michael Brownnutt, Markus Kumph, Peter Rabl, and Rainer Blatt (2015), *Ion-trap measurements of electric-field noise near surfaces*, arXiv:1409.6572.
solved_when: A predictive microscopic explanation is available that accounts for the full experimental landscape of ion-trap heating measurements and survives changes in fabrication and surface-cleaning conditions.
why: Anomalous heating directly limits trap miniaturization, ion transport, and motional gates — the operations a scaled trapped-ion architecture depends on — so without such an explanation these design choices remain guided by empirical trial and error.
key_works: Michael Brownnutt, Markus Kumph, Peter Rabl, and Rainer Blatt (2015), *Ion-trap measurements of electric-field noise near surfaces*, arXiv:1409.6572.

title: Integrated optical delivery for many ion zones
open: How can a large trapped-ion architecture deliver individually controlled, phase-stable optical fields to many distinct ion zones at once, without excessive optical power, alignment burden, fabrication variation, or crosstalk?
status: Integrated and broadcast control approaches exist as partial solutions, but complete optical control of large networks remains an open scaling challenge. Key work: Moses et al. (2023), *A Race Track Trapped-Ion Quantum Processor*, arXiv:2305.03828.
solved_when: A demonstration shows individually addressable, phase-stable optical delivery to many ion zones in an integrated architecture, with optical power, alignment tolerances, fabrication variation, and crosstalk all kept at manageable levels.
why: Without integrated delivery, the complexity of free-space optics grows with the number of zones and can overwhelm the advantages that integrated traps are meant to provide.
key_works: Moses et al. (2023), *A Race Track Trapped-Ion Quantum Processor*, arXiv:2305.03828.

title: Parallel entangling gates with shared motional resources
open: Can a trapped-ion architecture run many entangling gates at the same time on shared motional modes while keeping errors as low as isolated gates? Formally, achieve dense parallel entangling operation despite spectator excitation, mode crowding, transport-induced mode changes, and correlated gate errors.
status: High-fidelity individual gates have been demonstrated, but they do not settle the question of dense simultaneous operation. Key works: Pino et al. (2021), *Demonstration of the trapped-ion quantum-CCD computer architecture*, arXiv:2003.01293; Moses et al. (2023), *A Race Track Trapped-Ion Quantum Processor*.
solved_when: Simultaneous multi-gate operation is demonstrated with gate fidelities and error rates comparable to individually executed gates, with spectator excitation, mode crowding, transport-induced mode changes, and correlated gate errors demonstrably suppressed.
why: Parallel throughput is what converts long coherence times into fast computation; without it, a long-coherence device remains slow.
key_works: Pino et al. (2021), *Demonstration of the trapped-ion quantum-CCD computer architecture*, arXiv:2003.01293; Moses et al. (2023), *A Race Track Trapped-Ion Quantum Processor*.

title: Cooling during computation without damaging stored information
open: Can a trapped-ion machine run sympathetic cooling, ion transport, and repeated gates together so that motional entropy is steadily removed without accumulating memory, scattering, or species-crosstalk errors?
status: Cooling primitives exist; sustained many-zone scheduling with a complete logical error budget remains an integration problem. Key works: Pino et al. (2021), *Demonstration of the trapped-ion quantum-CCD computer architecture*, arXiv:2003.01293; Brownnutt et al. (2015), *Ion-trap measurements of electric-field noise near surfaces*.
solved_when: A sustained many-zone schedule integrates cooling, transport, and repeated gates, accompanied by a complete logical error budget showing that memory, scattering, and species-crosstalk errors remain within acceptable bounds.
why: Transport and gates continually replenish the motion that must be removed, so without integrated cooling during computation the stored quantum information degrades as the machine runs.
key_works: Pino et al. (2021), *Demonstration of the trapped-ion quantum-CCD computer architecture*, arXiv:2003.01293; Brownnutt et al. (2015), *Ion-trap measurements of electric-field noise near surfaces*.

title: Networked ion gates competitive with local fault tolerance
open: Can remote entangling gates between trapped-ion modules be made faithful and fast enough that computing over an optical network outperforms simply enlarging or reconfiguring a single local processor? Formally, the goal is to raise remote entangling-gate fidelity and throughput to the point where modular networked ion computation is the competitive engineering choice.
status: Distributed computation across an optical link has been demonstrated, so the existence of a remote gate is not the remaining problem; the open issue is fidelity and throughput competitiveness. Key work: D. Main et al. (2025), *Distributed Quantum Computing across an Optical Network Link*, arXiv:2407.00835.
solved_when: Networked, modular ion-trap computation demonstrably beats local fault-tolerant alternatives in performance — remote entangling-gate fidelity and throughput sufficient to make photonic modularity preferable to enlarging or reconfiguring a local processor.
why: It determines whether photonic modularity is a genuine performance advantage for trapped-ion computing rather than merely a connectivity demonstration.
key_works: D. Main et al. (2025), *Distributed Quantum Computing across an Optical Network Link*, arXiv:2407.00835.

title: Complete logical recovery from atom loss
open: Can a quantum computer built from neutral atoms recover completely — at the logical level — when an atom is lost mid-computation? That is, can we detect the loss, replace or reroute the missing carrier, restore the encoded state, and resume computation with a quantified logical failure probability?
status: Erasure conversion and reconfigurable logical processors provide the key ingredients; see Wu et al. (2022), *Erasure conversion for fault-tolerant quantum computing in alkaline earth Rydberg atom arrays*, arXiv:2201.03540, and Dolev Bluvstein et al. (2024), *Logical quantum processor based on reconfigurable atom arrays*. The full cost of recovery, however, is unresolved and depends on when and where the loss occurs.
solved_when: A demonstrated recovery procedure that detects loss, replaces or reroutes the carrier, restores the code, and continues computation with an explicitly quantified logical failure probability, including the recovery cost's dependence on when and where the loss occurs.
why: It converts a dominant physical failure mode of neutral-atom platforms into a routine, quantifiable logical maintenance operation rather than a computation-ending event.
key_works: Wu et al. (2022), *Erasure conversion for fault-tolerant quantum computing in alkaline earth Rydberg atom arrays*, arXiv:2201.03540; Dolev Bluvstein et al. (2024), *Logical quantum processor based on reconfigurable atom arrays*.

title: Correlation-aware benchmarking of parallel Rydberg gates
open: When many Rydberg entangling gates run simultaneously across a neutral-atom array, how correlated are the errors they leave behind, and how can those correlations be suppressed? Concretely, this asks for a characterization and mitigation of correlated errors in large parallel gate layers arising from common laser noise, blockade imperfections, and spatial intensity variation.
status: High-fidelity parallel entangling gates have been demonstrated, as in Simon J. Evered et al. (2023), *High-fidelity parallel entangling gates on a neutral atom quantum computer*, arXiv:2304.05420; however, the reported aggregate fidelity does not fully specify the error correlations relevant to error correction.
solved_when: A benchmarking protocol exists that measures not just aggregate parallel-gate fidelity but the structure of error correlations across simultaneously gated atoms, together with a demonstrated suppression of the identified common-mode error sources (common laser noise, blockade imperfections, spatial intensity variation).
why: Common-mode gate errors can dominate logical performance, so without understanding and suppressing them, the aggregate fidelity of parallel gates does not predict how well error correction will actually work on these devices.
key_works: Simon J. Evered et al. (2023), *High-fidelity parallel entangling gates on a neutral atom quantum computer*, arXiv:2304.05420.

title: Motional robustness of repeated neutral-atom gates
open: Can neutral-atom gates retain their fidelity when the same atoms are excited, transported, heated, and recooled over and over again — and can we build a model that connects the atoms' motional state to the logical error rate of each gate?
status: Strong individual and parallel gate results exist, but they do not establish arbitrarily long gate sequences under evolving motion. Key work: Evered et al. (2023), *High-fidelity parallel entangling gates on a neutral atom quantum computer*, arXiv:2304.05420.
solved_when: A model linking motional state to logical error is established, and gate performance is maintained through arbitrarily long sequences of excitation, transport, heating, and recooling rather than isolated or parallel gate demonstrations.
why: Internal-state coherence alone does not capture the full atom's computational behavior; without accounting for evolving motion, long computations on neutral-atom hardware cannot be trusted.
key_works: Evered et al. (2023), *High-fidelity parallel entangling gates on a neutral atom quantum computer*, arXiv:2304.05420.

title: Mid-circuit atom readout without spectator damage
open: Can we repeatedly measure a chosen subset of atoms in a neutral-atom array while leaving neighboring data qubits undamaged and keeping the error model clean enough for fault-tolerant decoding? Formally, this asks for mid-circuit selective readout whose accumulated spectator-qubit disturbance stays within a decodable error budget across many repetitions.
status: Logical-processor demonstrations supply partial evidence that this is achievable; repeated large-scale selective readout remains a demanding combined optical and architectural problem. Key work: Bluvstein et al. (2024), *Logical quantum processor based on reconfigurable atom arrays*, arXiv:2312.03982.
solved_when: Selective mid-circuit readout of designated atoms is demonstrated repeatedly at scale, with neighboring data qubits preserved and an error model maintained that is suitable for fault-tolerant decoding.
why: Quantum error correction requires frequent mid-circuit measurement without globally resetting the machine; without it, repeated syndrome extraction in atom arrays is blocked.
key_works: Bluvstein et al. (2024), *Logical quantum processor based on reconfigurable atom arrays*, arXiv:2312.03982.

title: Physically costed qLDPC routing in mobile arrays
open: Can the high-rate parity checks of a qLDPC code be physically routed in a reconfigurable atom array once every real cost of moving atoms is accounted for — transport time, collision avoidance, cooling, optical access, and correlated-motion errors?
status: Reconfigurability changes connectivity constraints but does not make movement free. Key works: Bluvstein et al. (2024), *Logical quantum processor based on reconfigurable atom arrays*; Bravyi et al. (2024), *High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory*.
solved_when: An implementation of high-rate code checks is demonstrated with all of these physical effects explicitly included and modeled: transport time, collision avoidance, cooling, optical access, and correlated-motion errors.
why: It tests a leading route for realizing sparse nonlocal quantum codes: unless reconfigurability survives realistic motion costs, qLDPC advantages over local codes may not transfer to this hardware.
key_works: Bluvstein et al. (2024), *Logical quantum processor based on reconfigurable atom arrays*; Bravyi et al. (2024), *High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory*.

title: Erasure detection with controlled false-positive and false-negative rates
open: Can erasure flags in neutral-atom quantum processors be co-optimized with the decoder so that missed losses, false alarms, detection latency, and the disturbance caused by checking are all managed together rather than treated as separate overheads? Formally, this asks for a joint design of the physical erasure-detection procedure and the error-decoding strategy under imperfect flag information.
status: Erasure conversion is known to improve theoretical thresholds, but imperfect flags change both decoding and architecture costs. Wu et al. (2022), *Erasure conversion for fault-tolerant quantum computing in alkaline earth Rydberg atom arrays*, arXiv:2201.03540.
solved_when: A detection-and-decoding scheme is demonstrated in which the false-negative rate (missed losses) and false-positive rate (false alarms) of erasure flags are controlled quantities that feed into the decoder, with detection latency and the disturbance from checking explicitly accounted for in the overall architecture cost.
why: A supposedly located error is useful only when its location information is reliable; unreliable flags simultaneously corrupt decoding and inflate hardware costs.
key_works: Wu et al. (2022), *Erasure conversion for fault-tolerant quantum computing in alkaline earth Rydberg atom arrays*, arXiv:2201.03540.

title: Foundry-scale spin-qubit yield with complete operations
subfield: Semiconductor spins, defects, and rare-earth systems
open: Can spin-qubit devices be produced at foundry scale such that large arrays reproducibly perform the complete set of operations — initialization, readout, single-qubit gates, two-qubit gates, and tuning — at a fidelity suitable for fault tolerance?
status: The state of the art is a 300-mm foundry silicon spin-qubit unit cell exceeding 99% fidelity in all operations (Paul Steinacker et al. (2025), *A 300mm foundry silicon spin qubit unit cell exceeding 99% fidelity in all operations*, arXiv:2410.15590). This is a major partial result, not a complete large-array yield demonstration.
solved_when: Reproducible large arrays are demonstrated in which initialization, readout, one-qubit gates, two-qubit gates, and tuning all meet a common fault-tolerance specification, with every operation exceeding 99% fidelity as achieved in the 300-mm foundry unit cell.
why: Manufacturing compatibility matters only if the full operation set scales; a process that cannot yield all operations together at array scale cannot support fault-tolerant quantum computing regardless of its foundry pedigree.
key_works: Paul Steinacker et al. (2025), *A 300mm foundry silicon spin qubit unit cell exceeding 99% fidelity in all operations*, arXiv:2410.15590.

title: Predictive control of spin-qubit device variability
subfield: Semiconductor spins, defects, and rare-earth systems
open: Can spin-qubit devices be modeled and controlled well enough that valley splitting, charge disorder, residual isotope effects, and device-to-device control differences are predicted and compensated without tuning effort that grows exponentially with array size?
status: Foundry demonstrations, including Steinacker et al. (2025), *A 300mm foundry silicon spin qubit unit cell exceeding 99% fidelity in all operations*, have identified concrete residual error mechanisms, but uniform autonomous operation across large arrays remains unresolved; see also Guido Burkard et al. (2023), *Semiconductor spin qubits*.
solved_when: A method demonstrably predicts and compensates these variability sources, achieving uniform autonomous operation across large arrays with tuning effort that does not scale exponentially in device count.
why: Uncontrolled variability turns nominally scalable fabrication into operationally unscalable systems, blocking large spin-qubit arrays.
key_works: Steinacker et al. (2025), *A 300mm foundry silicon spin qubit unit cell exceeding 99% fidelity in all operations*; Guido Burkard et al. (2023), *Semiconductor spin qubits*.

title: Long-distance two-dimensional coherent spin transport
subfield: Semiconductor spins, defects, and rare-earth systems
open: Can spin information be coherently shuttled across a large two-dimensional network of semiconductor qubits? Formally, achieve long-distance transport in a 2D array while simultaneously suppressing valley transitions, charge loss, unwanted phase accumulation, and spatially varying noise.
status: Coherence-protection results for mobile silicon spins are advancing, but short-path preservation falls short of a complete network demonstration. Key work: Jan A. Krzywda et al. (2026), *Coherence Protection for Mobile Spin Qubits in Silicon*, arXiv:2602.09179.
solved_when: A demonstration of coherent spin transport across a two-dimensional network — not just a short single path — is achieved with valley transitions, charge loss, phase accumulation, and spatially varying noise all controlled along the way.
why: It would allow spatially separating storage, interaction, and readout zones in a spin-based processor without dense local wiring at every qubit site.
key_works: Jan A. Krzywda et al. (2026), *Coherence Protection for Mobile Spin Qubits in Silicon*, arXiv:2602.09179.

title: Error correction with simultaneous spin shuttling
subfield: Semiconductor spins, defects, and rare-earth systems
open: Can repeated cycles of a logical error-correcting code be executed while multiple spins are being shuttled simultaneously? A demonstration would need to include measurements of correlated errors introduced by transport and an accounting of the scheduling overhead.
status: Existing results on mobile-spin coherence supply the necessary ingredients, but logical fault tolerance requires the entire transport-and-measurement cycle to be demonstrated together; key works include Krzywda et al. (2026), *Coherence Protection for Mobile Spin Qubits in Silicon*, arXiv:2602.09179, and Burkard et al. (2023), *Semiconductor spin qubits*.
solved_when: A full repeated logical-code cycle is carried out with multiple spins in simultaneous motion, with the correlated transport errors measured and the scheduling overhead quantified.
why: It determines whether shuttling genuinely reduces the cost of a spin-based architecture rather than merely relocating the noise burden elsewhere.
key_works: Krzywda et al. (2026), *Coherence Protection for Mobile Spin Qubits in Silicon*, arXiv:2602.09179; Burkard et al. (2023), *Semiconductor spin qubits*.

title: Fast spin readout at acceptable power and wiring cost
subfield: Semiconductor spins, defects, and rare-earth systems
open: Can a single-shot spin readout architecture be designed that simultaneously achieves fast readout, low assignment error, minimal back-action, and large-scale multiplexing, all within the cryogenic power and wiring budget of a large error-correcting array? More formally, is there a joint operating point for these constraints that supports repeated error-correction cycles in a scalable device?
status: Strong individual readout results exist, but they do not determine a scalable joint operating point; see Guido Burkard, Thaddeus Ladd, Andrew Pan, John Nichol, and Jason Petta (2023), *Semiconductor spin qubits*, DOI:10.1103/RevModPhys.95.025003.
solved_when: A demonstrated readout scheme achieves fast single-shot spin readout with low assignment error and back-action, multiplexed across many qubits, at cryogenic dissipation and wiring cost compatible with repeated large-array error correction.
why: Readout can dominate both the error-correction cycle time and the complexity of the classical interface, so without a scalable joint operating point the full stack of large spin-qubit arrays stalls at measurement.
key_works: Guido Burkard, Thaddeus Ladd, Andrew Pan, John Nichol, and Jason Petta (2023), *Semiconductor spin qubits*, DOI:10.1103/RevModPhys.95.025003.

title: Higher-temperature group-IV spin–photon nodes
subfield: Semiconductor spins, defects, and rare-earth systems
open: Can a group-IV spin–photon node simultaneously maintain useful spin coherence, optical indistinguishability, collection efficiency, and gate fidelity at temperatures that materially simplify cooling?
status: Current models of group-IV color centers identify phonon-limited tradeoffs among the key properties, and improving any one property alone has not established a complete node; see Isaac B. W. Harris and Dirk Englund (2024), *Coherence of group-IV color centers*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.109.085414.
solved_when: A demonstrated group-IV node operating at elevated temperature exhibits, at the same time, useful spin coherence, optical indistinguishability, collection efficiency, and gate fidelity — not merely improvement of one property in isolation.
why: Such a node would reduce the infrastructure burden of solid-state quantum networks by simplifying the cryogenics required.
key_works: Isaac B. W. Harris and Dirk Englund (2024), *Coherence of group-IV color centers*, DOI:10.1103/PhysRevB.109.085414.

title: Deterministic telecom-defect integration in silicon photonics
subfield: Semiconductor spins, defects, and rare-earth systems
open: Can we deterministically integrate telecom-wavelength color centers into silicon photonic circuits at scale, so that large arrays of emitters are individually addressable and usable as quantum nodes?
status: Individual components have been demonstrated — electrical manipulation of telecom color centers in silicon (A. M. Day et al. (2024), DOI:10.1038/s41467-024-48968-w) and multiplexed color centers in a silicon photonic cavity array (2025, Optica 12, 1400) — but deterministic complete-node yield remains a stronger target.
solved_when: Large arrays of individually addressable telecom emitters are fabricated with useful deterministic complete-node yield, frequency tuning, spin control, and low-loss photonic coupling.
why: A solution would let quantum interconnects be built on mature silicon photonics manufacturing rather than specialized platforms.
key_works: A. M. Day et al. (2024), *Electrical manipulation of telecom color centers in silicon*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-024-48968-w; *Multiplexed color centers in a silicon photonic cavity array* (2025), Optica 12, 1400.

title: Scalable rare-earth nuclear registers with optical networking
subfield: Semiconductor spins, defects, and rare-earth systems
open: Can rare-earth nuclear-spin registers be scaled into a connected quantum computing architecture — combining reproducible registers, high-fidelity local operations, and repeated optical entanglement generation without destroying stored information?
status: Deterministic local registers and Bell-state preparation have been demonstrated, but a scalable connected computing architecture remains open. Key work: Andrei Ruskuc, Chun-Ju Wu, Jake Rochman, Joonhee Choi, and Andrei Faraon (2022), *Nuclear spin-wave quantum register for a solid-state qubit*, arXiv:2108.12723; DOI:10.1038/s41586-021-04293-6.
solved_when: A scalable connected architecture exists that simultaneously supports deterministic nuclear-spin registers, high-fidelity local operations, and repeated optical entanglement generation while preserving stored quantum information.
why: It would combine long-lived nuclear-spin storage with optically accessible interfaces, enabling memory-rich networked quantum processors.
key_works: Andrei Ruskuc, Chun-Ju Wu, Jake Rochman, Joonhee Choi, and Andrei Faraon (2022), *Nuclear spin-wave quantum register for a solid-state qubit*, arXiv:2108.12723; DOI:10.1038/s41586-021-04293-6.

title: End-to-end fault-tolerant fusion-based computation
open: Can a photonic quantum computer suppress logical errors and perform universal computation end to end, with every hardware imperfection — source, propagation, switching, fusion, detector, and feed-forward — present at once rather than engineered away?
status: Fusion-based architectures and modular photonic systems are established milestones, but a complete fault-tolerant computation demonstration remains lacking. Key works: Sara Bartolucci et al. (2023), *Fusion-based quantum computation*, arXiv:2101.09310; H. Aghaee Rad et al. (2025), *Scaling and networking a modular photonic quantum computer*.
solved_when: A sustained demonstration of logical error suppression and universal computation is achieved under the combined imperfections of source, propagation, switching, fusion, detector, and feed-forward, testing the full loss budget rather than isolated components.
why: It exercises the entire loss budget in a single experiment, closing the gap between component-level demonstrations and a genuinely fault-tolerant photonic machine.
key_works: Sara Bartolucci et al. (2023), *Fusion-based quantum computation*, arXiv:2101.09310; H. Aghaee Rad et al. (2025), *Scaling and networking a modular photonic quantum computer*.

title: Large banks of mutually indistinguishable efficient photon sources
open: Can we build a large bank of photon sources that simultaneously delivers high collection efficiency, purity, indistinguishability, stability, and manufacturing yield at scale?
status: Excellent individual sources exist, but no complete bank has been shown to meet all requirements concurrently. A manufacturable platform is proposed in R. Alexander et al. (2025), *A manufacturable platform for photonic quantum computing*, arXiv:2404.17570; DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-08820-7.
solved_when: A bank of many sources is demonstrated in which all of the above requirements — efficiency, purity, indistinguishability, stability, and yield — are met concurrently, with enough photons simultaneously usable for multiphoton experiments.
why: Multiphoton success rates compound source imperfections, so without such a bank the scaling of photonic quantum computing is bottlenecked by its own sources.
key_works: R. N. Alexander et al. (2025), *A manufacturable platform for photonic quantum computing*, arXiv:2404.17570; DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-08820-7.

title: Resource-state factories with bounded multiplexing overhead
open: Can we build photonic resource-state factories that produce entangled resource states at useful rates, once the unavoidable stochasticity — probabilistic fusion gates, buffering, switching loss, and discarded attempts — is fully accounted for rather than idealized away?
status: Resource-state constructions exist, and fusion-based quantum computation is established as an asymptotically universal model (Bartolucci et al. (2023), *Fusion-based quantum computation*, arXiv:2101.09310), but practical factory yield is not specified by these asymptotic-universality results. Related frameworks include stochastic manufacturing networks and percolation with finite buffers.
solved_when: A factory architecture is specified that delivers resource states at useful rates with an explicit, bounded multiplexing overhead arising from probabilistic fusion, buffering, switching loss, and discarded attempts.
why: Factory overhead can dominate the cost of a complete optical computer, so uncontrolled multiplexing overhead would negate any advantage claimed at the abstract computation level.
key_works: Bartolucci et al. (2023), *Fusion-based quantum computation*, arXiv:2101.09310.

title: Feed-forward and optical delay without excessive loss
open: Can a photonic architecture integrate detection, decoding, switching, and delay so that photons survive the required classical decision latency with a useful total success probability?
status: Modular demonstrations establish feasibility at selected scales, but the joint latency–loss budget remains a scaling wall. Key work: Aghaee Rad et al. (2025), *Scaling and networking a modular photonic quantum computer*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-08406-9.
solved_when: The combined feed-forward system — detection, decoding, switching, and delay — achieves a total success probability that remains useful at scale, i.e., the joint latency–loss budget no longer forms a scaling wall.
why: Photons cannot simply wait in an ordinary register while a controller catches up; without low-loss delay integrated with fast classical decision-making, feed-forward-based photonic computing loses the very photons it is trying to process.
key_works: Aghaee Rad et al. (2025), *Scaling and networking a modular photonic quantum computer*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-08406-9.

title: Wafer-scale photonic loss and yield closure
open: Can a wafer-scale photonic platform be manufactured such that the losses accumulated across the entire system — propagation, coupling, component, and packaging — still meet the requirements of a complete fault-tolerant architecture?
status: Manufacturable photonic platforms are reported, but acceptable median component performance does not ensure acceptable whole-system yield. Key work: Alexander et al. (2025), *A manufacturable platform for photonic quantum computing*, arXiv:2404.17570.
solved_when: A demonstration shows manufacturing distributions in which cumulative propagation, coupling, component, and packaging losses satisfy a complete fault-tolerant architecture's requirements.
why: Many small losses multiply across a large optical circuit, so individually acceptable components do not guarantee a working whole system.
key_works: Alexander et al. (2025), *A manufacturable platform for photonic quantum computing*, arXiv:2404.17570.

title: High-rate detector arrays with computation-grade error models
open: Can photon-number-sensitive detector arrays be scaled to the rates required for computation while keeping their nonidealities — dead time, saturation, dark counts, timing uncertainty, readout heat, and correlated failures — within bounds that a fault-tolerant photonic machine can tolerate? Formally, this asks for detector arrays whose full error model, characterized in repeated operation, meets computation-grade thresholds rather than merely achieving high isolated efficiency.
status: Detector performance must currently be evaluated inside a repeated computation cycle, not only through isolated efficiency measurements; this in-context characterization remains the missing step. Key works: Alexander et al. (2025), *A manufacturable platform for photonic quantum computing*; Aghaee Rad et al. (2025), *Scaling and networking a modular photonic quantum computer*.
solved_when: A high-rate, photon-number-sensitive detector array is demonstrated whose dead time, saturation behavior, dark counts, timing uncertainty, readout heat load, and correlated-failure statistics are all characterized inside a repeated computation cycle and shown to support computation-grade operation, not just standalone detection efficiency.
why: In photonic architectures detectors are not passive measurement devices but active components of the logic itself, so their nonidealities feed directly into computational errors; scalable photonic quantum computing stalls without arrays that behave well enough to run inside the logical cycle.
key_works: Alexander et al. (2025), *A manufacturable platform for photonic quantum computing*; Aghaee Rad et al. (2025), *Scaling and networking a modular photonic quantum computer*.

title: Unambiguous nonabelian Majorana operations in solid-state devices
open: Can a solid-state Majorana platform be made to show genuinely nonabelian behavior — fusion outcomes and braiding operations — in a way that rules out the mundane explanations? Formally, this means demonstrating fusion-rule violations of Abelian statistics and noncommuting braiding operations with controls that exclude trivial Andreev-bound-state and measurement-artifact accounts of the observed signals.
status: The state of the art is parity-readout demonstrations, such as Morteza Aghaee et al. (2025), *Interferometric single-shot parity measurement in InAs–Al hybrid devices*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-08445-2, but these are not by themselves demonstrations of nonabelian statistics or topological protection. The theoretical framework remains Chetan Nayak et al. (2008), *Non-Abelian Anyons and Topological Quantum Computation*.
solved_when: Fusion and braiding behavior is demonstrated in the proposed solid-state platform, with control experiments that exclude trivial Andreev-state and measurement-artifact explanations.
why: It establishes the physical premise on which Majorana-based topological quantum computation rests; without it, the entire platform's claim to nonabelian anyons is unsupported.
key_works: Morteza Aghaee et al. (2025), *Interferometric single-shot parity measurement in InAs–Al hybrid devices*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-08445-2; Chetan Nayak et al. (2008), *Non-Abelian Anyons and Topological Quantum Computation*.

title: Exponentially improving topological-qubit protection
open: Does the logical protection of a topological qubit improve exponentially as the relevant device dimensions are scaled up? A convincing demonstration must isolate this scaling from the confounds of quasiparticle poisoning, readout errors, and ordinary calibration improvements.
status: A parity signal or long lifetime alone does not establish the required scaling law. Key works: Aghaee et al. (2025), *Interferometric single-shot parity measurement in InAs–Al hybrid devices*; Nayak et al. (2008), *Non-Abelian Anyons and Topological Quantum Computation*, arXiv:0707.1889.
solved_when: A measured scaling law of logical protection versus device dimensions is demonstrated, with poisoning, readout errors, and calibration improvements separately controlled so the observed improvement is attributable to the topological protection mechanism itself.
why: It tests the promised protection mechanism itself rather than a single favorable device, and without such scaling evidence the central claim of topological protection remains unverified.
key_works: Aghaee et al. (2025), *Interferometric single-shot parity measurement in InAs–Al hybrid devices*; Nayak et al. (2008), *Non-Abelian Anyons and Topological Quantum Computation*, arXiv:0707.1889.

title: Parity-poisoning control during topological computation
open: How much parity poisoning occurs across the full cycle of a topological qubit — preparation, measurement, coupling, and the braiding operations proposed for it — and can it be kept below a computation-compatible budget, including correlated poisoning between device segments? Formally, the goal is to quantify parity-change rates and correlations during every operational step and to demonstrate suppression mechanisms that hold during active computation rather than only in static characterization.
status: Static parity measurement has been demonstrated, but it does not establish a computation-compatible poisoning budget. Aghaee et al. (2025), *Interferometric single-shot parity measurement in InAs–Al hybrid devices*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-08445-2.
solved_when: Parity changes during preparation, measurement, coupling, and proposed braiding operations are quantified, including correlations between device segments, and suppressed to a budget compatible with topological computation.
why: Uncontrolled parity changes directly corrupt the encoded information, so without a poisoning budget valid during computation the encoded qubits cannot be trusted.
key_works: Aghaee et al. (2025), *Interferometric single-shot parity measurement in InAs–Al hybrid devices*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-08445-2.

title: A physical universal nonabelian-anyon computing platform
open: Can we build and experimentally certify a physical computing platform whose excitations are nonabelian anyons supporting universal protected gate operations? In full, the platform must also demonstrate initialization, readout, and manageable error rates.
status: Mathematical universality of suitable anyon models does not establish their controllable physical realization. A key reference is Chetan Nayak, Steven Simon, Ady Stern, Michael Freedman, and Sankar Das Sarma (2008), *Non-Abelian Anyons and Topological Quantum Computation*, arXiv:0707.1889; a related problem is the identification of nonabelian fractional quantum Hall phases.
solved_when: A physical platform exhibits experimentally certified nonabelian anyons that implement universal protected gate operations, together with initialization, readout, and manageable error rates.
why: A universal anyon platform could avoid some of the non-topological gate overheads required by more restricted anyon models.
key_works: Chetan Nayak, Steven Simon, Ady Stern, Michael Freedman, and Sankar Das Sarma (2008), *Non-Abelian Anyons and Topological Quantum Computation*, arXiv:0707.1889.

title: High-fidelity molecular gates beyond motion-sensitive demonstrations
open: Can a molecular entangling gate be experimentally demonstrated with performance that stays high under measured dipole-interaction fluctuations and realistic trap motion? More precisely, can the resilience of controlled-phase gates — so far established only in theory — be confirmed in the lab rather than only in calculation?
status: A 2026 proposal by Yan Lu and Xiao-Feng Shi (2026), *High-fidelity molecular quantum logic gates resilient to interaction fluctuation*, arXiv:2605.19741; DOI:10.1103/5k4z-dgn2, predicts resilient controlled-phase gates with favorable calculated fidelity, but this is not an experimental result.
solved_when: An experiment realizes molecular entangling gates whose fidelity remains high under the experimentally measured dipole-interaction fluctuations and realistic trap motion, going beyond motion-sensitive demonstrations.
why: It would unlock polar molecules' rich interactions and internal structure as resources for quantum computation, moving the platform beyond proof-of-principle operation.
key_works: Yan Lu and Xiao-Feng Shi (2026), *High-fidelity molecular quantum logic gates resilient to interaction fluctuation*, arXiv:2605.19741; DOI:10.1103/5k4z-dgn2.

title: Repeated molecular computation with coupled internal and motional states
open: Can an array of molecules sustain accurate quantum computation over long gate sequences, despite the many error channels that molecules introduce? Formally, this asks for a platform in which rotational, hyperfine, motional, and interaction-induced errors are all controlled simultaneously so that gate fidelity is preserved throughout repeated operation.
status: Two-body gate proposals and demonstrations of molecular entanglement provide partial foundations, but complete scalable error budgets remain undeveloped. Key work: Lu and Shi (2026), *High-fidelity molecular quantum logic gates resilient to interaction fluctuation*, arXiv:2605.19741.
solved_when: A scalable molecular array demonstrates accurate gates across long computation sequences, with a complete error budget accounting for rotational, hyperfine, motional, and interaction-induced errors.
why: Molecules offer internal structure useful for quantum computation, but that same richness brings additional error channels; without a scheme that suppresses all of them at once, the platform's advantages cannot be realized in practice.
key_works: Lu and Shi (2026), *High-fidelity molecular quantum logic gates resilient to interaction fluctuation*, arXiv:2605.19741.

title: Strong spin–photon coupling for electrons on solid neon
open: Can an electron floating on solid neon be made to couple coherently to a microwave photon through its spin, strongly and cleanly enough to support useful gates or networking — rather than only through its charge degree of freedom?
status: Electron charge-qubit control and interaction demonstrations exist, but they do not settle the spin-interface target. A cited work is Y. Tian et al. (2026), *Nb-Ti-N nanowire resonators and prospects for spin-photon coupling with electrons on solid neon*, DOI:10.1103/jq9v-n4rn.
solved_when: A demonstration of coherent spin–photon coupling for electrons on solid neon, at a strength and coherence quality sufficient for use in quantum gates or photonic networking, rather than charge–photon coupling alone.
why: Success would combine long-lived spin storage with electrically accessible circuit interfaces in a single platform.
key_works: Y. Tian et al. (2026), *Nb-Ti-N nanowire resonators and prospects for spin-photon coupling with electrons on solid neon*, DOI:10.1103/jq9v-n4rn.

title: Scalable multi-electron computation on solid neon
open: Can electrons trapped on solid neon be assembled into a scalable multi-qubit processor rather than a two-qubit demonstration? Concretely, this means reproducible electron arrays with individual initialization and control, working entangling gates, faithful readout, and a correlated-noise model that accounts for the whole device.
status: Two-qubit interactions and gates have been reported, so "first interaction" is no longer the open problem. Key work: Xinhao Li, Yizhong Huang, Xu Han, Xianjing Zhou, and Dafei Jin (2025), *Coherent manipulation of interacting electron qubits on solid neon*, arXiv:2503.23738.
solved_when: Interacting-electron devices on solid neon are demonstrated as reproducible arrays implementing initialization, individual control, entangling gates, and readout, together with a complete correlated-noise model of the architecture.
why: It tests whether this promising low-disorder substrate can support a complete computing architecture rather than isolated two-qubit physics.
key_works: Xinhao Li, Yizhong Huang, Xu Han, Xianjing Zhou, and Dafei Jin (2025), *Coherent manipulation of interacting electron qubits on solid neon*, arXiv:2503.23738.

title: Fault-tolerant remote gates with a net architectural benefit
open: Can we demonstrate remote logical gates whose combined error, latency, and resource cost makes a modular, networked architecture genuinely preferable to building the equivalent machine locally?
status: Physical remote gates and distributed algorithms have been demonstrated, but a useful logical-level crossover between distributed and local architectures remains an open, separate goal. Key work: Main et al. (2025), *Distributed Quantum Computing across an Optical Network Link*, arXiv:2407.00835.
solved_when: A fault-tolerant remote logical gate is demonstrated whose total error, latency, and resource overhead reaches a regime where modular computation outperforms the best local alternative on those same metrics.
why: It settles whether quantum networking actually helps build a larger computer, rather than merely adding cost.
key_works: Main et al. (2025), *Distributed Quantum Computing across an Optical Network Link*, arXiv:2407.00835.

title: Heterogeneous quantum-node interoperability
open: Can heterogeneous quantum nodes built on different qubit platforms be connected into a single functioning system that preserves entanglement? Formally, the goal is an interconnect maintaining entanglement fidelity, timing compatibility, and frequency conversion across platforms, with an auditable end-to-end error model.
status: Individual interfaces and homogeneous links exist as partial results, while interchangeable computing modules remain an integration target. Key works: Hai-Tao Tu et al. (2026), *Quantum-memory-assisted on-demand microwave-optical transduction*, arXiv:2509.18834; Main et al. (2025), *Distributed Quantum Computing across an Optical Network Link*.
solved_when: Different qubit platforms are connected in operation, preserving entanglement fidelity, with timing compatibility and frequency conversion achieved and a complete end-to-end error model that can be audited.
why: The best memory, processor, and communication qubit may be different physical systems, so a working heterogeneous link would let each task use its optimal platform.
key_works: Hai-Tao Tu et al. (2026), *Quantum-memory-assisted on-demand microwave-optical transduction*, arXiv:2509.18834; Main et al. (2025), *Distributed Quantum Computing across an Optical Network Link*.

title: Efficient low-noise microwave–optical transduction
open: Can a microwave–optical transducer be built that simultaneously achieves useful conversion efficiency, low added noise, and sufficient bandwidth while operating in the heat and magnetic-field environment that superconducting devices tolerate?
status: Coherent conversion demonstrations exist, but favorable performance in one metric does not close the complete interface budget. A recent example is Ujjwal Gautam, Nasser Gohari Kamel, Sourabh Kumar, and Daniel Oblak (2026), *Coherent microwave-to-optical transduction with Yb:YSO spins strongly coupled to a 3D resonator*, arXiv:2609.02226.
solved_when: A demonstrated transduction interface meets the complete budget at once — conversion efficiency, added noise, bandwidth, and compatibility with superconducting-device heat and magnetic constraints — rather than favoring any single metric.
why: Such a device links microwave quantum processors to low-loss optical networks, enabling distributed quantum computation and interconnects.
key_works: Ujjwal Gautam, Nasser Gohari Kamel, Sourabh Kumar, and Daniel Oblak (2026), *Coherent microwave-to-optical transduction with Yb:YSO spins strongly coupled to a 3D resonator*, arXiv:2609.02226.

title: On-demand transduction integrated with a working processor
open: Can a memory-assisted on-demand transducer be physically coupled to a functioning processor's computational qubits, delivering entanglement on demand to the very components performing computation? Formally, the target is repeated, on-demand entanglement transfer between the transduction stage and working computational qubits without degrading the local computation.
status: Memory-assisted on-demand microwave-optical transduction has been demonstrated (Hai-Tao Tu et al., 2026, *Quantum-memory-assisted on-demand microwave-optical transduction*, arXiv:2509.18834; DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-75752-9), but integration with a working processor and fidelity under repeated operation remain open and stronger requirements.
