solved_when: An integrated system demonstrates on-demand transduction coupled to actual computational qubits with repeated entanglement transfer across multiple rounds while local computation remains undamaged.
why: In a distributed quantum computer, synchronization between processor and interconnect matters as much as raw conversion efficiency; without on-demand delivery timed to computation, the pieces cannot compose into a machine.
key_works: Hai-Tao Tu et al. (2026), *Quantum-memory-assisted on-demand microwave-optical transduction*, arXiv:2509.18834; DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-75752-9.

title: Deadline-aware entanglement routing
open: Can we route and schedule stochastic entanglement generation so that fidelity, memory expiration, application deadlines, and fairness are jointly controlled? Formally, this asks for optimal—or reliably near-optimal—policies under realistic coupled constraints rather than isolated heuristics for each constraint.
status: Networking formulations of the problem exist, but optimal or reliably near-optimal policies under realistic coupled constraints remain unresolved. The networking challenges are surveyed in *Networking Challenges in Distributed Quantum Computing* (2018), arXiv:1810.08421. Related classical problems include stochastic shortest paths and perishable-inventory scheduling.
solved_when: A routing and scheduling policy is given that provably achieves optimal or reliably near-optimal joint control of fidelity, memory expiration, application deadlines, and fairness under realistic coupled constraints.
why: An available path is useless if its entanglement expires before use; without jointly accounting for these constraints, distributed quantum applications cannot rely on the entanglement they are delivered.
key_works: *Networking Challenges in Distributed Quantum Computing* (2018), arXiv:1810.08421.

title: Distributed resource-state construction under loss
open: Can we build multipartite graph or code states across unreliable, lossy links using only bounded memory and realistic heralding, while still achieving a favorable logical-computation rate?
status: Fusion and networking protocols currently supply the relevant primitives, but a complete finite-resource distributed construction remains workload-dependent. Key works: Bartolucci et al. (2023), *Fusion-based quantum computation*, arXiv:2101.09310; Aghaee Rad et al. (2025), *Scaling and networking a modular photonic quantum computer*.
solved_when: A complete distributed construction exists that produces multipartite graph or code states under link loss with bounded memory, realistic heralding, and a favorable logical-computation rate.
why: Multipartite resources can reduce repeated remote-gate overhead in distributed quantum computation.
key_works: Bartolucci et al. (2023), *Fusion-based quantum computation*, arXiv:2101.09310; Aghaee Rad et al. (2025), *Scaling and networking a modular photonic quantum computer*.

title: Cross-layer optimization of distributed quantum applications
open: Can compilation, code choice, entanglement generation, routing, and classical control for a distributed quantum application be optimized jointly rather than layer by layer, so that the resulting design carries guarantees tied to end-to-end application success instead of isolated link metrics?
status: Current solutions treat networking and compilation separately, and such separate approaches do not determine the best end-to-end design. Related efforts include *Networking Challenges in Distributed Quantum Computing* (2018), arXiv:1810.08421, and Main et al. (2025), *Distributed Quantum Computing across an Optical Network Link*.
solved_when: A co-design methodology or system exists that jointly optimizes compilation, code choice, entanglement generation, routing, and classical control, and its performance is certified against application-level success criteria (e.g., distributed completion time and reliability) rather than per-link metrics, demonstrating that it determines end-to-end designs at least as good as — and in cases where local improvements backfire, better than — the composition of separately optimized layers.
why: Local improvements can worsen distributed completion time or reliability, so without joint optimization the best end-to-end design may be missed or, worse, degraded by seemingly beneficial component upgrades.
key_works: *Networking Challenges in Distributed Quantum Computing* (2018), arXiv:1810.08421; Main et al. (2025), *Distributed Quantum Computing across an Optical Network Link*.

title: Verified compilation of dynamic quantum programs
open: Can a full production quantum compiler toolchain be given machine-checked correctness guarantees for realistic dynamic programs — those with mid-circuit measurement, reset, classical branching, loops, and resource constraints?
status: Verified optimizers and dynamic assembly languages exist — Kesha Hietala et al. (2020), *A Verified Optimizer for Quantum Circuits*, arXiv:1912.02250, and Andrew Cross et al. (2022), *OpenQASM 3: A broader and deeper quantum assembly language*, arXiv:2104.14722 — but complete semantic coverage across a production toolchain is not established by either alone.
solved_when: A verified compiler pipeline provides complete semantic coverage — preserving program semantics through optimization and assembly — for dynamic programs featuring mid-circuit measurement, reset, classical branching, and loops, subject to resource constraints, across a production toolchain rather than an isolated component.
why: A compiler bug can silently invalidate the results of a computation even on perfectly functioning quantum hardware, so verified compilation is the guardrail that makes physical outputs trustworthy.
key_works: Kesha Hietala et al. (2020), *A Verified Optimizer for Quantum Circuits*, arXiv:1912.02250; Andrew Cross et al. (2022), *OpenQASM 3: A broader and deeper quantum assembly language*, arXiv:2104.14722.

title: Verified lowering from logical operations to calibrated pulses
open: Can we formally certify that a calibrated pulse sequence faithfully implements a verified logical circuit? This requires closing the semantic gap between gate-level proofs and pulse-level executions through explicit, checkable assumptions about calibration, crosstalk, leakage, timing, and approximation error.
status: Gate-level verification does not certify the physical meaning of a calibrated pulse sequence. Related work includes Hietala et al. (2020), *A Verified Optimizer for Quantum Circuits*, arXiv:1912.02250, which verifies optimization at the logical level, and Krantz et al. (2019), *A quantum engineer's guide to superconducting qubits*, which characterizes pulse-level hardware without formal verification.
solved_when: A verified lowering pipeline exists in which every logical operation in a circuit is compiled down to calibrated pulses with a proof (or certificate) that the pulse sequence implements the logical circuit, relative to explicitly stated assumptions covering calibration error, crosstalk, leakage, timing, and approximation error.
why: It closes the semantic gap between a proof about software and the experiment actually executed, so that verified-circuit guarantees carry over to real hardware behavior.
key_works: Hietala et al. (2020), *A Verified Optimizer for Quantum Circuits*, arXiv:1912.02250; Krantz et al. (2019), *A quantum engineer’s guide to superconducting qubits*.

title: Portable semantics for cross-device quantum execution
open: Can we specify portable behavioral contracts for quantum programs covering timing, measurement, reset, randomness, and failure reporting — contracts that hold across devices without pretending those devices share identical noise or instruction semantics?
status: Common languages help express programs; they do not by themselves guarantee equivalent physical behavior. Cross et al. (2022), *OpenQASM 3: A broader and deeper quantum assembly language*, arXiv:2104.14722.
solved_when: A specification exists that defines portable behavioral contracts for timing, measurement, reset, randomness, and failure reporting across devices, without assuming identical noise or instruction semantics.
why: It enables reproducible quantum software without hiding device-specific assumptions.
key_works: Cross et al. (2022), *OpenQASM 3: A broader and deeper quantum assembly language*, arXiv:2104.14722.

title: Empirically calibrated full-stack resource estimators
open: Can we build full-stack resource estimators whose predictions of runtime, physical resources, energy, and failure probability are repeatedly checked against executed logical workloads, so that the estimates carry empirical validation rather than model assumptions alone? Formally, the target is a data-driven estimation pipeline whose outputs remain calibrated as hardware and software stacks evolve.
status: Detailed resource models exist, but predictive calibration across changing hardware and software remains an open infrastructure target. Related work includes Fellous-Asiani et al. (2023), *Optimizing resource efficiencies for scalable full-stack quantum computers*, arXiv:2209.05469, and Gidney (2025), *How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers with less than a million noisy qubits*.
solved_when: Estimators exist whose quantitative predictions of runtime, physical resource counts, energy, and failure probability are repeatedly and demonstrably calibrated against executed logical workloads, maintained under changing hardware and software stacks.
why: It makes architectural and application claims falsifiable: proposed designs and algorithmic cost estimates could be checked against reality rather than accepted on model faith.
key_works: Fellous-Asiani et al. (2023), *Optimizing resource efficiencies for scalable full-stack quantum computers*, arXiv:2209.05469; Gidney (2025), *How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers with less than a million noisy qubits*.

title: Programmable real-time control with deterministic deadlines
open: Can a programmable quantum control stack support rich, adaptive programs while guaranteeing that every controller, decoder, and communication step meets a deterministic deadline — including under overload and fault conditions? Formally, the goal is a system in which feedback-path latency bounds are proven, not merely measured.
status: Expressive dynamic languages and real-time experiments exist as partial foundations — e.g., Cross et al. (2022), *OpenQASM 3*, arXiv:2104.14722, and Google Quantum AI (2025), *Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold* — but deadline-safe composition of these components remains difficult.
solved_when: Rich adaptive quantum programs can be executed with bounded controller, decoder, and communication latency, with guarantees that hold through overload and fault behavior.
why: A missed feedback deadline is not a software inconvenience — it can be a physical computation error.
key_works: Cross et al. (2022), *OpenQASM 3*, arXiv:2104.14722; Google Quantum AI (2025), *Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold*.

title: Identifiable context-dependent quantum noise models
open: Which noise parameters can actually be identified when quantum operations depend on simultaneous gates, execution history, drift, and hidden device states? More formally, characterize the identifiability of context-dependent noise models under realistic experimental access.
status: Standard characterization models simplify away these context dependencies, and fitting a model does not establish that its parameters are identifiable. Key work: Timothy Proctor et al. (2017), *What randomized benchmarking actually measures*, arXiv:1702.01853.
solved_when: A characterization exists of which context-dependent noise parameters (those affected by simultaneous gates, history, drift, and hidden states) are identifiable from accessible measurement data, together with criteria distinguishing genuinely inferable parameters from those a fit merely estimates without guarantee.
why: Without identifiability guarantees, a well-fitted noise model can be confidently wrong, causing compilation and error correction to fail silently.
key_works: Timothy Proctor et al. (2017), *What randomized benchmarking actually measures*, arXiv:1702.01853.

title: Certified approximation of resource-optimal quantum compilation
open: When a quantum circuit must be compiled under a cost that mixes non-Clifford gate count, depth, ancillas, routing, and architecture-dependent errors, can we produce useful approximation guarantees on how close the compiled result is to optimal? More formally, the goal is certified approximation for compilation objectives that jointly include all of these resource terms.
status: Exact optimization is intractable for broad formulations, and strong practical heuristics rarely come with complete optimality certificates. Key works: Hietala et al. (2020), *A Verified Optimizer for Quantum Circuits*, arXiv:1912.02250; Gidney (2025), *How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers with less than a million noisy qubits*.
solved_when: An algorithm or analysis exists that, for compilation objectives jointly accounting for non-Clifford count, depth, ancillas, routing, and architecture-dependent errors, yields a useful approximation guarantee with a complete optimality certificate.
why: It determines whether a reported resource improvement is close to the best attainable implementation, rather than an artifact of a heuristic with no certificate.
key_works: Hietala et al. (2020), *A Verified Optimizer for Quantum Circuits*, arXiv:1912.02250; Gidney (2025), *How to factor 2048 bit RSA integers with less than a million noisy qubits*.

title: Safe adaptive quantum control under drift
open: Can a quantum control system learn and update its controls online while a computation is running, without incurring unacceptable exploration cost, unstable feedback, or violating the computation's declared error budget? Formally, this asks for a safe adaptive control scheme that adapts to drift during valuable computation while provably preserving these guarantees.
status: Progress has been made on parameter tracking, notably real-time adaptive tracking of fluctuating relaxation rates (Berritta et al. (2026), *Real-Time Adaptive Tracking of Fluctuating Relaxation Rates*, DOI:10.1103/gk1b-stl3), but general safe adaptation during valuable computation remains unresolved.
solved_when: An online control-adaptation method is demonstrated that updates controls during execution while guaranteeing bounded exploration cost, stable feedback, and preservation of the declared error budget of the running computation.
why: Large quantum systems require continual adaptation, and without such guarantees, running jobs would have to be treated as uncontrolled experiments — sacrificing the very computation they are meant to execute.
key_works: Berritta et al. (2026), *Real-Time Adaptive Tracking of Fluctuating Relaxation Rates*, DOI:10.1103/gk1b-stl3.

title: Useful regimes of polynomial-cost error mitigation
open: Under what structural promises on circuits, observables, and noise does quantum error mitigation remain polynomial-cost while still being scientifically useful? Formally, the goal is a characterization of the restricted regimes in which mitigation avoids the general exponential overhead.
status: General exponential-overhead lower bounds rule out unrestricted cheap mitigation, as established by Ryuji Takagi, Suguru Endo, Shintaro Minagawa, and Mile Gu (2022), *Fundamental limits of quantum error mitigation*, arXiv:2109.04457; the open problem is identifying favorable restricted regimes.
solved_when: A characterization is given of the circuit, observable, and noise classes for which mitigation costs scale polynomially and yields scientifically useful outputs, identifying favorable restricted regimes beyond the unrestricted setting ruled out by exponential lower bounds.
why: It would direct mitigation efforts toward settings where cheap mitigation can work in principle, rather than expending resources on regimes where exponential overhead is unavoidable.
key_works: Ryuji Takagi, Suguru Endo, Shintaro Minagawa, and Mile Gu (2022), *Fundamental limits of quantum error mitigation*, arXiv:2109.04457.

title: Tight mitigation lower bounds for realistic noise
open: Can we characterize the exact cost of quantum error mitigation when the noise is physically realistic — biased, correlated, non-Markovian, and drifting over time? More precisely, can matching upper and lower resource bounds be derived for mitigation under such noise models?
status: Strong general limits are known for important noise models, but they do not yield a complete classification for physically realistic noise; see Takagi et al. (2022), *Fundamental limits of quantum error mitigation*, arXiv:2109.04457.
solved_when: For each of biased, correlated, non-Markovian, and drift-dependent noise models, matching lower and upper resource bounds for mitigation are established, giving a complete cost classification.
why: It tells experimentalists which noise regimes are provably unfavorable, so resources are not wasted on mitigation strategies that cannot succeed.
key_works: Takagi et al. (2022), *Fundamental limits of quantum error mitigation*, arXiv:2109.04457.

title: Probabilistic error cancellation with affordable characterization
open: Can probabilistic error cancellation be made practical by driving down the total cost — including the overhead of learning and periodically refreshing the noise model — while still certifying the residual bias left by imperfect characterization?
status: Quasiprobability-based cancellation is established, but both its sampling overhead and its characterization overhead can be prohibitive. Key reference: Cai et al. (2023), *Quantum Error Mitigation*, arXiv:2210.00921.
solved_when: A cancellation protocol is demonstrated whose combined cost of mitigation sampling plus noise-model learning and refreshing is reduced relative to established quasiprobability methods, together with a certified bound on residual bias arising from imperfect characterization.
why: A mitigation protocol cannot assume an exact noise model supplied for free; without affordable characterization and bias certification, cancellation remains unusable in practice despite its theoretical guarantees.
key_works: Cai et al. (2023), *Quantum Error Mitigation*, arXiv:2210.00921.

title: Virtual distillation with correlated state copies
open: What happens to virtual distillation when the state copies it consumes are not independent? The task is to establish effective protocols, with valid guarantees, for realistic settings where nominal copies share drift, preparation biases, or correlated errors.
status: Existing analyses assume idealized independent copies, which do not cover every realistic repeated preparation. Background: Cai et al. (2023), *Quantum Error Mitigation*, arXiv:2210.00921; Proctor et al. (2017), *What randomized benchmarking actually measures*.
solved_when: Protocols and guarantees are established for virtual distillation that remain valid under correlated copies — specifically, under shared drift, preparation biases, and correlated errors among repeated preparations.
why: Shared errors can survive, or even be amplified by, the nonlinear purification estimators at the heart of virtual distillation, so the technique's guarantees silently fail in realistic experiments.
key_works: Cai et al. (2023), *Quantum Error Mitigation*, arXiv:2210.00921; Proctor et al. (2017), *What randomized benchmarking actually measures*.

title: Verification of analog simulation beyond classical tractability
open: Can a scientifically relevant analog-simulation output be certified as correct when no classical computer can check it directly — using only independent controls, rigorous bounds, and cross-platform checks? In other words, what verification protocol establishes trust in analog simulators operating beyond classical tractability?
status: Agreement between the analog simulator and classical computation in tractable regimes is necessary but does not by itself validate the extrapolated hard regime; this is illustrated by Joseph Tindall et al. (2024), *Efficient tensor network simulation of IBM's Eagle kicked Ising experiment*, arXiv:2306.14887, and LeBlanc et al. (2015), *Solutions of the Two Dimensional Hubbard Model*, where classically tractable comparisons were ultimately achievable or contested.
solved_when: A verification protocol exists that certifies outputs in regimes where exact classical simulation is unavailable, relying on independent controls, bounds, and cross-platform checks rather than agreement in classically tractable regimes alone.
why: The most valuable analog-simulation results are precisely those hardest to verify directly, so without such a protocol the strongest claims of quantum advantage in simulation rest on unverifiable extrapolation.
key_works: Joseph Tindall et al. (2024), *Efficient tensor network simulation of IBM’s Eagle kicked Ising experiment*, arXiv:2306.14887; LeBlanc et al. (2015), *Solutions of the Two Dimensional Hubbard Model*.

title: Spoof-resistant interpretation of cross-entropy benchmarks
open: Which supplementary tests, if any, can make a cross-entropy-style benchmark score meaningful evidence that the intended quantum computation was actually performed, even when a classical adversary is explicitly optimizing against that score? Put formally, determine what additional conditions or tests beyond a high score on the chosen statistic suffice to rule out optimized classical spoofers.
status: It is currently understood that a high score on a selected statistic is not equivalent to distributional correctness or useful computational advantage. Bouland et al. (2018), *Quantum Supremacy and the Complexity of Random Circuit Sampling*; Andrew Cross et al. (2019), *Validating quantum computers using randomized model circuits*, arXiv:1811.12926.
solved_when: A characterization exists of additional tests (or test ensembles) such that passing them, together with a high cross-entropy score, distinguishes genuine quantum sampling from any explicitly optimized classical spoofer; equivalently, a checkable criterion under which the benchmark cannot be passed by distributionally incorrect outputs.
why: Without such tests, benchmark optimization can silently replace the task being benchmarked, so high scores certify neither distributional correctness nor useful computational advantage.
key_works: Bouland et al. (2018), *Quantum Supremacy and the Complexity of Random Circuit Sampling*; Andrew Cross et al. (2019), *Validating quantum computers using randomized model circuits*, arXiv:1811.12926.

title: Area law for general gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians
subfield: Many-body structure, simulation resources, and sensing
open: Does every ground state of a general bounded-locality, uniformly gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonian satisfy an entanglement-entropy area law, under appropriate standard assumptions? Formally, can one bound the entanglement entropy of a spatial subregion by a constant times its boundary length, uniformly over the ground-state manifold?
status: Open. One-dimensional theorems and special higher-dimensional cases do not establish the general two-dimensional result. Background: Jens Eisert, Marcus Cramer, and Martin Plenio (2010), *Area laws for the entanglement entropy—a review*, arXiv:0808.3773; Simons Institute (2024), *Quantum Complexity: Quantum PCP, Area Laws, and Quantum Gravity*.
solved_when: A proof (or counterexample under the stated assumptions) of an area-law bound for ground states of general bounded-locality, uniformly gapped two-dimensional Hamiltonians.
why: It would constrain ground-state complexity and provide theoretical support for tensor-network approximations of gapped two-dimensional systems.
key_works: Jens Eisert, Marcus Cramer, and Martin Plenio (2010), *Area laws for the entanglement entropy—a review*, arXiv:0808.3773; Simons Institute (2024), *Quantum Complexity: Quantum PCP, Area Laws, and Quantum Gravity*.

title: Efficient certified contraction of physically promised PEPS
subfield: Many-body structure, simulation resources, and sensing
open: What broad, physically checkable promises on a many-body state suffice to make its PEPS representation contractible in polynomial time with rigorous error bounds on observables? More precisely, identify classes of structural or physical assumptions — beyond generic tensor-network inputs — under which certified efficient contraction is provably possible.
status: Generic tensor-network contraction is known to be difficult, and neither an area law nor an apparently modest bond dimension by itself supplies an efficient contraction algorithm. Key works: Eisert, Cramer, and Plenio (2010), *Area laws for the entanglement entropy—a review*; Tindall et al. (2024), *Efficient tensor network simulation of IBM's Eagle kicked Ising experiment*.
solved_when: A set of broad, checkable physical promises is identified, together with an efficient contraction algorithm for PEPS satisfying them that carries rigorous observable-error bounds.
why: It fixes the classical boundary that quantum simulation must beat: without such promises, area laws or modest bond dimension alone give no efficient classical contraction, so the line between classical and quantum advantage remains unmapped.
key_works: Eisert, Cramer, and Plenio (2010), *Area laws for the entanglement entropy—a review*; Tindall et al. (2024), *Efficient tensor network simulation of IBM’s Eagle kicked Ising experiment*.

title: Optimal asymptotic magic-state conversion rates
subfield: Many-body structure, simulation resources, and sensing
open: What are the optimal asymptotic rates for converting and distilling between specified nonstabilizer (magic) states under explicit allowed operations — and how do those rates change when catalysts are available?
status: Existing monotones, protocols, and irreversibility results constrain the achievable rates, but no universal rate formula is known. Key works include *Irreversibility of bound magic states assisted by catalysis* (2026), DOI:10.1103/yj6l-lhph, and Michael Zurel and Jack Davis (2026), *Basis-independent stabilizerness and maximally noisy magic states*, arXiv:2602.22336.
solved_when: A universal rate formula (or equivalent characterization) is obtained for conversion and distillation rates between specified nonstabilizer states, both with and without catalytic assistance.
why: It quantifies the irreducible resource cost of non-Clifford computation, fixing how many noisy magic states are fundamentally needed per unit of distillable magic.
key_works: *Irreversibility of bound magic states assisted by catalysis* (2026), DOI:10.1103/yj6l-lhph; Michael Zurel and Jack Davis (2026), *Basis-independent stabilizerness and maximally noisy magic states*, arXiv:2602.22336.

title: Experimentally accessible universality of monitored transitions
subfield: Many-body structure, simulation resources, and sensing
open: When can an experimentally measurable transition — such as a change in transport or correlation behavior — be trusted as a faithful signature of a measurement-induced entanglement transition? The question is to determine the conditions, including noise, finite size, and nonintegrable dynamics, under which such accessible observables diagnose the entanglement transition.
status: A 2026 spin-chain study links ballistic–diffusive behavior to entanglement transitions — K. G. S. H. Gunawardana, Ali G. Moghaddam, and Teemu Ojanen (2026), *Postselection-free ballistic-diffusive transition in monitored spin chains*, arXiv:2605.27350 — but a broad experimentally robust equivalence is not established.
solved_when: A general, experimentally robust equivalence is established between measurable transport or correlation transitions and measurement-induced entanglement transitions, holding in the presence of noise, finite-size effects, and nonintegrable dynamics.
why: It would expose many-body phenomena that otherwise require heavy postselection through observables accessible in experiments.
key_works: K. G. S. H. Gunawardana, Ali G. Moghaddam, and Teemu Ojanen (2026), *Postselection-free ballistic-diffusive transition in monitored spin chains*, arXiv:2605.27350.

title: Error-corrected sensing with finite-speed imperfect control
subfield: Many-body structure, simulation resources, and sensing
open: How much of the promised Heisenberg-limit advantage of error-corrected quantum sensing survives once error correction is implemented with realistic hardware — correction operations of finite duration, noisy ancillas, imperfect gates, and realistic resource costs? Can this residual metrological advantage be quantified and demonstrated?
status: Idealized conditions under which Heisenberg scaling can be achieved with quantum error correction are established; what remains open is how the physical overhead of correction changes the attainable advantage. Key work: Sisi Zhou, Mengzhen Zhang, John Preskill, and Liang Jiang (2018), *Achieving the Heisenberg limit in quantum metrology using quantum error correction*, arXiv:1706.02445.
solved_when: A quantitative characterization and experimental demonstration of the metrological advantage attainable under finite-duration correction, noisy ancillas, imperfect gates, and realistic resource costs is achieved.
why: It tests whether computing-grade control can genuinely improve sensors outside the idealized limits in which current theory is framed.
key_works: Sisi Zhou, Mengzhen Zhang, John Preskill, and Liang Jiang (2018), *Achieving the Heisenberg limit in quantum metrology using quantum error correction*, arXiv:1706.02445.

title: Multiparameter sensing with incompatible correction requirements
subfield: Many-body structure, simulation resources, and sensing
open: What precision can be achieved when a sensor must estimate several parameters at once, and preserving one signal conflicts with correcting noise or measuring another? Formally, determine the achievable precision region for multiparameter estimation under such incompatibility constraints.
status: Single-parameter correctability criteria are known not to fully characterize multiparameter tradeoffs under realistic controls. Key works: Zhou et al. (2018), *Achieving the Heisenberg limit in quantum metrology using quantum error correction*, arXiv:1706.02445.
solved_when: A characterization of the achievable precision region is given, resolving the multiparameter tradeoffs that single-parameter correctability criteria fail to capture under realistic controls.
why: Real sensors often need to estimate vector fields, frequencies, or several coupled physical parameters, so single-parameter guarantees do not suffice.
key_works: Zhou et al. (2018), *Achieving the Heisenberg limit in quantum metrology using quantum error correction*, arXiv:1706.02445.

title: Public rare-event syndrome archives
open: Can the community build a versioned, cross-platform public archive of rare-event syndrome data — raw syndrome streams, rare bursts, leakage flags, calibration history, and the metadata needed to reproduce logical-failure analyses — that serves quantum error correction research as a sustained shared resource?
status: This is a proposed infrastructure target; no such archive exists yet. Published demonstrations provide valuable data — notably Google Quantum AI (2025), *Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold*, and McEwen et al. (2022), *Resolving catastrophic error bursts from cosmic rays* — but these are single supplementary datasets rather than the sustained interoperable archive being called for.
solved_when: A versioned, cross-platform dataset exists containing raw syndrome streams, rare bursts, leakage flags, calibration history, and sufficient metadata to reproduce logical-failure analyses — a sustained interoperable archive rather than a single supplementary dataset.
why: Rare logical failures are difficult to study from averaged metrics; access to raw rare-event data would let researchers analyze catastrophic and infrequent error mechanisms directly.
key_works: Google Quantum AI (2025), *Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold*; McEwen et al. (2022), *Resolving catastrophic error bursts from cosmic rays*.

title: Longitudinal quantum-hardware drift benchmarks
open: Can the community produce and share long-duration quantum-hardware measurement datasets — repeated measurements over operationally meaningful periods, with interventions and missingness explicitly recorded — sufficient to evaluate drift prediction and adaptive control prospectively?
status: Currently only a proposed benchmark target; existing snapshots and selectively reported recalibration improvements do not supply this evaluation. Related work includes Berritta et al. (2026), *Real-Time Adaptive Tracking of Fluctuating Relaxation Rates*, and Bausch et al. (2024), *Learning high-accuracy error decoding for quantum processors*.
solved_when: A public dataset of repeated measurements over such periods exists, with interventions and missingness recorded, enabling prospective evaluation of drift prediction and adaptive control methods.
why: It enables honest testing of controllers and decoders under changing hardware, rather than under idealized stationary assumptions.
key_works: Berritta et al. (2026), *Real-Time Adaptive Tracking of Fluctuating Relaxation Rates*; Bausch et al. (2024), *Learning high-accuracy error decoding for quantum processors*.

title: Comparable logical-computation benchmarks
open: Can the community agree on benchmark tasks that meaningfully compare logical computation across different quantum error-correcting code families, going beyond memory-only demonstrations? Concretely, such tasks should measure logical throughput and reliability while accounting for the full pipeline — rejected runs, decoding, factory operation, and classical feedback.
status: Currently a proposed infrastructure target, beyond physical gate counts and memory-only demonstrations. Key works: Thomas Lubinski et al. (2023), *Application-Oriented Performance Benchmarks for Quantum Computing*, arXiv:2110.03137; Bravyi et al. (2024), *High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory*.
solved_when: A defined and maintained set of benchmark tasks exists that compares logical throughput and reliability across code families and includes rejected runs, decoding, factories, and classical feedback.
why: It makes "logical qubit" claims comparable across architectures, which physical gate counts and memory-only demonstrations currently cannot do.
key_works: Thomas Lubinski et al. (2023), *Application-Oriented Performance Benchmarks for Quantum Computing*, arXiv:2110.03137; Bravyi et al. (2024), *High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory*.

title: Hidden-test application benchmarks with matched classical baselines
open: Can the community establish and maintain application benchmark suites whose specifications are frozen in advance, whose test instances are held out until evaluation, and whose classical baselines are continuously strengthened by independent optimization — with quantum preprocessing and readout costs fully counted? In formal terms, this is an infrastructure and protocol problem rather than a theorem: the goal is a persistent benchmarking process whose validity survives adversarial classical improvement.
status: Proposed benchmark target. Application-oriented benchmarks exist (e.g., Lubinski et al. (2023), *Application-Oriented Performance Benchmarks for Quantum Computing*, arXiv:2110.03137), and strong classical counterexamples have been demonstrated (e.g., Tindall et al. (2024), *Efficient tensor network simulation of IBM's Eagle kicked Ising experiment*), but no suite yet guarantees validity against continuing classical improvements.
solved_when: A maintained application suite exists with (i) frozen specifications, (ii) held-out test instances, (iii) independently produced classical baselines that are updated as classical methods improve, and (iv) quantum preprocessing and readout costs included in the accounting.
why: Without such suites, handpicked instances and stale classical baselines can masquerade as quantum advantage; with them, application-level claims of quantum utility become auditable.
key_works: Lubinski et al. (2023), *Application-Oriented Performance Benchmarks for Quantum Computing*, arXiv:2110.03137; Tindall et al. (2024), *Efficient tensor network simulation of IBM’s Eagle kicked Ising experiment*.

title: An adversarial classical-simulation challenge archive
open: Can we build and maintain a public archive that tracks every claimed quantum-computational-advantage instance through its full adversarial lifecycle — the exact scoring rules, computational budgets, and instances as published, together with subsequent classical attacks and their reproducible outcomes?
status: This is a proposed infrastructure target, motivated by demonstrations whose classical baselines changed after publication — e.g., Tindall et al. (2024), *Efficient tensor network simulation of IBM's Eagle kicked Ising experiment*, arXiv:2306.14887, responding to Cross et al. (2019), *Validating quantum computers using randomized model circuits*. No such archive currently exists.
solved_when: A continuously updated archive exists that preserves the claimed advantage instances, exact scoring rules, computational budgets, subsequent classical attacks, and reproducible outcomes for the demonstrations it covers.
why: It turns classical progress into cumulative evidence rather than disconnected rebuttals, so the community can see at a glance which advantage claims still stand.
key_works: Tindall et al. (2024), *Efficient tensor network simulation of IBM’s Eagle kicked Ising experiment*, arXiv:2306.14887; Cross et al. (2019), *Validating quantum computers using randomized model circuits*.

title: Energy per correct answer datasets
open: Can we produce datasets that report the complete energy cost of every statistically valid answer produced by a quantum computing facility — including not only the hardware power draw but also cooling, controls, decoding, rejected runs, and amortized calibration? Formally, this is a measurement-and-data problem: define and publish a full-stack, facility-level accounting of energy per correct (statistically validated) answer.
status: This is currently a proposed measurement target. Full-stack resource models exist, but hardware-only power figures do not measure this quantity. A related resource is Fellous-Asiani et al. (2023), *Optimizing resource efficiencies for scalable full-stack quantum computers*, arXiv:2209.05469.
solved_when: A public dataset exists that measures energy per statistically valid answer at the full facility level, accounting for cooling, controls, decoding, rejected runs, and amortized calibration.
why: Such datasets would allow credible comparison of quantum computers with classical accelerators and with alternative quantum architectures; without them, hardware-only power figures systematically understate the true cost of producing an answer.
key_works: Fellous-Asiani et al. (2023), *Optimizing resource efficiencies for scalable full-stack quantum computers*, arXiv:2209.05469.

title: Reproducible negative-result repositories
open: Can we build a repository that archives failed scaling attempts, unsuccessful mitigations, unstable calibrations, and adverse fabrication runs with sufficient methods and metadata for reuse?
status: Currently a proposed infrastructure target only. Ordinary publication incentives do not automatically produce such a balanced record. Related concerns include publication bias and reproducibility infrastructure; the challenge is framed against the backdrop of de Leon et al. (2021), *Materials challenges and opportunities for quantum computing hardware*, and Cai et al. (2023), *Quantum Error Mitigation*.
solved_when: A sustained repository exists that captures negative results across failed scaling attempts, unsuccessful mitigation, unstable calibrations, and adverse fabrication runs, each documented with sufficient methods and metadata for reuse.
why: It prevents repeated dead ends and selection-biased engineering models.
key_works: de Leon et al. (2021), *Materials challenges and opportunities for quantum computing hardware*; Cai et al. (2023), *Quantum Error Mitigation*.

title: Chemistry benchmarks with independently controlled uncertainty
open: Can we build benchmark families for quantum chemistry in which the geometry, Hamiltonian, active space, reference uncertainty, and scientifically relevant outputs are each explicitly versioned and independently checked — so that no part of the target a quantum algorithm must hit is left implicit?
status: A proposed infrastructure target extending existing resource studies and electronic-structure comparisons, including Lee et al. (2022/2023), *Is there evidence for exponential quantum advantage in quantum chemistry?* and von Burg et al. (2021), *Quantum computing enhanced computational catalysis*.
solved_when: A publicly available benchmark family exists whose geometry, Hamiltonian, active space, reference uncertainty, and scientifically relevant outputs are explicitly versioned and independently checked.
why: It prevents comparing quantum numerical error against an uncertain or changing chemical target, which would invalidate any claimed advantage.
key_works: Lee et al. (2022/2023), *Is there evidence for exponential quantum advantage in quantum chemistry?*; von Burg et al. (2021), *Quantum computing enhanced computational catalysis*.

title: Data-access and QRAM cost benchmarks
open: Can the community agree on standardized ways to report data-access and QRAM costs in quantum algorithm evaluations, covering coherent-memory construction, updates, query fidelity, classical preprocessing, and amortization assumptions? In other words, what benchmark format makes oracle-complexity claims directly comparable to physical implementation costs?
status: A proposed benchmark target addressing a recurring mismatch between oracle complexity and physical implementation; no standard yet exists. Related key works: Giovannetti, Lloyd, and Maccone (2008), *Quantum random access memory*, arXiv:0708.1879; Tang (2019), *A quantum-inspired classical algorithm for recommendation systems*.
solved_when: A benchmark standard exists that specifies reporting of coherent-memory construction, updates, query fidelity, classical preprocessing, and amortization assumptions, and is adopted for quantum algorithm evaluations.
why: It makes claimed data-processing speedups comparable under honest access models, closing the recurring gap between abstract oracle complexity and physical implementation cost.
key_works: Giovannetti, Lloyd, and Maccone (2008), *Quantum random access memory*, arXiv:0708.1879; Tang (2019), *A quantum-inspired classical algorithm for recommendation systems*.

title: Cross-vendor reproducibility of physical and logical metrics
open: Can the community establish executable benchmarking protocols that reproduce reported quantum-computing metrics across different hardware providers, while preserving raw measurement outcomes, calibration context, exclusion rules, and uncertainty?
status: This is a proposed infrastructure target; currently, common metric names do not guarantee common experimental procedures. Key works: Cross et al. (2019), *Validating quantum computers using randomized model circuits*, arXiv:1811.12926; Lubinski et al. (2023), *Application-Oriented Performance Benchmarks for Quantum Computing*.
solved_when: Such protocols exist and demonstrably reproduce reported metrics across providers, retaining raw outcomes, calibration context, exclusion rules, and uncertainty quantification.
why: It enables meaningful procurement decisions, fair research comparison, and reliable replication of experimental results.
key_works: Cross et al. (2019), *Validating quantum computers using randomized model circuits*, arXiv:1811.12926; Lubinski et al. (2023), *Application-Oriented Performance Benchmarks for Quantum Computing*.

title: Sustained independent replication funding
open: How can we design funding mechanisms that pay independent teams to reproduce full-stack quantum-computing claims, publish adverse findings, and maintain verification capability across hardware generations?
status: Proposed funding-design problem. DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative already includes independent validation, but the broader need is sustained, accessible replication rather than an absence of all programs. Key works: DARPA (2024), *Moving Quantum Computing from Hype to Prototype*; DARPA, *Quantum Benchmarking Initiative*.
solved_when: A funding mechanism exists that provides sustained, accessible support for independent replication of full-stack claims, including the publication of adverse findings and the maintenance of verification capability across hardware generations.
why: Expensive verification should not depend entirely on the organization making the claim; independent, sustained replication capacity is what keeps full-stack claims accountable.
key_works: DARPA (2024), *Moving Quantum Computing from Hype to Prototype*; DARPA, *Quantum Benchmarking Initiative*.

title: Durable research access to useful quantum testbeds
open: How can researchers without ownership of or private negotiating power over leading quantum systems be guaranteed durable access to them? The goal is an access model delivering predictable multiyear availability, technical support, raw-data rights, and reproducibility guarantees for such researchers.
status: This is a proposed access-and-funding target. Programs such as NSF's National Quantum Virtual Laboratory are partial institutional responses; see NSF (2024), *NSF National Quantum Virtual Laboratory advances with first five projects*, and NSF, *Quantum Information Science*.
solved_when: A funded program or institutional mechanism exists that provides researchers who cannot own or privately negotiate access with predictable multiyear access, technical support, raw-data rights, and reproducibility guarantees on leading quantum testbeds.
why: Short promotional access windows are poorly suited to longitudinal hardware science, which requires sustained, repeatable experimentation on the same systems.
key_works: NSF (2024), *NSF National Quantum Virtual Laboratory advances with first five projects*; NSF, *Quantum Information Science*.

title: Open fabrication access and reusable process qualification
open: Can the quantum hardware community establish shared fabrication access with documented process interfaces and qualification data that any research group can reuse, so that no single group must rebuild an entire manufacturing stack to run experiments?
status: This is a proposed institutional target, not yet an achieved arrangement. Manufacturing-focused quantum hubs exist, but broad access and portable process knowledge still require explicit arrangements. Related precedents include shared semiconductor foundries and open process-design kits. Key works: U.S. Economic Development Administration, *The Bloch Quantum Tech Hub*; de Leon et al. (2021), *Materials challenges and opportunities for quantum computing hardware*.
solved_when: A funded shared-fabrication arrangement exists offering open fabrication runs, documented process interfaces, and independently reusable process qualification data available to research groups without recreating a manufacturing stack.
why: It removes duplicated manufacturing effort across groups and makes hardware research reproducible, since results no longer depend on each lab's private, undocumented process.
key_works: U.S. Economic Development Administration, *The Bloch Quantum Tech Hub*; de Leon et al. (2021), *Materials challenges and opportunities for quantum computing hardware*.

title: Maintenance funding for critical open quantum software
open: How can the essential software layer of quantum computing — decoders, compilers, verification tools, and benchmark infrastructure — be sustained once the research grants that created them expire?
status: Currently a proposed funding target only; the field's default practice — publishing a research implementation — is not a maintenance model.
solved_when: A durable support mechanism exists that provides ongoing maintenance funding for this critical open quantum software, together with explicit commitments assigning ownership and guaranteeing compatibility.
why: Without maintenance, otherwise useful research can be invalidated or stranded when the tools it depends on stop being kept up.
key_works: Hietala et al. (2020), *A Verified Optimizer for Quantum Circuits*; Lubinski et al. (2023), *Application-Oriented Performance Benchmarks for Quantum Computing*; NSF, *Quantum Information Science*.

title: Quantum technician and manufacturing workforce pipelines
open: How can we identify and fund training pathways that demonstrably deliver the cryogenic, photonic, fabrication, packaging, and control skills needed to sustain quantum operations at scale?
status: Current public strategies acknowledge quantum-related skills gaps, but the unresolved target is measured training-to-deployment effectiveness (NSF (2026), *NSF FY 2026–2030 Strategic Plan*; U.S. EDA, *The Bloch Quantum Tech Hub*).
solved_when: Funded training pathways exist with measured training-to-deployment effectiveness showing they supply the needed cryogenic, photonic, fabrication, packaging, and control skills.
why: Scaling quantum systems requires technicians and manufacturing expertise, not only additional theoretical researchers.
key_works: NSF (2026), *NSF FY 2026–2030 Strategic Plan*; U.S. EDA, *The Bloch Quantum Tech Hub*.

title: Independently verified economically useful quantum computation
open: Can a quantum computer perform a computation whose independently assessed economic value exceeds both the full cost of running the quantum system and the cost of the best credible classical alternative?
status: This is an explicit system-level target, not synonymous with sampling advantage or a favorable asymptotic runtime; DARPA's benchmarking program uses a related utility-scale criterion (DARPA, *Quantum Benchmarking Initiative*). Babbush et al. (2021), *Focus beyond quadratic speedups for error-corrected quantum advantage*, is a key related work.
solved_when: A demonstrated computation has independently assessed value strictly exceeding its complete quantum-system cost and the cost of the strongest credible classical alternative.
why: It would establish quantum computing as an economically productive capability rather than merely a scientific achievement.
key_works: DARPA, *Quantum Benchmarking Initiative*; Babbush et al. (2021), *Focus beyond quadratic speedups for error-corrected quantum advantage*.

title: Hundredfold reduction in usable non-Clifford spacetime cost
open: Can the physical spacetime cost per delivered non-Clifford logical operation be reduced by at least 100× relative to a frozen, fully specified baseline, while keeping failure probability and physical noise matched?
status: This is an engineering moonshot, not an established conjecture. Cultivation and addressable-code results provide concrete alternative routes: Gidney et al. (2024), *Magic state cultivation: growing T states as cheap as CNOT gates*, arXiv:2409.17595; He et al. (2025), *Quantum Codes with Addressable and Transversal Non-Clifford Gates*.
solved_when: A construction or protocol achieves at least a 100× reduction in physical spacetime per delivered non-Clifford logical operation against a frozen, fully specified baseline, at matched failure probability and physical noise.
why: Non-Clifford resources dominate many important fault-tolerant workloads, so a hundredfold cut in their usable spacetime cost would directly shrink the machines needed to run them.
key_works: Gidney et al. (2024), *Magic state cultivation: growing T states as cheap as CNOT gates*, arXiv:2409.17595; He et al. (2025), *Quantum Codes with Addressable and Transversal Non-Clifford Gates*.

title: Tenfold reduction in full-system energy per correct answer
open: Can a quantum computer deliver correct answers to a fixed, validated workload while consuming at least ten times less energy when the entire system is counted? Formally, the target is a full-system energy reduction of at least 10× per correct answer, with the accounting including cooling, controllers, decoding, calibration, and unsuccessful attempts.
status: Resource-efficiency models identify substantial tradeoffs; a measured complete-system improvement is considered stronger evidence than a lower-power component alone. Fellous-Asiani et al. (2023), *Optimizing resource efficiencies for scalable full-stack quantum computers*, arXiv:2209.05469.
solved_when: A measured complete-system energy reduction of at least 10× is demonstrated on a fixed validated workload, with the energy accounting covering cooling, controllers, decoding, calibration, and unsuccessful attempts.
why: A tenfold cut in full-system energy would make large quantum systems substantially more affordable and physically deployable.
key_works: Fellous-Asiani et al. (2023), *Optimizing resource efficiencies for scalable full-stack quantum computers*, arXiv:2209.05469.

title: Tenfold reduction in delivered high-fidelity entanglement cost
open: Can the delivered cost of a usable remote Bell pair be cut tenfold, holding distance, fidelity, and availability fixed, while honestly counting everything that contributes to that cost — hardware, multiplexing, memory, discarded attempts, and operation?
status: The target stands open. Improvements in conversion efficiency or raw heralding rate alone do not satisfy it, since the cost accounting spans the full delivered system. Key works: Main et al. (2025), *Distributed Quantum Computing across an Optical Network Link*; Tu et al. (2026), *Quantum-memory-assisted on-demand microwave-optical transduction*.
solved_when: A system delivers remote Bell pairs at fixed distance, fidelity, and availability with a total cost per usable pair — accounting for hardware, multiplexing, memory, discarded attempts, and operation — that is 10× lower than the incumbent baseline.
why: A tenfold cost reduction could change the viability of modular quantum computers and quantum repeaters.
key_works: Main et al. (2025), *Distributed Quantum Computing across an Optical Network Link*; Tu et al. (2026), *Quantum-memory-assisted on-demand microwave-optical transduction*.

title: Month-long unattended useful logical service
open: Can an error-corrected quantum computer run useful workloads continuously for a month without human intervention, maintaining itself as dependable infrastructure rather than a laboratory experiment? Formally, the target is a system delivering month-long useful logical operation with automatic calibration, automatic component recovery, verified outputs, and an auditable record of downtime and failed jobs.
status: Continuous coherent hardware operation has been demonstrated on shorter experimental timescales, but service-level logical continuity adds recovery, computation, and verification requirements beyond what has been shown. Key works: Chiu et al. (2025), *Continuous operation of a coherent 3,000-qubit system*, arXiv:2506.20660; Google Quantum AI (2025), *Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold*.
solved_when: A quantum system operates useful error-corrected workloads for a full month with automatic calibration, automatic component recovery, verified outputs, and an auditable record of downtime and failed jobs.
why: Achieving this converts a laboratory processor into dependable scientific infrastructure that users can trust unattended, rather than a device requiring constant expert supervision.
key_works: Chiu et al. (2025), *Continuous operation of a coherent 3,000-qubit system*, arXiv:2506.20660; Google Quantum AI (2025), *Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold*.
